title: Differential Equations I
blurb: Weeks 1–6: separable, exact, linear, Bernoulli, homogeneous, Riccati and Clairaut equations, applications and higher-order linear equations. Includes the 2023 midterm, solved.

chapters.title: Integration toolkit
chapters.lead: Every method in this course ends with “now integrate both sides”. This short refresher collects exactly the derivatives, integrals and tricks the lecturer's solutions use, so the calculus never stops you in the middle of a DE.
chapters.src: Collected from the worked solutions in Week+3.pdf and Week+4.pdf
chapters.html:
You already know calculus; it is just rusty. You do not need everything from Calculus I. The differential-equation methods in this course keep using the same dozen or so facts. Learn these well and the DE part becomes the only thing you have to think about.

→
How a DE solution really works
Each method (Bernoulli, homogeneous, Riccati, …) is a substitution that turns a scary equation into one of two easy kinds: separable (put all \(u\)'s on one side, all \(x\)'s on the other, integrate) or linear (multiply by an integrating factor, integrate). So the last step is always an integral.

1. Derivatives you must know instantly

\(f(x)\)\(f'(x)\)\(f(x)\)\(f'(x)\)
\(x^n\)\(n x^{n-1}\)\(\sin x\)\(\cos x\)
\(\ln|x|\)\(\dfrac1x\)\(\cos x\)\(-\sin x\)
\(e^{ax}\)\(a e^{ax}\)\(\tan x\)\(\sec^2 x = 1+\tan^2 x\)
\(\dfrac1x = x^{-1}\)\(-\dfrac{1}{x^2}\)\(\arctan x\)\(\dfrac{1}{1+x^2}\)

Three rules do the rest:

  • Chain rule — the heart of every substitution. If \(u = y^{-1}\) and \(y\) depends on \(x\), then \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = -y^{-2}\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Never forget the \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) at the end.
  • Product rule — \((\mu u)' = \mu u' + \mu' u\). The integrating-factor trick is this rule read backwards.
  • Implicit differentiation — \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(y^2) = 2y\,y'\), \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{y}) = e^{y} y'\). You need it in orthogonal trajectories and in Clairaut equations.
Chain rule as used in Week 3, p.4If \(u = y^{1-n}\), find \(\dfrac{du}{dx}\).
  1. Differentiate the power: \(\dfrac{d}{dy}\,y^{1-n} = (1-n)y^{-n}\).
  2. Multiply by the inner derivative \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) (\(y\) is a function of \(x\)).
\(\dfrac{du}{dx} = (1-n)\,y^{-n}\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}\)

2. Integrals that keep coming back

IntegralAnswer (+ C)Where it appears
\(\int x^n\,dx,\ n\neq -1\)\(\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}\)everywhere
\(\int \dfrac{dx}{x}\)\(\ln|x|\)every separable equation
\(\int \dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx\)\(\ln|f(x)|\)integrating factors
\(\int e^{ax}\,dx\)\(\dfrac1a e^{ax}\)linear equations
\(\int \tan x\,dx\)\(-\ln|\cos x|\)Bernoulli Example 16
\(\int \cot x\,dx\)\(\ln|\sin x|\)Bernoulli Exercise 5.4
\(\int \sec^2 x\,dx\)\(\tan x\)substitution \(u = x+y\)
\(\int \cos^2 x\,dx\)\(\dfrac x2 + \dfrac{\sin 2x}{4}\)substitution \(u = x+y\)
\(\int \dfrac{dx}{1+x^2}\)\(\arctan x\)special transformation
\(\int \dfrac{dx}{a^2+x^2}\)\(\dfrac1a\arctan\dfrac xa\)special transformation
★
The one integral to rule them all
\(\displaystyle\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)|\). Whenever the top is (a multiple of) the derivative of the bottom, the answer is a logarithm. \(\int \frac{2x}{x^2+1}dx = \ln(x^2+1)\), \(\int \frac{1}{x\ln x}dx = \ln|\ln x|\) (Week 4 quiz).

3. Substitution (u-substitution)

Pick the "inside" piece \(z\), compute \(dz\), and rewrite the whole integral in \(z\). The lecturer does this in the margin of almost every solution.

Integral of tan x — Week 3, p.5Compute \(\displaystyle\int \tan x\,dx\).
  1. Write \(\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\).
  2. Let \(z = \cos x\), so \(dz = -\sin x\,dx\) (the numerator is almost \(dz\)).
  3. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}dx = -\int\frac{dz}{z} = -\ln|z| = -\ln|\cos x|\).
\(\int \tan x\,dx = -\ln|\cos x| + C\), so \(e^{-\int\tan x\,dx} = e^{\ln|\cos x|} = \cos x\) (up to sign)
Week 4, p.16 (quiz)Compute \(\displaystyle\int \frac{\ln x}{x}\,dx\).
  1. Let \(z = \ln x\), \(dz = \dfrac1x dx\).
  2. \(\displaystyle\int z\,dz = \frac{z^2}{2}\).
\(\displaystyle\int\frac{\ln x}{x}dx = \frac{(\ln x)^2}{2} + C\)
Week 3, p.23Compute \(\displaystyle\int \frac{u}{u^2-1}\,du\).
  1. Let \(z = u^2-1\), \(dz = 2u\,du\), so \(u\,du = \tfrac12 dz\).
  2. \(\displaystyle\int \frac{u\,du}{u^2-1} = \frac12\int\frac{dz}{z} = \frac12\ln|u^2-1|\).
\(\tfrac12\ln|u^2-1| + C\)

4. Integration by parts

\[ \int f\,g'\,dx = f\,g - \int f'\,g\,dx \]
Integration by parts

Choose \(f\) = the part that gets simpler when differentiated (a polynomial like \(x\), or \(\ln x\)); \(g'\) = the part you can integrate (like \(e^{-x}\), \(\dfrac1{x^2}\)).

Typical in linear equationsCompute \(\displaystyle\int x e^{-x}\,dx\).
  1. \(f = x\) (\(f' = 1\)), \(g' = e^{-x}\) (\(g = -e^{-x}\)).
  2. \(\displaystyle\int xe^{-x}dx = -xe^{-x} + \int e^{-x}dx = -xe^{-x} - e^{-x}\).
\(\displaystyle\int xe^{-x}dx = -(x+1)e^{-x} + C\)
Needed in Bernoulli problems with ln xCompute \(\displaystyle\int \frac{\ln x}{x^2}\,dx\).
  1. \(f = \ln x\) (\(f' = \tfrac1x\)), \(g' = x^{-2}\) (\(g = -\tfrac1x\)).
  2. \(\displaystyle -\frac{\ln x}{x} + \int\frac{1}{x^2}dx = -\frac{\ln x}{x} - \frac1x\).
\(\displaystyle\int\frac{\ln x}{x^2}dx = -\frac{\ln x + 1}{x} + C\)

5. Partial fractions

When a separable equation gives you \(\int \frac{\text{polynomial}}{(\ldots)(\ldots)}\), split the fraction into simple pieces, each of which integrates to a logarithm.

Week 4, p.19 (quiz Q2)Split \(\dfrac{1}{u(u-1)}\) and integrate.
  1. Write \(\dfrac{1}{u(u-1)} = \dfrac Au + \dfrac{B}{u-1}\).
  2. Cover-up: at \(u=0\): \(A = \dfrac{1}{0-1} = -1\); at \(u=1\): \(B = \dfrac11 = 1\).
  3. \(\displaystyle\int\Big(\frac{1}{u-1} - \frac1u\Big)du = \ln|u-1| - \ln|u| = \ln\Big|\frac{u-1}{u}\Big|\).
\(\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{u(u-1)} = \ln\left|\frac{u-1}{u}\right| + C\)
Week 3, p.32 (Example 20)Split \(\dfrac{4-3z}{(3z+1)(z-1)}\).
  1. \(\dfrac{4-3z}{(3z+1)(z-1)} = \dfrac{A}{3z+1} + \dfrac{B}{z-1}\), so \(4-3z = A(z-1) + B(3z+1)\).
  2. Compare coefficients (the lecturer's way): \(z\): \(A + 3B = -3\); constant: \(-A + B = 4\). Adding: \(4B = 1\), \(B = \tfrac14\), \(A = -\tfrac{15}{4}\).
  3. Then \(\displaystyle\int\frac{-15/4}{3z+1}dz = -\frac54\ln|3z+1|\) (the inner derivative 3 divides out) and \(\displaystyle\int \frac{1/4}{z-1}dz = \frac14\ln|z-1|\).
\(-\tfrac54\ln|3z+1| + \tfrac14\ln|z-1| + C\)

6. Logs, exponentials and the integrating factor

\[ e^{\ln f} = f,\qquad e^{-\ln f} = \frac1f,\qquad e^{a\ln x} = x^{a},\qquad a\ln x = \ln x^{a},\qquad \ln A + \ln B = \ln(AB) \]
Rules used in every integrating factor
  • \(e^{-\int \frac3x dx} = e^{-3\ln x} = x^{-3} = \dfrac{1}{x^3}\) (Week 3, p.40).
  • \(e^{-\int\frac{dx}{x+1}} = e^{-\ln(x+1)} = \dfrac{1}{x+1}\) (Week 3, p.15).
  • \(e^{\int \frac{dx}{x\ln x}} = e^{\ln(\ln x)} = \ln x\) (Week 4, p.18).
  • \(4\ln|\cos x| = \ln\cos^4 x\) (Week 3, p.6).
i
Absolute values inside the integrating factor
Strictly \(e^{\ln|\cos x|} = |\cos x|\). The lecturer simply writes \(\cos x\): any nonzero constant multiple of an integrating factor still works, and on an interval \(|\cos x| = \pm\cos x\). You may do the same.

The linear-equation engine

Bernoulli, Riccati and many substitutions all end in a linear equation. This is the routine the lecturer writes every time:

\[ \frac{du}{dx} + P(x)\,u = Q(x),\qquad \mu(x) = e^{\int P(x)\,dx},\qquad \int\frac{d}{dx}\big(\mu\,u\big)\,dx = \int \mu\,Q\,dx \;\Rightarrow\; u = \frac{1}{\mu}\Big(\int \mu Q\,dx + C\Big) \]
First-order linear equation

Why it works: after multiplying by \(\mu\), the left side \(\mu u' + \mu P u\) is exactly \((\mu u)'\) by the product rule, because \(\mu' = P\mu\).

7. Handling the constant like the lecturer

The constant of integration may be renamed freely, as long as it stays an arbitrary constant. The lecturer's favourite move: write the constant as a logarithm so the logs combine.

Pattern from Week 3, p.24Solve \(\ln|z| = \ln|x| + C\) for \(z\).
  1. Write the constant as \(\ln|C|\) with \(C\neq0\): \(\ln|z| = \ln|x| + \ln|C| = \ln|Cx|\).
  2. Remove the logs: \(|z| = |Cx|\), so \(z = \pm Cx\).
  3. Rename: \(K = \pm C\), with \(K\neq0\). So \(z = Kx\), \(K\neq0\).
  4. Check \(z = 0\) separately (it was lost when you divided by \(z\)). If \(z=0\) also solves the equation, allow \(K = 0\) too and call the constant \(D\in\mathbb R\).
\(\ln|z| = \ln|x| + C \;\Longrightarrow\; z = Dx,\ D\in\mathbb R\) (when \(z=0\) is also a solution)
  • \(e^{x+C} = e^{C}e^{x} = Ke^{x}\) with \(K = \pm e^{C}\neq 0\) (Week 3, p.44).
  • \(\tfrac14\ln|A| = \ln|Cu|\) gives \(|A| = C^4u^4\) — rename \(\tilde C = C^4 \gt 0\), then \(A = K u^4\), \(K = \pm\tilde C\neq0\) (Week 3, p.33).
  • \(\frac{1}{m-1}\cdot\frac{1}{z^{m-1}} = x + C\) can be rewritten with \(\tilde C = (m-1)C\) (Week 3, p.43).
!
Dividing means losing
Every time you divide by something (\(y\), \(u\), \(u^2-1\), \(z-1\) …) to separate variables, write "for … \(\neq 0\)" and afterwards plug those values back into the original equation. Some are solutions you must list, some are already inside the family, and some are not solutions at all. The lecturer checks this on every example — and it is worth points.

In one minute

  • Every method ends in a separable or a linear equation, then an integral.
  • Chain rule: \(\dfrac{d}{dx}y^{k} = k y^{k-1}y'\) — the key to every substitution.
  • \(\int\frac{f'}{f} = \ln|f|\); \(\int\tan x = -\ln|\cos x|\); \(\int\cot x = \ln|\sin x|\).
  • By parts for \(x e^{ax}\), \(\ln x\cdot x^{k}\); partial fractions for \(\frac{1}{(\ldots)(\ldots)}\).
  • \(e^{\ln f} = f\), \(e^{a\ln x} = x^a\): integrating factors simplify to plain functions.
  • Linear: \(\mu = e^{\int P}\), \((\mu u)' = \mu Q\).
  • \(\ln|y| = \ln|x| + \ln|C| \Rightarrow y = Kx\); then check the value you divided by (maybe \(K=0\) is allowed).

chapters.title: Differential equations and their solutions
chapters.lead: After this chapter you can look at any equation and say at once: ODE or PDE, which order, linear or non-linear. You will also know exactly what a solution is, and the difference between general, particular and singular solutions.
chapters.html:
What is a differential equation?

In ordinary algebra the unknown is a number (solve \(x^2=4\)). In a differential equation the unknown is a function \(y(x)\), and the equation tells you something about its derivatives.

✓
Definition 1 (Week+1-3.pdf p.6)
A differential equation is an equation involving one or more derivatives of an unknown function.

ODE or PDE?

Look at what the unknown function depends on.

  • If it depends on one variable only (\(y=y(x)\)), you only see ordinary derivatives \(\frac{dy}{dx}, y'', \dots\). That is an ordinary differential equation (ODE).
  • If it depends on several variables (\(u=u(x,y)\)), you see partial derivatives \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\). That is a partial differential equation (PDE).
Example 1 · Week+1-3.pdf p.7Classify: (1) \(\frac{dy}{dx}+y=x^2\); (2) \(y''=-k^2y\); (3) \(\frac{d^4y}{dx^4}+\left(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^2+\cos x=0\); (4) \(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}=0\).
  1. In (1), (2), (3) the unknown \(y\) depends only on \(x\). (only ordinary derivatives appear)
  2. In (4) the unknown \(u\) depends on \(x\) and \(y\). (partial derivatives \(\partial/\partial x\), \(\partial/\partial y\))
(1), (2), (3) are ODEs; (4) is a PDE. In this course we only solve ODEs.

Order

✓
Definition 2 (p.8)
The order of a differential equation is the order of the highest derivative occurring in it. Any \(n\)-th order ODE can be written as \(F(x,y,y',\dots,y^{(n)})=0\). Here \(y\) is the dependent variable and \(x\) is the independent variable.
!
Order is not power
The order is about how many times you differentiate, not about exponents. In \(\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^3=y^2\) the highest derivative is \(y'\), so the order is 1 (the cube is a power, not a third derivative). In Example 1 (3), \(\left(y''\right)^2\) has a square, but \(y^{(4)}\) is there, so the order is 4.

Linear or non-linear?

✓
Definition 3 (p.9)
An equation that can be written as \[ a_0(x)y^{(n)}(x)+a_1(x)y^{(n-1)}(x)+\cdots+a_n(x)y(x)=f(x), \] where \(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n\) (with \(a_0\neq0\)) and \(f\) are functions of \(x\) only, is a linear differential equation of order \(n\). It is linear in \(y,y',\dots,y^{(n)}\). An equation that does not satisfy this definition is non-linear.

A practical way to test linearity: look only at \(y\) and its derivatives. The equation is linear when

  • \(y, y', y'',\dots\) appear only to the first power,
  • they are never multiplied with each other (no \(y\,y'\)),
  • they are never inside another function (no \(\sin y\), \(e^{y}\), \(\sqrt{y}\)).

The coefficients may be any functions of \(x\): \(x^2y'\) or \(\frac{1}{1+x^2}y'\) or \(\sin(x)\,y\) are all fine.

Example 2 · p.10Which are linear? (1) \(y''+x^2y'+\sin(x)y=e^x\); (2) \(xy''+\frac{1}{1+x^2}y'=\sin x\); (3) \(y''+x\sin(y')-xy=x^2\); (4) \(y'=\sqrt{y/x}\); (5) \(y''+(2y')^2=e^x\).
  1. (1) and (2): every term is (function of \(x\)) × (\(y\), \(y'\) or \(y''\)). (\(\sin x\) and \(\frac{1}{1+x^2}\) are coefficients; they only contain \(x\))
  2. (3): \(y'\) sits inside \(\sin\). (a function of the unknown)
  3. (4): \(y\) sits inside a square root.
  4. (5): \(y'\) is squared.
(1), (2) linear (both order 2); (3), (4), (5) non-linear.
Exercises 1 · p.11Classify by type, order and linearity: (1) \(y\frac{dy}{dx}=x\); (2) \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}-16y=0\); (3) \(\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^3=y^2\); (4) \(\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}\right)=xyu\); (5) \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial u}{\partial y}=0\).
  1. (1) ODE, order 1, non-linear. (\(y\cdot y'\) is a product of the unknown with its derivative)
  2. (2) ODE, order 2, linear. (\(a_0=1, a_1=0, a_2=-16, f=0\))
  3. (3) ODE, order 1, non-linear. (\(y'\) is cubed and \(y\) is squared)
  4. (4) PDE, order 1, non-linear. (product of two derivatives of \(u\))
  5. (5) PDE, order 1, linear. (each derivative appears alone, to the first power)
(1) ODE·1·non-lin. (2) ODE·2·lin. (3) ODE·1·non-lin. (4) PDE·1·non-lin. (5) PDE·1·lin.
i
Note
Definition 3 on the slide is written for ODEs. For the two PDEs we use the same idea (the unknown \(u\) and its partial derivatives appear only to the first power and are not multiplied together).

What is a solution?

✓
Definition 4 (p.12)
A solution of an \(n\)-th order differential equation on an interval \(I\) is any function \(y=y(x)\) that is (at least) \(n\)-times differentiable on \(I\) and that satisfies the differential equation identically for all \(x\) in \(I\).

Two words matter here. Identically means the equation must hold for every \(x\) in \(I\), not just at a few points. Interval means a solution always comes with a domain; where the formula or the equation is undefined, the solution stops.

Example 3 · p.13(1) Show that \(y=e^{2x}\) is a solution of \(y'=2y\) for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). (2) Where can solutions of \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}(y-1)\) live?
  1. Differentiate the candidate: \(y'=2e^{2x}\). (chain rule)
  2. Substitute: left side \(2e^{2x}\), right side \(2y=2e^{2x}\). They agree for every real \(x\).
  3. For (2): \(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\) is undefined when \(x\le 0\). (square root of a negative / division by 0)
(1) \(y=e^{2x}\) is a solution on \(\mathbb{R}\). (2) Any solution can only be defined for \(x\gt 0\).

Explicit and implicit solutions

A solution can come in two shapes (p.14): explicit \(y=\varphi(x)\) (\(y\) is alone on one side) or implicit \(\Phi(x,y)=0\) (a relation between \(x\) and \(y\)).

Explicit solution (Def. 5)
A function \(y=\varphi(x)\) that satisfies \(F(x,y,y',\dots,y^{(n)})=0\) for all \(x\) in \(I\) when substituted for \(y\).
Implicit solution (Def. 6)
A relation \(\Phi(x,y)=0\) that defines one or more explicit solutions of the equation on \(I\).
Example 4 · p.15Show that \(x^2+y^2=4\) is an implicit solution of \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}\). On which interval?
  1. Solve the relation for \(y\): \(y=\pm\sqrt{4-x^2}\). (the relation hides two functions)
  2. Check one branch: \(y=\sqrt{4-x^2}\Rightarrow y'=\frac{-x}{\sqrt{4-x^2}}=-\frac{x}{y}\). The other branch works the same way.
  3. At \(x=\pm2\) we get \(y=0\), but the equation contains \(\frac{x}{y}\), so it is only defined for \(y\neq0\). (remove the endpoints)
\(x^2+y^2=4\) contains two explicit solutions \(y=\pm\sqrt{4-x^2}\), valid for \(-2\lt x\lt 2\).
★
Checking an implicit solution fast
Differentiate the relation implicitly: \(2x+2yy'=0\Rightarrow y'=-x/y\). That is exactly the equation, so it is a solution.

General, particular and singular solutions

Example 5 · p.16Find all solutions of \(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=5x\).
  1. Integrate once: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac52x^2+c_1\). (\(c_1\) arbitrary constant)
  2. Integrate again: \(y=\frac56x^3+c_1x+c_2\). (a second constant \(c_2\))
\(y=\frac56x^3+c_1x+c_2\) — the general solution (two constants for a 2nd-order equation).
General solution (Def. 7, p.17)
A solution of an \(n\)-th order ODE that contains \(n\) arbitrary constants.
Particular solution (Def. 8, p.19)
A solution that does not contain any arbitrary constants. Assigning fixed values to the constants of the general solution gives a particular solution (Remark 2).
Singular solution (Def. 9, p.20)
A solution that cannot be obtained from the general solution by any choice of the \(n\) arbitrary constants.

Example 6 (p.17). \(y''=e^{-x}\). Integrating twice: general solution \(y=e^{-x}+c_1x+c_2\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).

Example 7 (p.19). Choosing \(c_1=1, c_2=0\) gives \(y=e^{-x}+x\), a particular solution of \(y''=e^{-x}\).

!
Remark 1 (p.18): not every equation has a general solution
\(\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2+(y-1)^2=0\). A sum of two squares is 0 only if both are 0, so \(y'=0\) and \(y=1\). The only solution is \(y(x)\equiv1\). It has no arbitrary constant, so this equation has no general solution.
Example 8 · p.20For \(\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2-4y=0\), show that \(y=(x+c)^2\) is the general solution and that \(y\equiv0\) is a singular solution.
  1. \(y=(x+c)^2\Rightarrow y'=2(x+c)\), so \((y')^2-4y=4(x+c)^2-4(x+c)^2=0\). (one constant, first order \(\to\) general solution)
  2. Particular solutions: \(c=2\) gives \(y=(x+2)^2\); \(c=-5\) gives \(y=(x-5)^2\).
  3. \(y\equiv0\): \(y'=0\), and \(0-0=0\). So it is a solution.
  4. Can \((x+c)^2\) be \(0\) for all \(x\)? No: whatever \(c\) is, \((x+c)^2\gt0\) for \(x\neq-c\). (no choice of \(c\) works)
General solution \(y=(x+c)^2\); \(y\equiv0\) is a singular solution.
→
How to prove something is singular
Two steps. (1) Plug it into the equation: it must be a solution. (2) Show that no value of the constant(s) in the general solution produces it for all \(x\).

Exercises 1.1 (p.21), solved

Exercises 1.1 #1 · p.21Show that \(y''-y=0\) has the general solution \(y=c_1\cosh x+c_2\sinh x\). Find \(c_1,c_2\) so that \(y(0)=0\), \(y'(0)=1\).
  1. \((\cosh x)'=\sinh x\), \((\sinh x)'=\cosh x\). So \(y'=c_1\sinh x+c_2\cosh x\) and \(y''=c_1\cosh x+c_2\sinh x=y\). Hence \(y''-y=0\). (2 constants, 2nd order \(\to\) general)
  2. \(y(0)=c_1\cosh0+c_2\sinh0=c_1=0\). (\(\cosh0=1,\ \sinh0=0\))
  3. \(y'(0)=c_1\sinh0+c_2\cosh0=c_2=1\).
\(c_1=0,\ c_2=1\): the particular solution is \(y=\sinh x\).
Exercises 1.1 #2 · p.21Find \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(y''-4y'+4y=0\) has the general solution \(y=e^{\alpha x}(c_1x+c_2)\).
  1. \(y'=\alpha e^{\alpha x}(c_1x+c_2)+c_1e^{\alpha x}\). (product rule)
  2. \(y''=\alpha^2e^{\alpha x}(c_1x+c_2)+2\alpha c_1e^{\alpha x}\).
  3. Substitute and divide by \(e^{\alpha x}\neq0\): \((\alpha^2-4\alpha+4)(c_1x+c_2)+(2\alpha-4)c_1=0\).
  4. This must hold for all \(c_1,c_2\) and all \(x\): \(\alpha^2-4\alpha+4=(\alpha-2)^2=0\) and \(2\alpha-4=0\).
\(\alpha=2\): \(y=e^{2x}(c_1x+c_2)\).
Exercises 1.1 #3 · p.21Show that \(2y\frac{dy}{dx}=x\left(4+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\right)\) has the particular solution \(y=x^2+1\), and find the one-parameter family that forms the general solution.
  1. \(y=x^2+1,\ y'=2x\): left \(2(x^2+1)(2x)=4x^3+4x\); right \(x(4+4x^2)=4x+4x^3\). Equal. ✓
  2. Try the family \(y=cx^2+h\) (same shape as the particular solution): \(y'=2cx\).
  3. Left: \(2(cx^2+h)(2cx)=4c^2x^3+4chx\). Right: \(x(4+4c^2x^2)=4x+4c^2x^3\).
  4. Compare the \(x\) terms: \(4ch=4\Rightarrow h=\frac1c\).
General solution \(y=cx^2+\frac1c\) (\(c\neq0\)); \(c=1\) gives \(x^2+1\).
i
The slide says y = cx + h, but …
The slide asks for \(h\) so that \(y=cx+h\) is the general solution. If you try that, you get \(2c^2=4+c^2\) and \(2ch=0\), so only \(c=\pm2,\ h=0\) works (that is not a one-parameter family). The family that fits the particular solution \(x^2+1\) is \(y=cx^2+h\) with \(h=1/c\). We think the slide dropped the square.
Exercises 1.1 #4 · p.21Show that \(y=x\frac{dy}{dx}+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2\) has the general solution \(y=cx+c^2\) and that \(y=-\frac14x^2\) is a singular solution.
  1. \(y=cx+c^2,\ y'=c\): right side \(xc+c^2=y\). ✓ (1 constant, 1st order \(\to\) general)
  2. \(y=-\frac14x^2,\ y'=-\frac x2\): right side \(x\left(-\frac x2\right)+\frac{x^2}{4}=-\frac{x^2}{4}=y\). ✓
  3. Could \(cx+c^2=-\frac14x^2\) for all \(x\)? The left side is a line, the right side a parabola; no \(c\) makes them equal.
\(y=cx+c^2\) is the general solution; \(y=-\frac14x^2\) is a singular solution.

In one minute

  • A DE contains derivatives of an unknown function. One independent variable \(\to\) ODE; partial derivatives \(\to\) PDE.
  • Order = highest derivative (not the highest power).
  • Linear: \(y,y',\dots\) only to the 1st power, not multiplied together, not inside \(\sin, e^{\cdot}, \sqrt{\ }\); coefficients depend on \(x\) only.
  • A solution is \(n\)-times differentiable on an interval \(I\) and satisfies the equation for all \(x\in I\). It can be explicit \(y=\varphi(x)\) or implicit \(\Phi(x,y)=0\).
  • General = \(n\) arbitrary constants; particular = no constants; singular = a solution that no choice of constants produces.
  • To show a function is a solution: differentiate and substitute. To show it is singular: also show no constant gives it.
  • Some equations have no general solution (\((y')^2+(y-1)^2=0\) has only \(y\equiv1\)).

chapters.title: Initial value problems and the existence–uniqueness theorem
chapters.lead: Here you learn to pick the one solution that passes through a given point, and to use Theorem 1 to say whether such a solution exists and is unique, without solving anything.
chapters.html:
One-parameter families

A first-order equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)\) usually has infinitely many solutions. Solving it gives a formula with one constant, \(y=\Phi(x,c)\). The slides call this the one-parameter family of solutions (p.22).

Each value of \(c\) is one curve. An extra condition such as \(y(0)=1\) chooses one curve from the family.

Example 9 · Week+1-3.pdf p.22\(y=\cos x+c\) is a one-parameter family of solutions of \(y'=-\sin x\). Which one satisfies \(y(0)=1\)?
  1. Check the family: \((\cos x+c)'=-\sin x\). ✓
  2. Use the condition: \(y(0)=\cos0+c=1+c=1\). (put \(x=0\), \(y=1\))
  3. So \(c=0\).
\(y=\cos x\) is the only solution with \(y(0)=1\).

What an IVP looks like

A problem of this kind is an initial value problem (IVP). It always has two parts (p.23):

\[ \begin{cases} \dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y) & \text{differential equation}\\[4pt] y(x_0)=y_0 & \text{initial condition} \end{cases} \]
Initial value problem

The recipe is always the same:

  1. Find the general solution (one constant \(c\)).
  2. Put \(x=x_0\) and \(y=y_0\) into it and solve for \(c\).
  3. Write the solution with that \(c\), and say on which interval it lives.

Theorem 1: existence and uniqueness

Before solving, we may ask: does the IVP have a solution at all? Is there only one? Theorem 1 answers both questions by looking only at \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial y\).

✓
Theorem 1 (Existence and Uniqueness), p.24
Let \(f(x,y)\) and \(\frac{\partial}{\partial y}f(x,y)\) be continuous on the rectangle \(R:=\{(x,y):\ |x-x_0|\le a,\ |y-y_0|\le b\}\). Then there is a unique solution of the IVP \[ \begin{cases}\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)\\ y(x_0)=y_0\end{cases} \] in some interval \(I:\ |x-x_0|\lt h\), where \(h\gt0\).

How to use it, step by step:

  1. Write the equation as \(y'=f(x,y)\) and name \(f\).
  2. Compute \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) (treat \(x\) as a constant).
  3. Find where \(f\) is continuous and where \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) is continuous. Typical trouble spots: division by zero, \(\sqrt{\ }\) of something negative, \(\ln\) of something \(\le0\).
  4. If the point \((x_0,y_0)\) lies inside a region where both are continuous, you can draw a small rectangle \(R\) around it: a unique solution exists near \(x_0\).
  5. If \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) is not continuous at \((x_0,y_0)\), the theorem says nothing. There may be no solution, one, or several.
!
What the theorem does NOT say
It only promises a solution on some small interval \(|x-x_0|\lt h\). It does not tell you how big \(h\) is, and it does not promise the solution lives on all of \(\mathbb{R}\). Also, if the hypotheses fail, that does not prove non-uniqueness; it just means the theorem can't help.
Example 10 · p.25Consider \(\frac{dy}{dx}=x\sqrt{y},\ y(x_0)=y_0\). What does Theorem 1 say for \((x_0,y_0)=(1,2)\)? And for \((0,0)\)?
  1. \(f(x,y)=x\sqrt y\) is continuous for \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \(y\ge0\). (square root needs \(y\ge0\))
  2. \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac{x}{2\sqrt y}\) is continuous for \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \(y\gt0\). (now \(y=0\) also breaks it: division by 0)
  3. \((1,2)\): \(y_0=2\gt0\), so both are continuous on a small rectangle around it. A unique solution exists on some interval \(1-h\lt x\lt 1+h\).
  4. \((0,0)\): \(y_0=0\) is on the boundary where \(\partial f/\partial y\) fails. The theorem does not apply.
  5. Indeed there are two solutions through \((0,0)\): \(y\equiv0\) (\(0=x\cdot0\)) and \(y=\frac{x^4}{16}\) (\(y'=\frac{x^3}{4}\) and \(x\sqrt{x^4/16}=x\cdot\frac{x^2}{4}=\frac{x^3}{4}\)).
At \((1,2)\): unique solution near \(x=1\). At \((0,0)\): two solutions, \(y\equiv0\) and \(y=\frac{x^4}{16}\); uniqueness does not hold.
★
Shortcut for the region
Write down \(f\) and \(f_y\). Every place where one of them divides by zero, takes an even root of a negative number, or takes \(\ln\) of a non-positive number is a forbidden set. The theorem guarantees a unique solution through every point in the open region that avoids all forbidden sets.

Exercises 2 (p.26), solved

Exercises 2 #1 · p.26Show that the IVP \(\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x),\ y(x_0)=y_0\), where \(p,q\) are continuous functions and \(x_0,y_0\in\mathbb{R}\), admits a unique solution in an interval \(|x-x_0|\lt h\) for some \(h\gt0\).
  1. Put it in the form \(y'=f(x,y)\): \(f(x,y)=q(x)-p(x)y\).
  2. \(f\) is continuous everywhere: \(p,q\) are continuous and \(y\) is a polynomial. (sums and products of continuous functions are continuous)
  3. \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=-p(x)\), which is continuous. (the \(q(x)\) term has no \(y\))
  4. So both are continuous on any rectangle around \((x_0,y_0)\). Theorem 1 applies.
A unique solution exists on some interval \(|x-x_0|\lt h\). (Every linear first-order IVP with continuous \(p,q\) has this property.)
Exercises 2 #2 · p.26Show that \(\frac{dy}{dx}=1+y^2,\ y(0)=0\) admits a unique solution in some neighbourhood of 0.
  1. \(f(x,y)=1+y^2\) is a polynomial, so continuous on all of \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
  2. \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2y\), also continuous everywhere.
  3. Any rectangle around \((0,0)\) works, so Theorem 1 gives a unique solution on some \(|x|\lt h\).
Unique solution near \(x=0\). (It is \(y=\tan x\), which you can find with Chapter 4's method.)
i
Why only some neighbourhood?
Even though \(f=1+y^2\) is perfect everywhere, the solution \(y=\tan x\) blows up at \(x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\). So it exists only on \(-\frac\pi2\lt x\lt\frac\pi2\), not on all of \(\mathbb{R}\). This is exactly why the theorem only promises an interval \(|x-x_0|\lt h\).

More practice in the same style

Practice (modeled on p.25)For \(y'=y^{2/3}\), where does Theorem 1 guarantee a unique solution through \((x_0,y_0)\)? Check \((0,0)\).
  1. \(f=y^{2/3}\) is continuous for all \((x,y)\). (cube root is defined for negative numbers too)
  2. \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=\frac23y^{-1/3}=\frac{2}{3\sqrt[3]{y}}\): not defined at \(y=0\).
  3. So uniqueness is guaranteed through every point with \(y_0\neq0\).
  4. At \((0,0)\): \(y\equiv0\) works, and so does \(y=\frac{x^3}{27}\) (\(y'=\frac{x^2}{9}=\left(\frac{x^3}{27}\right)^{2/3}\)).
Unique for every \(y_0\neq0\). Through \((0,0)\) there are at least two solutions: \(y\equiv0\) and \(y=x^3/27\).
Practice: interval of existenceSolve \(y'=-2xy^2,\ y(0)=-1\) (the equation of Example 11 (3) in Chapter 4) and give the largest interval containing 0 where the solution exists.
  1. The general solution is \(y=\frac{1}{x^2+C}\) (see Chapter 4).
  2. \(y(0)=\frac1C=-1\Rightarrow C=-1\), so \(y=\frac{1}{x^2-1}\).
  3. The formula breaks at \(x=\pm1\). A solution lives on an interval, and the one that contains \(x_0=0\) is \((-1,1)\).
\(y=\frac{1}{x^2-1}\) on \(-1\lt x\lt1\).
!
Same equation, different interval
With \(y(0)=1\) the same equation gives \(y=\frac{1}{x^2+1}\), defined on all of \(\mathbb{R}\). The interval depends on the initial condition, not only on the equation.

In one minute

  • IVP = equation \(y'=f(x,y)\) + initial condition \(y(x_0)=y_0\).
  • To solve: general solution, plug in \((x_0,y_0)\), find \(c\), state the interval.
  • Theorem 1: if \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial y\) are continuous on a rectangle around \((x_0,y_0)\), there is a unique solution on some \(|x-x_0|\lt h\).
  • Check \(f_y\), not just \(f\). Typical failure: \(\sqrt y\) or \(y^{2/3}\) at \(y=0\).
  • If the hypotheses fail, the theorem is silent. Example 10: two solutions \(0\) and \(x^4/16\) through \((0,0)\).
  • The guarantee is local: \(y'=1+y^2\) is perfect everywhere, but \(y=\tan x\) only lives on \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\).
  • Linear IVPs \(y'+p(x)y=q(x)\) with continuous \(p,q\) always have a unique solution near \(x_0\).

chapters.title: Separable equations
chapters.lead: The first real solving method: move all the y's to one side and all the x's to the other, then integrate. You will also learn the step most students forget, which is checking for lost (singular) solutions.
chapters.html:
Two ways to write a first-order equation

The slides (p.27) use two forms, and you must be able to switch between them:

  • Derivative form: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y)\).
  • Differential form: \(M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0\).

Going from one to the other is just algebra with \(dx\) and \(dy\). For example \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-2y^2x\) is the same as \(2y^2x\,dx+dy=0\).

What makes an equation separable

✓
Definition 10 (Separable Equations), p.28
An equation of the form \[ f(y)\frac{dy}{dx}=g(x) \] is called a separable equation.

In words: you can put everything with \(y\) (including \(dy\)) on one side and everything with \(x\) (including \(dx\)) on the other side.

The most common shape on exams is the one in Remark 3 (p.30):

\[ \frac{dy}{dx}=g(x)\,h(y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{h(y)}\,dy=g(x)\,dx\qquad (h(y)\neq0) \]
Separable: right side = (function of x) × (function of y)
★
Quick separability test
Try to factor the right side into a product \(g(x)\cdot h(y)\). \(\ x^2+x^2y^2=x^2(1+y^2)\) factors, so it is separable. \(\ x+y\) does not factor, so it is not.

The solution technique

From p.29: first write the equation as \(f(y)\,dy=g(x)\,dx\). Then integrate both sides:

\[ \underbrace{\int^{y} f(\zeta)\,d\zeta}_{F(y)}=\underbrace{\int^{x} g(\eta)\,d\eta}_{G(x)}+c \]
General solution \(F(y)=G(x)+c\), \(c\) arbitrary

One constant on one side is enough: two constants \(c_1,c_2\) on both sides combine into one.

The lost-solution check (Remark 3)

When you divide by \(h(y)\), you silently assume \(h(y)\neq0\). But if \(h(y_1)=0\) for some number \(y_1\), then the constant function \(y\equiv y_1\) gives \(y'=0\) and \(g(x)h(y_1)=0\). So it is a solution, and dividing threw it away.

✓
Remark 3, p.30
The equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}=g(x)h(y)\) is separable because it can be written as \(\frac{1}{h(y)}dy=g(x)dx\), provided that \(h(y)\neq0\). What happens if \(h(y)=0\)? In that case we get lost solutions. If these solutions are not included in the general solution for definite values of the arbitrary constants, then they are called singular solutions.
→
The lecturer's recipe (mirror this on the exam)
  1. Name the form (derivative or differential) and show it is separable by labelling \(h(y)\) and \(g(x)\).
  2. Write "for \(h(y)\neq0\)" and separate: \(\frac{1}{h(y)}dy=g(x)dx\).
  3. Integrate both sides; add one constant \(C\); write "general solution".
  4. Write "if \(h(y)=0\)": find those constants \(y=y_1\) and check them in the equation.
  5. Decide: is \(y=y_1\) contained in the general solution for some \(C\)? If not, it is a singular solution.

The same idea works in differential form: if you divide by something containing \(x\), such as \(x+1\), check the vertical lines \(x=\text{const}\) too (see Exercise 3.1 #1 below).

Example 11 (p.31), solved

Example 11 (1) · p.31Solve \(e^{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=x\cos x\).
  1. Already in the form \(f(y)y'=g(x)\) with \(f(y)=e^y\), \(g(x)=x\cos x\). Separate: \(e^y\,dy=x\cos x\,dx\). (nothing to divide by, so nothing is lost)
  2. \(\int e^y\,dy=e^y\).
  3. \(\int x\cos x\,dx=x\sin x-\int\sin x\,dx=x\sin x+\cos x\). (by parts: \(u=x\), \(dv=\cos x\,dx\))
  4. \(e^y=x\sin x+\cos x+C\).
\(y=\ln\left(x\sin x+\cos x+C\right)\), wherever \(x\sin x+\cos x+C\gt0\).
Example 11 (2) · p.31Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy\).
  1. \(g(x)=2x\), \(h(y)=y\). For \(y\neq0\): \(\frac{dy}{y}=2x\,dx\).
  2. Integrate: \(\ln|y|=x^2+C\). (\(\int\frac{dy}{y}=\ln|y|\))
  3. Exponentiate: \(|y|=e^{C}e^{x^2}\), so \(y=Ke^{x^2}\) with \(K=\pm e^{C}\neq0\).
  4. If \(y=0\): \(y'=0\) and \(2x\cdot0=0\). ✓ So \(y\equiv0\) is a solution.
  5. Is it included? Yes: take \(K=0\) in \(y=Ke^{x^2}\).
\(y=Ke^{x^2}\), \(K\) arbitrary (\(K=0\) gives \(y\equiv0\)). Here \(y=0\) is not singular.
Example 11 (3) · p.32 (handwritten)Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-2y^2x\).
  1. Derivative form. \(-2y^2x=(-y^2)\cdot(2x)\): \(h(y)=-y^2\), \(g(x)=2x\). Separable.
  2. For \(y\neq0\): \(-\int\frac{1}{y^2}dy=\int2x\,dx\).
  3. \(-\int y^{-2}dy=\frac1y\), so \(\frac1y=x^2+C\), \(C\) arbitrary constant.
  4. General solution: \(y=\frac{1}{x^2+C}\).
  5. If \(y=0\): \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\) and \(-2x\cdot0^2=0\). ✓ So \(y=0\) is also a solution (lost solution).
  6. \(\frac{1}{x^2+C}\) is never 0, for any \(C\).
General solution \(y=\frac{1}{x^2+C}\); \(y=0\) is a singular solution, since it cannot be included in the general solution by any choice of \(C\).
!
Same check, different verdict
In 11(2) the lost solution \(y=0\) comes back with \(K=0\), so it is not singular. In 11(3) it never comes back, so it is singular. Always write out both: "\(y=0\) is a solution" and then whether it is contained in the general solution.

Exercises 3.1 (p.33): "find the solutions and domain of validity"

Exercises 3.1 #1 · p.34 (handwritten)Solve \((y^2+1)\,dx+(x+1)\,dy=0\).
  1. Differential form. Write \(y\)-terms on the left, \(x\)-terms on the right. For \(x\neq-1\): \(\frac{1}{y^2+1}dy=-\frac{1}{x+1}dx\).
  2. Integrate both sides: \(\int\frac{dy}{1+y^2}=-\int\frac{dx}{x+1}\).
  3. \(\arctan y=-\ln|x+1|+C\), \(C\) arbitrary constant. (general solution)
  4. For \(x=-1\): \(dx=0\). Substitute into the equation: \((y^2+1)\cdot0+(x+1)dy=0\cdot dy=0\). ✓ So \(x=-1\) is also a solution.
  5. \(x=-1\) is not included in the general solution, so it is a singular solution.
  6. Domain: explicitly \(y=\tan\left(C-\ln|x+1|\right)\), valid on intervals that avoid \(x=-1\) and where \(|C-\ln|x+1||\lt\frac\pi2\). (\(\tan\) blows up at \(\pm\pi/2\))
\(\arctan y+\ln|x+1|=C\); also the singular solution \(x=-1\). (\(y^2+1\) is never 0, so no constant \(y\) is lost.)
Exercises 3.1 #2 · p.35 (handwritten)Solve \(e^{y^2}\ln(x)\,dx-y\,dy=0\).
  1. Differential form. Rewrite: \(\frac{y}{e^{y^2}}dy=\ln x\,dx\). (\(e^{y^2}\gt0\), nothing lost; \(\ln x\) needs \(x\gt0\))
  2. Left: \(\int ye^{-y^2}dy\). Put \(u=y^2\), \(du=2y\,dy\): \(\frac12\int e^{-u}du=-\frac12e^{-u}=-\frac12e^{-y^2}\).
  3. Right: \(\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x\). (by parts)
  4. \(-\frac12e^{-y^2}=x\ln x-x+C\).
  5. Multiply by \(-2\): \(e^{-y^2}=-2x\ln x+2x+\tilde C\), where \(\tilde C=-2C\) is an arbitrary constant.
\(e^{-y^2}=2x-2x\ln x+\tilde C\), for \(x\gt0\) (and where the right side is in \((0,1]\), so that \(y=\pm\sqrt{-\ln(\dots)}\) is real).
i
The handwritten line has a slip
Multiplying \(x\ln x-x+C\) by \(-2\) gives \(-2x\ln x+2x-2C\). The handwritten line has \(+x\) and \(\tilde C=-C\); the correct factors are \(+2x\) and \(\tilde C=-2C\). (Checked with sympy.)
Exercises 3.1 #3 · p.33Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}-x^2y^2=x^2\).
  1. Move the \(x^2y^2\): \(\frac{dy}{dx}=x^2+x^2y^2=x^2(y^2+1)\). Separable. (this is the hint written on the slide)
  2. \(y^2+1\neq0\) always, so \(\frac{dy}{1+y^2}=x^2dx\) loses nothing.
  3. \(\arctan y=\frac{x^3}{3}+C\).
\(y=\tan\left(\frac{x^3}{3}+C\right)\), valid where \(\left|\frac{x^3}{3}+C\right|\lt\frac\pi2\). No singular solutions.
Exercises 3.1 #4 · p.36–37 (handwritten)Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos(y)\sin(x)\).
  1. \(h(y)=\cos y\), \(g(x)=\sin x\): separable.
  2. For \(\cos y\neq0\): \(\int\frac{1}{\cos y}dy=\int\sin x\,dx\), i.e. \(\int\sec y\,dy=\int\sin x\,dx\).
  3. \(\ln|\sec y+\tan y|=-\cos x+C\), \(C\) arbitrary constant. (standard integral of \(\sec y\))
  4. For \(\cos y=0\): \(y=\frac\pi2+k\pi\), \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\). Then \(\frac{dy}{dx}=0\) and \(\cos y\sin x=0\cdot\sin x=0\). ✓
  5. At \(\cos y=0\), \(\sec y\) is undefined, so these lines are not in the general solution.
\(\ln|\sec y+\tan y|=-\cos x+C\); singular solutions \(y(x)=\frac\pi2+k\pi\), \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\).
Exercises 3.1 #5 · p.37–38 (handwritten)Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=(y^2-1)\ln x\). (The slide says: be careful for \(y=\mp1\)!)
  1. \(h(y)=y^2-1\), \(g(x)=\ln x\) (so \(x\gt0\)). For \(y\neq\mp1\): \(\int\frac{1}{y^2-1}dy=\int\ln x\,dx\).
  2. Partial fractions: \(\frac{1}{y^2-1}=\frac{A}{y-1}+\frac{B}{y+1}\Rightarrow A+B=0,\ A-B=1\Rightarrow A=\frac12,\ B=-\frac12\).
  3. Right side by parts (\(u=\ln x\), \(dv=dx\)): \(x\ln x-\int\frac1x\cdot x\,dx=x\ln x-x\).
  4. \(\frac12\left(\ln|y-1|-\ln|y+1|\right)=x\ln x-x+C\), i.e. \(\frac12\ln\left|\frac{y-1}{y+1}\right|=x\ln x-x+C\).
  5. Solve for \(y\): \(\frac{y-1}{y+1}=Kx^{2x}e^{-2x}\) (\(K=\pm e^{2C}\)), so \(y=\frac{1+Kx^{2x}e^{-2x}}{1-Kx^{2x}e^{-2x}}\).
  6. Constant solutions: \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) make \(y^2-1=0\), so \(y'=0=0\cdot\ln x\). ✓ Both are solutions.
  7. In the explicit family, \(K=0\) gives \(y=1\). No \(K\) gives \(y=-1\): with \(A=Kx^{2x}e^{-2x}\), \(\frac{1+A}{1-A}=-1\) would need \(1+A=-1+A\), i.e. \(1=-1\).
\(\frac12\ln\left|\frac{y-1}{y+1}\right|=x\ln x-x+C\) (\(x\gt0\)), plus \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\). With the family written as \(y=\frac{1+Kx^{2x}e^{-2x}}{1-Kx^{2x}e^{-2x}}\), \(K\) arbitrary, \(y=1\) is included (\(K=0\)) and only \(y=-1\) is singular.
i
The handwritten solution ends with ln C x^x, but …
On p.37–38 the right side \(x\ln x-x+\ln C\) is rewritten as \(\ln\left(Cx^{x}\right)\). That drops the \(-x\): the correct form is \(\ln\left(Cx^{x}e^{-x}\right)\). The \(\ln\left(Cx^x\right)\) version does not satisfy the equation.
!
Singular depends on how you write the family
In the \(\ln\) form, both \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) are outside the formula. After solving for \(y\) and letting \(K=0\), \(y=1\) comes back. So on the exam, list all constant solutions explicitly, and say which ones the family you wrote contains.

In one minute

  • Separable: \(f(y)y'=g(x)\), or \(y'=g(x)h(y)\) (the right side factors into an \(x\)-part times a \(y\)-part).
  • Separate \(\frac{dy}{h(y)}=g(x)dx\), integrate both sides, add one constant.
  • Always say "for \(h(y)\neq0\)" and then check \(h(y)=0\): each root \(y_1\) gives a constant solution \(y\equiv y_1\).
  • Lost solution not obtainable from the general solution for any \(C\) = singular solution (e.g. \(y=0\) for \(y'=-2xy^2\)).
  • Some lost solutions come back with \(K=0\) (\(y'=2xy\): \(y=Ke^{x^2}\)), so they are not singular.
  • In differential form, dividing by an \(x\)-expression such as \(x+1\) can lose a vertical line \(x=-1\).
  • State the domain: \(\ln x\) needs \(x\gt0\), \(\tan\) needs its argument in \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\), and so on.

chapters.title: Exact equations
chapters.lead: Some equations are secretly the total differential of a function F(x,y). Spot them with one test, rebuild F in two ways, and the answer is simply F(x,y) = C.
chapters.html:
The idea: dF = 0 means F is constant

If \(F(x,y)\) is a function of two variables, a small change in \(x\) and \(y\) changes \(F\) by

✓
Definition 11 (Total differential), Week 2-2.pdf p.1
Let \(F\) be a function of two real variables with continuous first partial derivatives in a domain \(D\). The total differential of \(F\) is \[ dF=\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}dx+\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}dy\quad\text{for all }(x,y)\in D. \]

Now look at an equation in differential form, \(M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0\). It has the same shape as \(dF\). If we can find \(F\) with

\[ \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=M(x,y)\quad\text{and}\quad\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=N(x,y), \]

then the equation says \(dF=0\). A function whose change is always zero is constant, so

\[ dF=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F(x,y)=C,\qquad C\ \text{arbitrary constant} \]
The general solution of an exact equation (p.2)
✓
Definition 12, p.3
The differential equation \(M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0\) is said to be exact in a domain \(D\) if there exists a function \(F\) such that \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=M(x,y)\) and \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=N(x,y)\) for all \((x,y)\in D\).

The test for exactness

✓
Theorem 2 (Test for Exactness), p.4
Let \(M,N\) and their first-order partial derivatives \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}\) and \(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\) be continuous in a rectangular domain \(D\). Then \(M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0\) is exact for all \((x,y)\in D\) if and only if \[ \frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}. \]

Why it works (the lecturer's handwritten arrows on p.4): if the equation is exact, then \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{\partial^2F}{\partial y\,\partial x}\) and \(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\left(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}\right)=\frac{\partial^2F}{\partial x\,\partial y}\). Mixed partial derivatives of a nice function are equal, so \(M_y=N_x\).

!
Cross the letters
Differentiate \(M\) (the \(dx\) coefficient) with respect to \(y\), and \(N\) (the \(dy\) coefficient) with respect to \(x\). Computing \(M_x\) and \(N_y\) is the classic slip. Also keep the sign: in \(y\,dx-x\,dy=0\), \(N=-x\), not \(x\).

Building F: two ways

Example 12 on p.5–6 is worked out both ways side by side. Learn one well, but know both.

1st way: start from \(M\)

  1. \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=M\Rightarrow F=\int M\,dx+g(y)\). (\(y\) is held constant, so the "constant" may depend on \(y\))
  2. Differentiate in \(y\) and set \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=N\).
  3. Solve for \(g'(y)\) (all \(x\) must cancel), integrate to get \(g(y)\).

2nd way: start from \(N\)

  1. \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=N\Rightarrow F=\int N\,dy+h(x)\).
  2. Differentiate in \(x\) and set \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=M\).
  3. Solve for \(h'(x)\) (all \(y\) must cancel), integrate to get \(h(x)\).
★
Which way is faster?
Integrate whichever of \(M\,dx\) or \(N\,dy\) is easier. In Exercise 3.2 #3 below, \(N=x^2\) is trivial to integrate in \(y\), so the 2nd way is quicker.
Example 12 · Week 2-2.pdf p.5–6Find the general solution of \(2xe^y\,dx+\left(x^2e^y+\cos y\right)dy=0\).
  1. \(M=2xe^y\), \(N=x^2e^y+\cos y\).
  2. \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=2xe^y\), \(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=2xe^y\). Equal, so the given equation is exact.
  3. 1st way. \(F=\int2xe^y\,dx+g(y)=x^2e^y+g(y)\).
  4. \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=x^2e^y+g'(y)\overset{!}{=}x^2e^y+\cos y\Rightarrow g'(y)=\cos y\Rightarrow g(y)=\sin y+c_1\).
  5. \(F=x^2e^y+\sin y+c_1=c_2\), so \(x^2e^y+\sin y=c_2-c_1=C\).
  6. 2nd way. \(F=\int\left(x^2e^y+\cos y\right)dy+h(x)=x^2e^y+\sin y+h(x)\).
  7. \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=2xe^y+h'(x)\overset{!}{=}2xe^y\Rightarrow h'(x)=0\Rightarrow h(x)=0\). (one choice is enough)
\(x^2e^y+\sin y=C\), \(C\) arbitrary constant (both ways give the same answer).
i
Constants
The lecturer sometimes keeps \(c_1\) from \(g(y)\) and then merges it: \(F=c_2\Rightarrow\ldots=c_2-c_1=C\). It is equally correct to take \(g\) without a constant, since the final \(=C\) absorbs it.
!
g(y) must not contain x
If after setting \(F_y=N\) your \(g'(y)\) still contains \(x\), you made a mistake (or the equation is not exact). Go back and check \(M_y=N_x\) and your integral.

Exercises 3.2 (p.7), solved

Exercises 3.2 #4 · p.8–9 (handwritten)Solve \(\frac{1}{x+y^2}dx+\left(3+\frac{2y}{x+y^2}\right)dy=0\).
  1. \(M=\frac{1}{x+y^2}\), \(N=3+\frac{2y}{x+y^2}\).
  2. \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{-2y}{(x+y^2)^2}\) and \(\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=\frac{-2y}{(x+y^2)^2}\). Equal, so the equation is exact.
  3. \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial x}=M\): \(F=\int\frac{1}{x+y^2}dx+g(y)=\ln|x+y^2|+g(y)\).
  4. \(\frac{\partial F}{\partial y}=N\): \(\frac{1}{x+y^2}\cdot2y+g'(y)=\frac{2y}{x+y^2}+3\Rightarrow g'(y)=3\Rightarrow g(y)=3y\).
  5. Hence \(F(x,y)=\ln|x+y^2|+3y\).
\(\ln|x+y^2|+3y=C\), \(C\) arbitrary constant.
Exercises 3.2 #1 · p.7Solve \(\left(\sec(x+y)\right)^2dx+\left(2y+\left(\sec(x+y)\right)^2\right)dy=0\).
  1. \(M=\sec^2(x+y)\), \(N=2y+\sec^2(x+y)\).
  2. \(M_y=2\sec^2(x+y)\tan(x+y)\) and \(N_x=2\sec^2(x+y)\tan(x+y)\). Equal, so the equation is exact. (\((\sec u)'=\sec u\tan u\), chain rule)
  3. \(F=\int\sec^2(x+y)\,dx+g(y)=\tan(x+y)+g(y)\).
  4. \(F_y=\sec^2(x+y)+g'(y)=2y+\sec^2(x+y)\Rightarrow g'(y)=2y\Rightarrow g(y)=y^2\).
\(\tan(x+y)+y^2=C\).
Exercises 3.2 #2 · p.7Solve \(\left(2(x+y)-3x^2\right)dx+2(x+y)\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M=2x+2y-3x^2\), \(N=2x+2y\). \(M_y=2=N_x\), so the equation is exact.
  2. \(F=\int(2x+2y-3x^2)\,dx+g(y)=x^2+2xy-x^3+g(y)\).
  3. \(F_y=2x+g'(y)=2x+2y\Rightarrow g(y)=y^2\).
\(x^2+2xy+y^2-x^3=C\), i.e. \((x+y)^2-x^3=C\).
Exercises 3.2 #3 · p.7Solve \(\left(2xy+x\cos x+\sin x\right)dx+x^2\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M_y=2x\), \(N_x=2x\). Exact.
  2. 2nd way (easier): \(F=\int x^2\,dy+h(x)=x^2y+h(x)\).
  3. \(F_x=2xy+h'(x)\overset{!}{=}2xy+x\cos x+\sin x\Rightarrow h'(x)=x\cos x+\sin x\).
  4. \(h(x)=\int x\cos x\,dx+\int\sin x\,dx=(x\sin x+\cos x)+(-\cos x)=x\sin x\). (by parts for \(x\cos x\))
\(x^2y+x\sin x=C\).
Exercises 3.2 #5 · p.7Determine a function \(M\) such that \(M(x,y)\,dx+\left(2x^2y-1\right)dy=0\) is exact, and then solve it.
  1. Exactness requires \(M_y=N_x=\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(2x^2y-1)=4xy\).
  2. Integrate in \(y\): \(M=2xy^2+k(x)\), where \(k(x)\) is any function of \(x\) only. (differentiating in \(y\) kills \(k(x)\))
  3. Simplest choice \(k=0\): \(M=2xy^2\).
  4. \(F=\int2xy^2\,dx+g(y)=x^2y^2+g(y)\); \(F_y=2x^2y+g'(y)=2x^2y-1\Rightarrow g(y)=-y\).
\(M=2xy^2\) (more generally \(2xy^2+k(x)\)); solution \(x^2y^2-y=C\).

An exact IVP

Practice (modeled on p.5–6)Solve \(\left(3x^2y+e^y\right)dx+\left(x^3+xe^y-2y\right)dy=0,\ y(0)=1\).
  1. \(M_y=3x^2+e^y\), \(N_x=3x^2+e^y\). Exact.
  2. \(F=\int(3x^2y+e^y)\,dx+g(y)=x^3y+xe^y+g(y)\).
  3. \(F_y=x^3+xe^y+g'(y)=x^3+xe^y-2y\Rightarrow g(y)=-y^2\).
  4. General solution \(x^3y+xe^y-y^2=C\). At \((0,1)\): \(0+0-1=C\).
\(x^3y+xe^y-y^2=-1\).

In one minute

  • Exact means \(M\,dx+N\,dy=dF\) for some \(F\); then the solution is \(F(x,y)=C\).
  • Test (Theorem 2): \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\). Always write both partial derivatives and the verdict.
  • 1st way: \(F=\int M\,dx+g(y)\), then \(F_y=N\) gives \(g'(y)\).
  • 2nd way: \(F=\int N\,dy+h(x)\), then \(F_x=M\) gives \(h'(x)\).
  • \(g'(y)\) may contain only \(y\); if an \(x\) is left, something is wrong.
  • For an IVP, plug \((x_0,y_0)\) into \(F(x,y)=C\) to get \(C\).

chapters.title: Integrating factors
chapters.lead: When an equation fails the exactness test, you can often repair it by multiplying by a well-chosen \(\mu(x)\) or \(\mu(y)\). This chapter shows how to decide which one, how to compute it, and how to finish. It is exactly midterm Question 2.
chapters.html:
The idea

If \(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\) is not exact, it is sometimes possible to make it exact by multiplying the whole equation by a non-zero function (p.10).

✓
Definition 13, Week 2-2.pdf p.10
A non-zero function \(\mu=\mu(x,y)\) is called an integrating factor for \(M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0\) if the differential equation \[ \mu(x,y)M(x,y)\,dx+\mu(x,y)N(x,y)\,dy=0 \] is exact.

Applying the exactness test to \(\mu M\) and \(\mu N\) gives a condition on \(\mu\):

✓
Theorem 3, p.11
\(\mu=\mu(x,y)\) is an integrating factor for \(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\) if and only if it is a solution of the partial differential equation \[ N\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial x}-M\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial y}=\mu\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right).\qquad(\ast) \]

Solving a PDE is usually no easier than the original problem. So we only look for the two special kinds \(\mu=\mu(x)\) and \(\mu=\mu(y)\).

Where the formulas come from

If \(\mu\) depends only on \(x\) (handwritten, p.11–12): then \(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial x}=\frac{d\mu}{dx}\) and \(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial y}=0\). From \((\ast)\):

\[ N\frac{d\mu}{dx}=\mu\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right)\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{d\mu}{dx}=\mu\cdot\underbrace{\frac1N\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right)}_{\text{must depend only on }x,\ =f(x)} \]

This is a separable equation for \(\mu\): \(\int\frac{d\mu}{\mu}=\int f(x)dx\), so \(\ln|\mu|=\int f(x)dx\) and \(\mu=\mp e^{\int f(x)dx}\). Since we need only one integrating factor, take \(\mu(x)=e^{\int f(x)dx}\).

If \(\mu\) depends only on \(y\): now \(\frac{\partial\mu}{\partial x}=0\), and \((\ast)\) becomes \(-M\frac{d\mu}{dy}=\mu\left(M_y-N_x\right)\). Notice the minus sign in front of \(M\). It carries into the formula:

\[ \frac{d\mu}{dy}=-\mu\cdot\underbrace{\frac1M\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right)}_{=g(y)}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu(y)=e^{-\int g(y)\,dy}. \]

Theorem 4: the two cases

✓
Theorem 4, p.13–14 (learn exactly as written)
Consider \(M(x,y)dx+N(x,y)dy=0\).
Case 1. There exists an integrating factor that depends only on \(x\) if and only if \[ \frac1N\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right)=f(x). \] Then an integrating factor is \(\displaystyle\mu(x)=\exp\left\{\int^x f(\eta)\,d\eta\right\}\).
Case 2. There exists an integrating factor that depends only on \(y\) if and only if \[ \frac1M\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right)=g(y). \] Then an integrating factor is \(\displaystyle\mu(y)=\exp\left\{-\int^y g(\zeta)\,d\zeta\right\}\).
!
The minus sign in Case 2
The lecturer marked it with a red "!" on p.14. With the slide's \(g(y)=\frac1M(M_y-N_x)\), the factor is \(e^{\boldsymbol{-}\int g}\). Forgetting the minus gives \(1/\mu\) instead of \(\mu\) (e.g. \(y^{-5}\) instead of \(y^{5}\)), and the new equation is not exact. Quick self-check: after multiplying, test \(\tilde M_y=\tilde N_x\) again.
→
How to decide (the lecturer's order)
  1. Label \(M\) and \(N\). Compute \(M_y\) and \(N_x\). If they differ, write "Not exact".
  2. Compute the difference \(M_y-N_x\) and simplify/factor it.
  3. Divide by \(N\). Only \(x\) left? Then Case 1, \(\mu(x)=e^{\int f}\).
  4. Otherwise divide by \(M\). Only \(y\) left? Then Case 2, \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int g}\).
  5. Multiply the equation by \(\mu\), rename \(\tilde M=\mu M\), \(\tilde N=\mu N\), and check \(\tilde M_y=\tilde N_x\).
  6. Solve the exact equation as in Chapter 5: \(F=\int\tilde M\,dx+g(y)\), \(F_y=\tilde N\). Answer \(F(x,y)=C\).
★
Factor the difference first
Factor \(M_y-N_x\) and compare it with \(N\) and \(M\). In Example 13, \(M_y-N_x=-2(xy-1)\) and \(N=x(xy-1)\): the bracket \((xy-1)\) cancels and only \(-\frac2x\) remains.

Example 13: μ(x)

Example 13 · p.15–18 (handwritten)Solve \((2x^2+y)\,dx+x(xy-1)\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M=2x^2+y\), \(N=x(xy-1)=x^2y-x\).
  2. \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=1\neq\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=2xy-1\). Not exact.
  3. \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=1-2xy+1=-2(xy-1)\).
  4. \(\frac1M(\ldots)=\frac{-2(xy-1)}{2x^2+y}\): not a function of \(y\) alone. \(\ \frac1N(\ldots)=\frac{-2(xy-1)}{x(xy-1)}=-\frac2x=f(x)\). ✓
  5. \(\mu(x)=e^{\int f(x)dx}=e^{-\int\frac2xdx}=e^{-2\ln|x|}=\frac{1}{x^2}\).
  6. Multiply: \(\left(2+\frac{y}{x^2}\right)dx+\left(y-\frac1x\right)dy=0\). Now \(\tilde M_y=\frac1{x^2}=\tilde N_x\). Exact.
  7. \(F=\int\left(2+\frac{y}{x^2}\right)dx+g(y)=2x-\frac yx+g(y)\).
  8. \(F_y=-\frac1x+g'(y)=y-\frac1x\Rightarrow g'(y)=y\Rightarrow g(y)=\frac12y^2+c_1\).
\(2x-\frac yx+\frac12y^2=C\), \(C\) arbitrary constant.

Example 14: μ = xmyn

Sometimes neither case works, and the problem gives you the shape of \(\mu\). Then multiply, apply the exactness test, and compare coefficients of matching powers.

Example 14 · p.15, 18–19 (handwritten)Determine the integrating factor of the form \(\mu(x,y)=x^my^n\) for \(y(3x-2y^2)\,dx+x(3x-5y^2)\,dy=0\), and solve.
  1. \(M=3xy-2y^3\), \(N=3x^2-5xy^2\). \(M_y=3x-6y^2\neq N_x=6x-5y^2\). Not exact.
  2. Multiply by \(x^my^n\): \(\tilde M=3x^{m+1}y^{n+1}-2x^my^{n+3}\), \(\tilde N=3x^{m+2}y^n-5x^{m+1}y^{n+2}\).
  3. \(\tilde M_y=3(n+1)x^{m+1}y^n-2(n+3)x^my^{n+2}\).
  4. \(\tilde N_x=3(m+2)x^{m+1}y^n-5(m+1)x^my^{n+2}\).
  5. Match the coefficients of \(x^{m+1}y^n\) and of \(x^my^{n+2}\): \(3(n+1)=3(m+2)\) and \(-2(n+3)=-5(m+1)\).
  6. So \(n-m=1\) and \(-2n+5m=1\). Then \(3m=3\): \(m=1\), \(n=2\). \(\mu=xy^2\).
  7. Now solve: \(\left(3x^2y^3-2xy^5\right)dx+\left(3x^3y^2-5x^2y^4\right)dy=0\) (check: \(\tilde M_y=9x^2y^2-10xy^4=\tilde N_x\)).
  8. \(F=\int(3x^2y^3-2xy^5)\,dx+g(y)=x^3y^3-x^2y^5+g(y)\); \(F_y=3x^3y^2-5x^2y^4+g'(y)\Rightarrow g'=0\).
\(\mu=xy^2\); general solution \(x^3y^3-x^2y^5=C\).

Exercises 3.3 (p.20), solved

Exercises 3.3 #1 · p.20Solve \((x+y-1)y\,dx+(x+2y-2)\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M=xy+y^2-y\), \(N=x+2y-2\). \(M_y=x+2y-1\), \(N_x=1\). Not exact.
  2. \(M_y-N_x=x+2y-2=N\). So \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)=1=f(x)\). (a constant counts as a function of \(x\) only)
  3. \(\mu(x)=e^{\int1\,dx}=e^x\).
  4. \(\tilde M=e^x(xy+y^2-y)\), \(\tilde N=e^x(x+2y-2)\); \(\tilde M_y=e^x(x+2y-1)=\tilde N_x\). ✓
  5. Easier from \(\tilde N\): \(F=\int e^x(x+2y-2)\,dy+h(x)=e^x(xy+y^2-2y)+h(x)\).
  6. \(F_x=e^x(xy+y^2-2y)+e^xy+h'(x)=e^x(xy+y^2-y)+h'(x)\overset{!}{=}\tilde M\Rightarrow h'=0\).
\(e^x\left(xy+y^2-2y\right)=C\).
Exercises 3.3 #2 · p.20Solve \(3xy\,dx+(9x^2+4y)\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M=3xy\), \(N=9x^2+4y\). \(M_y=3x\neq N_x=18x\). Not exact.
  2. \(M_y-N_x=-15x\). \(\frac1N(\ldots)=\frac{-15x}{9x^2+4y}\): contains \(y\), so no Case 1.
  3. \(\frac1M(\ldots)=\frac{-15x}{3xy}=-\frac5y=g(y)\). Case 2.
  4. \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int g(y)dy}=e^{\int\frac5ydy}=e^{5\ln|y|}=y^5\). (minus times minus)
  5. \(\tilde M=3xy^6\), \(\tilde N=9x^2y^5+4y^6\); \(\tilde M_y=18xy^5=\tilde N_x\). ✓
  6. \(F=\int3xy^6\,dx+g(y)=\frac32x^2y^6+g(y)\); \(F_y=9x^2y^5+g'(y)=9x^2y^5+4y^6\Rightarrow g=\frac47y^7\).
\(\frac32x^2y^6+\frac47y^7=C\).
Exercises 3.3 #3 · p.20Find \(m,n\) such that \(\mu=x^my^n\) is an integrating factor for \(y^2\,dx+x(x+y)\,dy=0\), and then solve it.
  1. \(\tilde M=x^my^{n+2}\), \(\tilde N=x^{m+2}y^n+x^{m+1}y^{n+1}\).
  2. \(\tilde M_y=(n+2)x^my^{n+1}\); \(\tilde N_x=(m+2)x^{m+1}y^n+(m+1)x^my^{n+1}\).
  3. \(\tilde M_y\) has no \(x^{m+1}y^n\) term, so \(m+2=0\). Matching \(x^my^{n+1}\): \(n+2=m+1\).
  4. \(m=-2\), \(n=-3\): \(\mu=x^{-2}y^{-3}\).
  5. Equation: \(\frac{1}{x^2y}dx+\left(\frac1{y^3}+\frac{1}{xy^2}\right)dy=0\).
  6. \(F=\int\frac{1}{x^2y}dx+g(y)=-\frac{1}{xy}+g(y)\); \(F_y=\frac{1}{xy^2}+g'(y)=\frac1{y^3}+\frac1{xy^2}\Rightarrow g=-\frac{1}{2y^2}\).
\(\mu=x^{-2}y^{-3}\); \(-\frac{1}{xy}-\frac{1}{2y^2}=C\).
Exercises 3.3 #4 · p.20–21 (handwritten)Use an integrating factor of the form \(\mu=\mu(xy)\) to find the general solution of \(y\,dx+x(1+x^2y^3)\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M=y\), \(N=x+x^3y^3\). \(M_y=1\neq N_x=1+3x^2y^3\). Not exact.
  2. Try \(\mu=(xy)^n\): \(\tilde M=x^ny^{n+1}\), \(\tilde N=x^{n+1}y^n+x^{n+3}y^{n+3}\).
  3. \(\tilde M_y=(n+1)x^ny^n\); \(\tilde N_x=(n+1)x^ny^n+(n+3)x^{n+2}y^{n+3}\).
  4. Equal iff \(n+3=0\): \(n=-3\), \(\mu=(xy)^{-3}\). Then the obtained equation is exact.
  5. Equation: \(x^{-3}y^{-2}dx+\left(x^{-2}y^{-3}+1\right)dy=0\).
  6. \(F=\int x^{-3}y^{-2}dx+g(y)=-\frac{1}{2x^2y^2}+g(y)\); \(F_y=\frac{1}{x^2y^3}+g'(y)=\frac{1}{x^2y^3}+1\Rightarrow g=y\).
\(\mu=(xy)^{-3}\); \(y-\frac{1}{2x^2y^2}=C\). (The slide stops at "Solve it!"; this is the finish.)
i
Note
When you multiply by something like \(\frac1{x^2}\) or \((xy)^{-3}\), the new equation is not defined on \(x=0\) or \(y=0\). The answers above are valid where \(\mu\) is defined and non-zero. The lecturer does not discuss these lines for integrating-factor problems.

Midterm-style: μ(y) with trig

Practice (modeled on 2023 midterm Q2)Find the general solution of \((2x-\cot y)\,dx+(x^2\cot y+x)\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M=2x-\cot y\), \(N=x^2\cot y+x\). \(M_y=\csc^2y\), \(N_x=2x\cot y+1\). Not exact.
  2. \(M_y-N_x=\csc^2y-1-2x\cot y=\cot^2y-2x\cot y=-\cot y\,(2x-\cot y)\). (\(\csc^2y-1=\cot^2y\))
  3. \(\frac1M(\ldots)=-\cot y=g(y)\). Case 2.
  4. \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int g}=e^{\int\cot y\,dy}=e^{\ln|\sin y|}=\sin y\).
  5. Multiply: \((2x\sin y-\cos y)\,dx+(x^2\cos y+x\sin y)\,dy=0\). \(\tilde M_y=2x\cos y+\sin y=\tilde N_x\). ✓
  6. \(F=\int(2x\sin y-\cos y)\,dx+g(y)=x^2\sin y-x\cos y+g(y)\); \(F_y=x^2\cos y+x\sin y+g'(y)\Rightarrow g'=0\).
\(x^2\sin y-x\cos y=C\).

In one minute

  • Integrating factor \(\mu\neq0\): multiplying by it makes \(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\) exact.
  • Compute \(M_y-N_x\), factor it, then divide by \(N\) and by \(M\).
  • \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)=f(x)\) gives \(\mu(x)=e^{\int f(x)dx}\).
  • \(\frac1M(M_y-N_x)=g(y)\) gives \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int g(y)dy}\) (note the minus).
  • Given a shape \(x^my^n\) or \((xy)^n\): multiply, test exactness, match coefficients.
  • After multiplying, re-check \(\tilde M_y=\tilde N_x\), then build \(F\) and write \(F=C\).
  • \(e^{-2\ln|x|}=1/x^2\), \(e^{5\ln|y|}=y^5\), \(e^{\ln|\sin y|}=\sin y\): simplify \(e^{\ln}\).

chapters.title: First-order linear equations
chapters.lead: The most reliable recipe of the course: put the equation in standard form, multiply by \(\mu=e^{\int p}\), and the left side becomes one derivative. You will also see when to swap the roles of x and y.
chapters.html:
Standard form

A linear equation of order \(n=1\) (Definition 3 with \(n=1\)) is \(a_0(x)y'(x)+a_1(x)y(x)=f(x)\). Dividing by \(a_0(x)\) (where \(a_0(x)\neq0\)) gives the form we always use (handwritten, p.22):

\[ y'+\underbrace{\frac{a_1(x)}{a_0(x)}}_{p(x)}\,y=\underbrace{\frac{f(x)}{a_0(x)}}_{q(x)}. \]
✓
Definition 14 (Linear Differential Equation), Week 2-2.pdf p.22
A first-order ordinary differential equation is linear in the dependent variable \(y\) and the independent variable \(x\) if it can be written in the form \[ \frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x). \]
!
Standard form first
The coefficient of \(y'\) must be exactly 1 before you read off \(p(x)\). For \(xy'-3y=x^2\), divide by \(x\): \(y'-\frac3xy=x\), so \(p(x)=-\frac3x\) (not \(-3\)), and the work is valid only on an interval with \(x\neq0\). Also keep the sign: in \(y'-\tan(x)y=\sec x\), \(p(x)=-\tan x\).

Theorem 5 and why it works

✓
Theorem 5, p.23
The linear differential equation \(\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x)\) has an integrating factor \[ \mu(x):=\exp\left\{\int^xp(\eta)\,d\eta\right\}. \] A one-parameter family of solutions for this equation is \[ y:=\frac{1}{\mu(x)}\left[\int^x\mu(\eta)q(\eta)\,d\eta+c\right]. \] Furthermore, this one-parameter family of solutions includes all solutions.

Why (handwritten, p.24): multiply \(y'+p(x)y=q(x)\) by \(\mu=e^{\int p(x)dx}\):

\[ e^{\int p\,dx}\,y'+p(x)e^{\int p\,dx}\,y=e^{\int p\,dx}\,q(x). \]

By the product rule, \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{\int p\,dx}\,y\right)=e^{\int p\,dx}\,p(x)\,y+e^{\int p\,dx}\,y'\). That is exactly the left side! So the equation is

\[ \frac{d}{dx}\big(\mu(x)\,y\big)=\mu(x)\,q(x). \]

Integrate both sides with respect to \(x\):

\[ \mu(x)\,y=\int\mu(x)q(x)\,dx+C\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad y(x)=e^{-\int p(x)dx}\left(\int e^{\int p(x)dx}q(x)\,dx+C\right) \]
General solution, C arbitrary constant (p.24–25)
→
The recipe in 5 lines
  1. Standard form \(y'+p(x)y=q(x)\); name \(p\) and \(q\); say "1st order linear diff. eqn."
  2. \(\mu(x)=e^{\int p(x)dx}\) (no constant needed; simplify \(e^{\ln}\)).
  3. Write \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(\mu y\right)=\mu q\).
  4. Integrate: \(\mu y=\int\mu q\,dx+C\). Do not forget \(C\).
  5. Divide by \(\mu\). For an IVP, now plug in \(x_0, y_0\).
!
Where the constant goes
Add \(C\) before dividing by \(\mu\). Then \(C\) gets multiplied by \(e^{-\int p}\): \(y=\ldots+Ce^{-\int p}\). Writing \(y=\frac1\mu\int\mu q\,dx\ +C\) is wrong.

Note that the linear method is the integrating-factor idea of Chapter 6: written as \((py-q)\,dx+dy=0\), we have \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)=p(x)\), so Case 1 gives \(\mu=e^{\int p}\).

Example 15 (an IVP)

Example 15 · p.25–27 (handwritten)Solve the initial value problem \(\frac{dy}{dx}+xy=xe^{x^2/2},\ y(0)=1\).
  1. \(p(x)=x\), \(q(x)=xe^{x^2/2}\). 1st order linear diff. eqn.
  2. \(\mu(x)=e^{\int p(x)dx}=e^{\int x\,dx}=e^{x^2/2}\).
  3. Multiply both sides: \(e^{x^2/2}y'+xe^{x^2/2}y=xe^{x^2}\). The left side is \(\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{x^2/2}y\right)\).
  4. Integrate: \(e^{x^2/2}y=\int xe^{x^2}dx\). Put \(u=x^2\), \(du=2x\,dx\): \(=\frac12\int e^u\,du=\frac12e^{x^2}+C\).
  5. Divide: \(y(x)=\frac12e^{x^2/2}+Ce^{-x^2/2}\).
  6. \(y(0)=\frac12e^0+Ce^0=1\Rightarrow C=\frac12\).
\(y(x)=\frac12e^{x^2/2}+\frac12e^{-x^2/2}\), for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).

Domain caveats

Theorem 5 (and Exercise 2 #1 in Chapter 3) needs \(p\) and \(q\) continuous on an interval \(I\). The solution lives on that interval. So:

  • If you divided by \(a_0(x)\), exclude its zeros (\(xy'+\ldots\) means \(x\neq0\): work on \(x\gt0\) or \(x\lt0\)).
  • \(\tan x\), \(\sec x\) need \(x\neq\frac\pi2+k\pi\): work on e.g. \(-\frac\pi2\lt x\lt\frac\pi2\).
  • \(\cot x\), \(\csc x\) need \(x\neq k\pi\): work on e.g. \(0\lt x\lt\pi\).
  • \(e^{\int p}\) often produces \(|x|\) or \(|\cos x|\). On an interval where the inside has a fixed sign, you may drop the absolute value (any non-zero constant multiple of \(\mu\) also works).

Exercises 4 (p.28), solved

Exercises 4 #1 · p.28Find the general solution of \(y'+3y=x\).
  1. \(p=3\), \(q=x\). \(\mu=e^{\int3\,dx}=e^{3x}\).
  2. \(\left(e^{3x}y\right)'=xe^{3x}\).
  3. \(\int xe^{3x}dx=\frac{x}{3}e^{3x}-\frac19e^{3x}\). (by parts: \(u=x\), \(dv=e^{3x}dx\))
  4. \(e^{3x}y=\frac x3e^{3x}-\frac19e^{3x}+C\).
\(y=\frac x3-\frac19+Ce^{-3x}\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).
Exercises 4 #2 · p.28Find the general solution of \(y'-\tan(x)y=\sec(x)\).
  1. \(p=-\tan x\), \(q=\sec x\); both continuous on \(-\frac\pi2\lt x\lt\frac\pi2\).
  2. \(\mu=e^{-\int\tan x\,dx}=e^{\ln|\cos x|}=\cos x\). (\(\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln|\cos x|\); \(\cos x\gt0\) there)
  3. \((y\cos x)'=\cos x\sec x=1\).
  4. \(y\cos x=x+C\).
\(y=(x+C)\sec x\) on \(-\frac\pi2\lt x\lt\frac\pi2\).
Exercises 4 #3 · p.28Solve \(y'+e^xy=e^x\).
  1. \(p=e^x\), \(q=e^x\). \(\mu=e^{\int e^xdx}=e^{e^x}\).
  2. \(\left(e^{e^x}y\right)'=e^xe^{e^x}\).
  3. \(\int e^xe^{e^x}dx=e^{e^x}\). (\(u=e^x\), \(du=e^xdx\))
  4. \(e^{e^x}y=e^{e^x}+C\).
\(y=1+Ce^{-e^x}\), \(x\in\mathbb{R}\). (The equation is also separable: \(y'=e^x(1-y)\).)
Exercises 4 #4 · p.28Solve \(y'+\cot(x)y=x\).
  1. \(p=\cot x\), continuous on \(0\lt x\lt\pi\). \(\mu=e^{\int\cot x\,dx}=e^{\ln|\sin x|}=\sin x\).
  2. \((y\sin x)'=x\sin x\).
  3. \(\int x\sin x\,dx=-x\cos x+\sin x\). (by parts)
  4. \(y\sin x=\sin x-x\cos x+C\).
\(y=1-x\cot x+C\csc x\) on \(0\lt x\lt\pi\).
Exercises 4 #5 · p.28Depending on the values of \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac\alpha xy=\beta\), where \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\).
  1. \(p=\frac\alpha x\), \(q=\beta\); work on \(x\gt0\). \(\mu=e^{\alpha\ln x}=x^\alpha\).
  2. \(\left(x^\alpha y\right)'=\beta x^\alpha\).
  3. Case \(\alpha\neq-1\): \(\int\beta x^\alpha dx=\frac{\beta x^{\alpha+1}}{\alpha+1}\). So \(x^\alpha y=\frac{\beta x^{\alpha+1}}{\alpha+1}+C\).
  4. Case \(\alpha=-1\): \(\int\beta x^{-1}dx=\beta\ln x\). So \(x^{-1}y=\beta\ln x+C\). (the power rule fails for exponent \(-1\))
\(\alpha\neq-1\): \(y=\frac{\beta}{\alpha+1}x+Cx^{-\alpha}\). \(\ \alpha=-1\): \(y=\beta x\ln x+Cx\). (\(x\gt0\))
Exercises 4 #6 · p.28 (handwritten start)Obtain the general solution of \(y^2\,dx+(3xy-1)\,dy=0\).
  1. As \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^2}{1-3xy}\) it is not linear in \(y\). Flip it: for \(y\neq0\), \(\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1-3xy}{y^2}=\frac1{y^2}-\frac3yx\).
  2. So \(\frac{dx}{dy}+\frac3y\,x=\frac1{y^2}\): linear in \(x\) (the unknown is now \(x(y)\)), with \(p(y)=\frac3y\), \(q(y)=\frac1{y^2}\).
  3. \(\mu(y)=e^{\int\frac3ydy}=e^{3\ln|y|}=y^3\) (on \(y\gt0\); \(-y^3\) works the same on \(y\lt0\)).
  4. \(\frac{d}{dy}\left(y^3x\right)=y^3\cdot\frac1{y^2}=y\Rightarrow y^3x=\frac{y^2}2+C\).
\(x=\frac{1}{2y}+\frac{C}{y^3}\), i.e. \(xy^3-\frac{y^2}{2}=C\). (Also \(y\equiv0\) satisfies the differential form: \(dy=0\) and \(y^2=0\).)
★
When to flip x and y
If the equation is not linear in \(y\) but \(x\) appears only to the first power (as in \(3xy\) above), solve for \(\frac{dx}{dy}\) instead and treat \(x\) as the unknown.

In one minute

  • Linear 1st order: \(y'+p(x)y=q(x)\). Get the coefficient of \(y'\) to be 1 first.
  • \(\mu(x)=e^{\int p(x)dx}\); then \(\frac{d}{dx}(\mu y)=\mu q\).
  • \(y=\frac1\mu\left(\int\mu q\,dx+C\right)\); the \(C\) goes inside the bracket.
  • Theorem 5: this family contains all solutions, so there are no singular solutions.
  • Domain: \(p,q\) continuous on \(I\); avoid zeros of the leading coefficient, \(\tan/\sec\) at \(\frac\pi2+k\pi\), \(\cot/\csc\) at \(k\pi\).
  • Typical \(\mu\): \(p=\frac ax\Rightarrow x^a\); \(p=-\tan x\Rightarrow\cos x\); \(p=\cot x\Rightarrow\sin x\); \(p=\text{const }k\Rightarrow e^{kx}\).
  • Not linear in \(y\)? Try linear in \(x\): \(\frac{dx}{dy}+p(y)x=q(y)\).

chapters.title: Bernoulli equations
chapters.lead: A Bernoulli equation is a linear equation spoiled by one power of y. After this chapter you can spot it, kill the power with u = y^(1−n), solve the linear equation, and remember the solution y = 0 that the substitution hides.
chapters.html:
The idea in one picture

A linear equation \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)\) is easy (integrating factor). A Bernoulli equation looks almost the same, but the right side has an extra factor \(y^n\):

\[ \frac{dy}{dx} + p(x)\,y = q(x)\,y^{n} \]
Definition 15 — Bernoulli equation (Week+3.pdf p.1)

That single \(y^n\) makes it nonlinear. The trick: divide by \(y^n\), and notice that what is left is the derivative of a new unknown \(u = y^{1-n}\). In terms of \(u\) the equation is linear again.

The two easy cases (p.2)

  • \(n = 0\): \(y^0 = 1\), so \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)\) — already linear.
  • \(n = 1\): \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)y\), i.e. \(y' + \big(p(x)-q(x)\big)y = 0\) — linear (and also separable: \(\frac{dy}{dx} = -\tilde p(x)\,y\)).

So the real Bernoulli work is for \(n\neq 0\) and \(n\neq 1\).

The substitution \(u = y^{1-n}\)

\[ u := y^{1-n}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{du}{dx} = (1-n)\,y^{-n}\,\frac{dy}{dx}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{1}{y^n}\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{1-n}\frac{du}{dx} \]
Theorem 6 (p.3): for n other than 0 and 1 this substitution makes Bernoulli linear

Here is the lecturer's derivation (p.4), step by step.

  1. First check \(y = 0\): then \(y' = 0\) and the equation reads \(0 + p\cdot0 = q\cdot 0\). — true. So \(y=0\) is a solution (when \(n \gt 0\)).
  2. For \(y\neq0\), divide everything by \(y^n\): \(\dfrac{1}{y^n}\dfrac{dy}{dx} + p(x)\,y^{1-n} = q(x)\) (\(\frac{1}{y^n}\,p\,y = p\,y^{1-n}\)).
  3. Replace \(\dfrac{1}{y^n}\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) by \(\dfrac{1}{1-n}\dfrac{du}{dx}\) and \(y^{1-n}\) by \(u\): \(\dfrac{1}{1-n}\dfrac{du}{dx} + p(x)\,u = q(x)\).
  4. Multiply by \((1-n)\):
\[ \frac{du}{dx} + \underbrace{(1-n)p(x)}_{\tilde p(x)}\,u = \underbrace{(1-n)q(x)}_{\tilde q(x)} \]
The linear equation you always get
i
Letters
The slides call the new unknown \(u\) (Theorem 6: \(u := y^{1-n}\)). Some books and teachers write \(v = y^{1-n}\) — it is the same thing. This guide follows the slides and uses \(u\).
★
Practical version: multiply instead of divide
In the worked examples the lecturer does not divide and then multiply; he multiplies the whole equation once by \((1-n)y^{-n}\) (for \(n=2\): by \(-\frac{1}{y^2}\); for \(n=3\): by \(-\frac{2}{y^3}\)). Then the first term is exactly \(\frac{du}{dx}\) and the second is a multiple of \(u\). Fewer steps, fewer sign errors.

The recipe

  1. Bring the equation to the form \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)y^n\). Read off \(p\), \(q\), \(n\).
  2. Note that \(y = 0\) is a solution if \(n \gt 0\).
  3. Set \(u = y^{1-n}\), \(u' = (1-n)y^{-n}y'\). Multiply the equation by \((1-n)y^{-n}\).
  4. Solve the linear equation \(u' + (1-n)p\,u = (1-n)q\) with \(\mu = e^{\int (1-n)p\,dx}\).
  5. Back-substitute \(u = y^{1-n}\) and state the general solution (plus \(y=0\)).

Example 16 — an initial value problem

Example 16 · Week+3.pdf p.3, solved p.5–7Solve \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \tan(x)\,y = \dfrac{4\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\,y^2\), \(y(0) = 1\).
  1. Identify: \(p(x) = \tan x\), \(q(x) = \dfrac{4\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\), \(n = 2\).
  2. \(u = y^{1-2} = \dfrac1y\), so \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = -\dfrac{1}{y^2}\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).
  3. For \(y\neq0\), multiply the equation by \(-\dfrac{1}{y^2}\): \(\;-\dfrac{1}{y^2}\dfrac{dy}{dx} - \tan x\cdot\dfrac1y = -\dfrac{4\sin x}{\cos^2x}\).
  4. Recognise \(u\): \(\dfrac{du}{dx} - \tan x\;u = -\dfrac{4\sin x}{\cos^2 x}\) (linear in \(u\)).
  5. Integrating factor: \(\mu(x) = e^{-\int\tan x\,dx} = e^{-\int\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}dx}\). With \(z = \cos x\), \(dz = -\sin x\,dx\): \(\mu = e^{\int \frac{dz}{z}} = e^{\ln z} = \cos x\).
  6. Multiply: \(\cos x\,\dfrac{du}{dx} - \sin x\;u = -4\tan x\), and the left side is \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(u\cos x)\).
  7. Integrate: \(u\cos x = -\int 4\tan x\,dx = 4\ln|\cos x| + C\).
  8. So \(\dfrac{1}{y} = u = \dfrac{4\ln|\cos x| + C}{\cos x}\), i.e. \(y = \dfrac{\cos x}{\ln\cos^4 x + C}\) (\(4\ln|\cos x| = \ln\cos^4x\)).
  9. Initial condition: \(y(0) = \dfrac{\cos 0}{\ln 1 + C} = \dfrac{1}{0 + C} = 1\Rightarrow C = 1\).
General solution \(y(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{\ln\cos^4 x + C}\) (and \(y=0\)); solution of the IVP: \(y(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{\ln\cos^4 x + 1}\).
i
The slide and the handwriting differ
The printed slide (p.3) says the right side is \(4\sin(x)\,y^2\); the handwritten solution (p.5) uses \(\dfrac{4\sin x}{\cos^2x}\,y^2\). The solution above follows the handwriting. With the printed version the same steps give \((u\cos x)' = -4\sin x\cos x\), \(u\cos x = 2\cos^2x + C\), \(y = \dfrac{\cos x}{2\cos^2 x + C}\) and, with \(y(0)=1\), \(C=-1\): \(y = \dfrac{\cos x}{2\cos^2x - 1} = \dfrac{\cos x}{\cos 2x}\). Both are checked with sympy.

Exercise 5.2 — \(n = 3\)

Exercise 5.2 · Week+3.pdf p.11, solved p.14–15Find the general solution of \(y' + \dfrac{1}{2(x+1)}\,y = (1-x^2)\,y^3\).
  1. \(p(x) = \dfrac{1}{2(x+1)}\), \(q(x) = 1-x^2\), \(n = 3\).
  2. \(u = y^{1-3} = y^{-2}\), \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = -2y^{-3}\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).
  3. Multiply by \(-\dfrac{2}{y^3}\): \(\;-\dfrac{2}{y^3}\dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{1}{x+1}\cdot\dfrac{1}{y^2} = -2(1-x^2)\).
  4. So \(\dfrac{du}{dx} - \dfrac{1}{x+1}\,u = -2(1-x)(1+x)\) (linear).
  5. \(\mu(x) = e^{-\int\frac{dx}{x+1}} = e^{-\ln(x+1)} = \dfrac{1}{x+1}\).
  6. \(\dfrac{1}{x+1}\dfrac{du}{dx} - \dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}u = -2(1-x)\), i.e. \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(\dfrac{u}{x+1}\Big) = 2(x-1)\) (the factor \(1+x\) cancels).
  7. Integrate: \(\dfrac{u}{x+1} = x^2 - 2x + C\), so \(u = (x+1)(x^2-2x+C)\).
\(\dfrac{1}{y^2} = (x+1)(x^2-2x+C)\), \(C\) arbitrary; plus the solution \(y = 0\).

Exercise 5.5 — when \(x\) is the Bernoulli variable

Sometimes the equation is not Bernoulli in \(y(x)\), but it is Bernoulli if you treat \(x\) as a function of \(y\). Flip the derivative: \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} = 1\Big/\dfrac{dy}{dx}\).

Exercise 5.5 · Week+3.pdf p.11–13Obtain the general solution of \(x\,y' = \dfrac{e^{y^2}}{y\,e^{y^2} - x^2}\).
  1. Flip (for \(x\neq0\); note \(x = 0\) is not a solution): \(\dfrac{1}{x}\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{y e^{y^2} - x^2}{e^{y^2}} = y - e^{-y^2}x^2\).
  2. Multiply by \(x\): \(\dfrac{dx}{dy} - y\,x = -e^{-y^2}x^3\). This is Bernoulli in \(x(y)\) with \(p(y) = -y\), \(q(y) = -e^{-y^2}\), \(n = 3\).
  3. \(u = x^{1-3} = x^{-2}\), \(\dfrac{du}{dy} = -2x^{-3}\dfrac{dx}{dy}\). Multiply by \(-2x^{-3}\): \(-2x^{-3}\dfrac{dx}{dy} + 2y\,x^{-2} = 2e^{-y^2}\).
  4. So \(\dfrac{du}{dy} + 2y\,u = 2e^{-y^2}\) (linear in \(u(y)\)).
  5. \(\mu(y) = e^{\int 2y\,dy} = e^{y^2}\); then \(\dfrac{d}{dy}\big(e^{y^2}u\big) = 2\).
  6. \(e^{y^2}u = 2y + C\), \(u = 2ye^{-y^2} + Ce^{-y^2}\).
\(\dfrac{1}{x^2} = 2y\,e^{-y^2} + C e^{-y^2}\), \(C\) arbitrary.

Try it yourself (homework Exercises 5, p.11)

Same recipe each time; answers checked with sympy.

Equation\(n\), \(u\)Linear equationGeneral solution
5.1 \(y' + \frac1x y = (1-x^2)y^2\)\(2,\ y^{-1}\)\(u' - \frac1x u = x^2-1\)\(\frac1y = x\big(\frac{x^2}{2} - \ln|x| + C\big)\)
5.3 \(y' + \tan(x)\,y = y^2\)\(2,\ y^{-1}\)\(u' - \tan x\,u = -1\)\(y = \dfrac{\cos x}{C - \sin x}\)
5.4 \(y' + \cot(x)\,y = \cos(x)\,y^3\)\(3,\ y^{-2}\)\(u' - 2\cot x\,u = -2\cos x\)\(\frac{1}{y^2} = 2\sin x + C\sin^2 x\)

In every case \(y = 0\) is an extra solution.

A substitution that creates a Bernoulli equation

Exam question 3 in 2023 was not written as a Bernoulli equation. A substitution turned it into one.

✓
Midterm 2023, Q3 pattern
\(e^{y}y' + e^{y} = e^{3y+2x}\). Notice \(e^{3y} = (e^{y})^3\) and \(e^y y' = (e^y)'\). With \(z = e^{y}\), \(z' = e^{y}y'\), the equation becomes \(z' + z = e^{2x}z^3\): Bernoulli with \(n = 3\). Then \(u = z^{-2} = e^{-2y}\), \(u' - 2u = -2e^{2x}\), \(\mu = e^{-2x}\), and the answer is \(e^{-2y} = -2xe^{2x} + Ce^{2x}\). Since \(z = e^{y}\) is never 0, there is no lost solution here.
★
How to spot such a substitution
Look for a function of \(y\) whose derivative (times \(y'\)) is sitting in the equation: \(e^{y}y'\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(z = e^{y}\); \(\cos y\,y'\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(z = \sin y\); \(2y\,y'\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(z = y^2\). After the substitution, the leftover powers of \(z\) tell you \(n\).

Remark 4 and Example 17 — a jump in \(q\)

The last part of the Bernoulli section is about a linear equation (\(n=0\)) whose right side jumps.

i
Remark 4 (p.8)
Sometimes the function \(q\) in the equation may not be continuous but may have a jump discontinuity. In this case the existence theorem does not necessarily guarantee the existence of a unique solution of the IVP.

What we do instead: solve on each side of the jump separately, then choose the constants so that the pieces join continuously.

Example 17 · Week+3.pdf p.8, solved p.9–10Find a continuous solution to \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + y = q(x)\), \(y(0) = 0\), where \(q(x) = 1\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(q(x) = -1\) for \(x \lt 0\).
  1. Linear equation: \(\mu(x) = e^{\int 1\,dx} = e^{x}\). Then \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(e^{x}y) = e^{x}q(x)\), so \(y = e^{-x}\displaystyle\int e^{x}q(x)\,dx + Ce^{-x}\).
  2. For \(x\ge0\), \(q = 1\): \(y = e^{-x}e^{x} + Ce^{-x} = 1 + Ce^{-x}\). From \(y(0) = 1 + C = 0\): \(C = -1\), so \(y = 1 - e^{-x}\).
  3. For \(x \lt 0\), \(q = -1\): \(y = -1 + \tilde Ce^{-x}\) with a new constant \(\tilde C\) (different interval, different constant).
  4. Continuity at 0: \(\lim_{x\to0^+}(1-e^{-x}) = 0\) must equal \(\lim_{x\to0^-}(-1+\tilde Ce^{-x}) = -1 + \tilde C\). So \(\tilde C = 1\).
\(y(x) = \begin{cases} 1 - e^{-x}, & x\ge 0\\ -1 + e^{-x}, & x \lt 0\end{cases}\)

Traps

!
Forgetting y = 0
For \(n \gt 0\), \(y \equiv 0\) solves every Bernoulli equation, but the formula for \(u = y^{1-n}\) can never produce it (you divided by \(y^n\)). In a "find all solutions" question you must write it down. (For \(n \lt 0\), \(y^n\) is undefined at 0, so \(y=0\) is not a solution.)
!
Multiplying only one side by (1−n)
The linear equation is \(u' + (1-n)p\,u = (1-n)q\). Both \(p\) and \(q\) get the factor \((1-n)\). For \(n = 2\) that is a factor \(-1\): \(y' + \tan x\,y = \ldots y^2\) becomes \(u' - \tan x\,u = -\ldots\). Losing this sign changes the integrating factor completely.
!
Stopping at u
The question asks for \(y\). Always finish with \(u = y^{1-n}\) put back, e.g. \(\frac{1}{y^2} = \ldots\) or \(y = \ldots\).
!
Wrong n
Read \(n\) after putting the equation in the form \(y' + py = qy^n\). In Exercise 5.5 the "\(y\)" is actually \(x\) and \(n = 3\) appears only after flipping and multiplying by \(x\).

In one minute

  • Bernoulli: \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)y^n\); \(n = 0,1\) are already linear.
  • Substitute \(u = y^{1-n}\) (slides' letter \(u\)); \(u' = (1-n)y^{-n}y'\).
  • Result: \(u' + (1-n)p\,u = (1-n)q\) — linear; solve with \(\mu = e^{\int(1-n)p\,dx}\).
  • Shortcut: multiply the original equation by \((1-n)y^{-n}\).
  • \(y = 0\) is an extra solution when \(n \gt 0\) — never forget it.
  • If \(x\) appears with a power instead of \(y\), flip to \(\frac{dx}{dy}\) and treat \(x\) as the unknown.
  • Hidden Bernoulli: \(z = e^{y}\), \(z = \sin y\), … (midterm Q3).
  • Jump in \(q\): solve on each side, match the pieces by continuity.

chapters.title: Homogeneous equations (y = ux)
chapters.lead: Some equations only care about the ratio y/x. After this chapter you can test for that, substitute y = ux to get a separable equation, and collect every solution — including the ones lost when you divide.
chapters.src: From Week+3.pdf, pages 16–28, and the quiz in Week+4.pdf, pages 15–19
chapters.html:
The idea

Look at \(y' = \dfrac{y}{x} + \dfrac{x}{y}\). The right side depends on \(x\) and \(y\) only through the ratio \(\frac yx\) (because \(\frac xy = 1/\frac yx\)). Such equations are called homogeneous. If we give the ratio its own name, \(u = \frac yx\), the equation becomes separable.

\[ M(x,y)\,dx + N(x,y)\,dy = 0 \text{ is homogeneous} \iff y' = f(x,y) = g\!\left(\frac yx\right) \]
Definition 16 (Week+3.pdf p.16)
i
Not the same word as later
"Homogeneous" here means "depends only on \(y/x\)". It has nothing to do with "homogeneous linear equation" (right side zero) that you will meet with second-order equations.

Testing for homogeneity

Way 1: write \(f\) as a function of \(y/x\)

Divide numerator and denominator by a suitable power of \(x\) and see whether only \(\frac yx\) remains.

Example 18.1 · Week+3.pdf p.17–18Is \((x^2-y^2)\,dx + 2xy\,dy = 0\) homogeneous?
  1. For \(x,y\neq0\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x^2-y^2}{2xy} = -\dfrac12\Big(\dfrac{x^2}{xy} - \dfrac{y^2}{xy}\Big) = \dfrac12\Big(\dfrac yx - \dfrac xy\Big)\).
  2. \(\dfrac xy = \dfrac{1}{y/x}\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac12\Big(\dfrac yx - \dfrac{1}{y/x}\Big) = g\big(\tfrac yx\big)\).
Yes — it is a homogeneous differential equation.
Example 18.2 · Week+3.pdf p.17, 19 (homework)Is \(\big(x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\big)dx - x\,dy = 0\) homogeneous?
  1. For \(x\neq0\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{x} = 1 + \sqrt{\dfrac{x^2+y^2}{x^2}} = 1 + \sqrt{1 + \big(\tfrac yx\big)^2}\) (for \(x \gt 0\); the slide writes it this way).
