Yes — \(\frac{dy}{dx} = g\big(\frac yx\big)\), homogeneous.

Way 2: homogeneous functions of the same degree

\[ F(\lambda x, \lambda y) = \lambda^{n}F(x,y) \]
Definition 17 (p.17): homogeneous function of degree n

Why this helps (p.20): put \(\lambda = \frac1x\). Then \(M\big(1, \frac yx\big) = \big(\frac1x\big)^n M(x,y)\), i.e.

\[ M(x,y) = x^n M\!\left(1, \tfrac yx\right),\qquad N(x,y) = x^n N\!\left(1, \tfrac yx\right) \]
So in dy/dx = −M/N the common power of x cancels (p.20)
✓
Conclusion 1 (p.21)
If \(M\) and \(N\) in \(M(x,y)dx + N(x,y)dy = 0\) are both homogeneous functions of the same degree \(n\), then the differential equation is a homogeneous differential equation.
★
Quick test
Equivalent and fastest in practice: replace \(x\to\lambda x\), \(y\to\lambda y\) in \(f(x,y) = y'\). If all the \(\lambda\)'s cancel (\(f(\lambda x,\lambda y) = f(x,y)\)), it is homogeneous. Eyeball version: every term in the numerator and denominator has the same total degree. \(\frac{x^2+y^2}{xy}\): all degree 2 — yes. \(\frac{x+y+1}{x}\): the "1" has degree 0 — no.

The substitution \(y = ux\)

\[ y = ux\ \ \Big(u = \frac yx\Big)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{dy}{dx} = u + x\,\frac{du}{dx} \]
Theorem 7 (p.21): homogeneous becomes separable

The derivative comes from the product rule: \(\frac{d}{dx}(u\cdot x) = \frac{du}{dx}\,x + u\cdot 1\). Then \(u + x u' = g(u)\), i.e. \(x\,\frac{du}{dx} = g(u) - u\): the variables separate as \(\dfrac{du}{g(u)-u} = \dfrac{dx}{x}\).

The recipe

  1. Show it is homogeneous (same degree for \(M\) and \(N\), or write \(y' = g(y/x)\)).
  2. Put \(y = ux\), \(y' = u + xu'\). Simplify to \(x\,u' = g(u) - u\).
  3. For \(g(u) - u \neq 0\): separate and integrate. Combine the logs and the constant.
  4. Check the values with \(g(u) - u = 0\): \(u = \text{const}\) gives the straight lines \(y = u_0 x\). Are they in the family? If not, list them.
  5. Back-substitute \(u = y/x\). In differential form, also check \(x = 0\).

Example 19 — the full lecture solution

Example 19 · Week+3.pdf p.21–25Solve \((x^2 - 3y^2)\,dx + 2xy\,dy = 0\).
  1. Test (1st way): \(M = x^2-3y^2\): \(M(\lambda x,\lambda y) = \lambda^2x^2 - 3\lambda^2y^2 = \lambda^2M\), degree 2. \(N = 2xy\): \(N(\lambda x,\lambda y) = 2\lambda x\lambda y = \lambda^2N\), degree 2. Same degree ⇒ homogeneous.
  2. Test (2nd way): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3y^2-x^2}{2xy} = \dfrac32\dfrac yx - \dfrac12\dfrac{1}{y/x} = g\big(\tfrac yx\big)\).
  3. \(y = ux\) (for \(x\neq0\)): \(x\dfrac{du}{dx} + u = \dfrac32u - \dfrac12\dfrac1u\), so \(x\dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac12\Big(u - \dfrac1u\Big) = \dfrac12\,\dfrac{u^2-1}{u}\) (separable).
  4. For \(u\neq\pm1\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{u}{u^2-1}du = \int\frac{dx}{2x}\). With \(z = u^2-1\), \(u\,du = \tfrac12dz\): \(\tfrac12\ln|z| = \tfrac12\ln|x| + \tfrac12\ln|C|\), \(C\neq0\).
  5. \(\ln|z| = \ln|Cx|\Rightarrow z = \pm Cx = Kx\), \(K\neq0\): \(u^2 - 1 = Kx\).
  6. Lost solutions: if \(u = \pm1\), then \(\frac{du}{dx} = 0\) and \(\frac{u^2-1}{u} = 0\): the \(u\)-equation holds. So \(u = \pm1\) are solutions too — they are exactly \(K = 0\). Hence \(u^2 - 1 = Dx\), \(D\in\mathbb R\).
  7. Back to \(y\): \(\dfrac{y^2}{x^2} - 1 = Dx\), i.e. \(y^2 = x^2 + Dx^3\).
  8. \(x = 0\): then \(dx = 0\) and the term \(2xy\,dy\) is 0 too, so the differential equation is satisfied. \(x = 0\) is also a solution (the lecturer calls it a singular solution).
General solution \(y^2 = x^2 + Dx^3\), \(D\in\mathbb R\) (contains \(y = \pm x\) for \(D = 0\)); also \(x = 0\).
i
Correction to the handwritten slide
On p.25 the final line reads \(y^2(x) = x^2 + Dx\). That is a slip: from \(\frac{y^2}{x^2} - 1 = Dx\) you get \(y^2 = x^2 + Dx^3\). Sympy confirms that \(y^2 = x^2 + Dx^3\) solves the equation and \(y^2 = x^2 + Dx\) does not.
!
x = 0 only counts in differential form
\(x = 0\) is a "solution" here because the equation is written as \(M\,dx + N\,dy = 0\) and both terms vanish on the line \(x = 0\). If the equation is given as \(y' = f(x,y)\) with \(x\) in a denominator (like the quiz below), \(x = 0\) is not even in the domain — do not list it.

Exercise 6.3 — a logarithm inside

Exercise 6.3 · Week+3.pdf p.26–28Find the general solution of \(x\,y' = \big(1 + \alpha\ln y - \alpha\ln x\big)\,y\), \(\alpha \gt 0\).
  1. For \(x\neq0\): \(y' = \Big(1 + \alpha\ln\dfrac yx\Big)\dfrac yx\) — a function of \(\frac yx\), so homogeneous.
  2. \(y = ux\): \(u + x\dfrac{du}{dx} = u + \alpha\,u\ln u\), so \(x\dfrac{du}{dx} = \alpha\,u\ln u\) (separable).
  3. For \(u\neq1\), \(u\neq0\) (note \(u = 1\) is a solution, and \(u\) cannot be 0 because of \(\ln u\)): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{u\ln u} = \int\frac{\alpha}{x}dx\).
  4. With \(z = \ln u\), \(dz = \frac1u du\): \(\ln|z| = \alpha\ln|x| + \ln C = \ln\big(C|x|^\alpha\big)\), \(C\neq0\).
  5. \(z = \pm Cx^\alpha = Kx^\alpha\), \(K\neq0\); so \(\ln u = Kx^\alpha\). Including \(u = 1\) (\(\ln u = 0\)): \(\ln u = Dx^{\alpha}\), \(D\) arbitrary.
\(\ln\dfrac yx = D\,x^{\alpha}\), \(D\) arbitrary constant (i.e. \(y = x\,e^{Dx^\alpha}\)).

The Week 4 quiz — "find all solutions" (same as midterm Q4)

✓
This exact equation was midterm 2023 Q4
\(y' = \dfrac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\) is homework Exercise 6.2 (p.26), the Week 4 quiz (Week+4.pdf p.18–19) and Question 4 of the 2023 midterm ("Find all solutions"). Learn both ways below.
Quiz Q2, 1st way · Week+4.pdf p.18–19 (finished here)Find all solutions of \(y' = \dfrac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\).
  1. \(y' = \dfrac13\Big(\dfrac yx\Big)^2 + \dfrac23\Big(\dfrac yx\Big)\) — homogeneous.
  2. \(y = ux\): \(u + x\dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac13u^2 + \dfrac23u\Rightarrow x\dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac13(u-1)u\) (separable).
  3. For \(u\neq0\), \(u\neq1\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{du}{u(u-1)} = \frac13\int\frac{dx}{x}\). Partial fractions: \(\frac{1}{u(u-1)} = \frac{1}{u-1} - \frac1u\).
  4. \(\ln\Big|\dfrac{u-1}{u}\Big| = \dfrac13\ln|x| + c\Rightarrow \dfrac{u-1}{u} = Kx^{1/3}\), \(K\neq0\).
  5. Solve for \(u\): \(u - 1 = Kx^{1/3}u\Rightarrow u = \dfrac{1}{1 - Kx^{1/3}}\), so \(y = \dfrac{x}{1 - Kx^{1/3}}\).
  6. Lost values. \(u = 1\) (\(y = x\)): it solves the equation and it is \(K = 0\) in the formula — already included. \(u = 0\) (\(y = 0\)): it solves the equation (\(0 = 0\)) but no value of \(K\) gives it — list it separately.
All solutions: \(y = \dfrac{x}{1 + Cx^{1/3}}\), \(C\in\mathbb R\) (renaming \(C = -K\)), and \(y = 0\).
Quiz Q2, 2nd way · Week+4.pdf p.19Same equation, as a Bernoulli equation.
  1. \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{3x^2}y^2 + \dfrac{2}{3x}y\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} - \dfrac{2}{3x}y = \dfrac{1}{3x^2}y^2\): Bernoulli, \(n = 2\).
  2. \(u = y^{-1}\), \(u' = -\frac{1}{y^2}y'\). Multiply by \(-\frac1{y^2}\): \(\dfrac{du}{dx} + \dfrac{2}{3x}u = -\dfrac{1}{3x^2}\) (linear).
  3. \(\mu = e^{\int\frac{2}{3x}dx} = x^{2/3}\); \(\big(x^{2/3}u\big)' = -\tfrac13x^{-4/3}\Rightarrow x^{2/3}u = x^{-1/3} + C\).
  4. \(u = \dfrac1x + Cx^{-2/3}\), i.e. \(\dfrac1y = \dfrac{1 + Cx^{1/3}}{x}\).
\(y = \dfrac{x}{1 + Cx^{1/3}}\), plus \(y = 0\) (Bernoulli with \(n = 2 \gt 0\)). Same answer as the first way.

More homework, with answers

Exercise (p.26)Separable equation in \(u\)Answer
6.1 \(y' = \dfrac{3y-x}{3x-y}\)\(x u' = \dfrac{u^2-1}{3-u}\)\(y - x = K(x+y)^2\), \(K\in\mathbb R\); and \(y = -x\)
6.4 \(y' = \dfrac{y^2+(\alpha+1)xy-\alpha x^2}{x\big((\alpha+1)x-(\alpha-1)y\big)}\)\(x u' = \dfrac{\alpha(u^2-1)}{(\alpha+1)-(\alpha-1)u}\)\(y - x = K\,x\,(x+y)^{\alpha}\); and \(y = -x\)

In both, \(u = 1\) (\(y = x\)) is inside the family (\(K = 0\)) but \(u = -1\) (\(y = -x\)) is an extra solution. For 6.1 the partial fractions are \(\frac{3-u}{(u-1)(u+1)} = \frac{1}{u-1} - \frac{2}{u+1}\).

The other quiz question (Week 4, p.15–18)

The same quiz had an equation you can solve in two ways — with an integrating factor (exact equations) or as a linear equation. It shows that one equation may fit several methods.

Quiz Q1 · Week+4.pdf p.15–18Solve \((\ln x - y)\,dx - x\ln x\,dy = 0\).
  1. 1st way: \(M_y = -1 \neq N_x = -\ln x - 1\) — not exact. \(\dfrac{M_y - N_x}{N} = \dfrac{\ln x}{-x\ln x} = -\dfrac1x\) depends on \(x\) only, so \(\mu = e^{-\int\frac1xdx} = \dfrac1x\).
  2. \(\frac1x(\ln x - y)dx - \ln x\,dy = 0\) is exact; \(F = -y\ln x + g(x)\), \(F_x = -\frac yx + g'(x) = \frac{\ln x}{x} - \frac yx\Rightarrow g = \frac{(\ln x)^2}{2}\).
  3. 2nd way: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{1}{x\ln x}y = \dfrac1x\) is linear; \(\mu = e^{\int\frac{dx}{x\ln x}} = \ln x\) and \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(y\ln x) = \dfrac{\ln x}{x}\).
\(-y\ln x + \dfrac{(\ln x)^2}{2} = C\) (both ways give the same).

Traps

!
The derivative of y = ux
\(y' = u + xu'\), not \(y' = u'\) and not \(y' = xu'\). Forgetting the "\(+u\)" is the most common way to lose the whole question.
!
Lost straight-line solutions
Separating needs \(g(u) - u \neq 0\). Each root \(u_0\) gives a line \(y = u_0x\) that solves the equation. Check whether a value of the constant reproduces it (then it is already in the general solution) or not (then list it). Example 19: \(y = \pm x\) included (\(D=0\)); quiz: \(y = x\) included, \(y = 0\) not; Exercise 6.1: \(y = -x\) not.
!
Same degree means the same n
\(x^2 + xy\) and \(x^3\) are both homogeneous functions, but of degrees 2 and 3, so \((x^2+xy)dx + x^3dy = 0\) is not a homogeneous equation.

In one minute

  • Homogeneous: \(y' = g(y/x)\); test with \(f(\lambda x,\lambda y) = f(x,y)\), or \(M, N\) homogeneous of the same degree.
  • Substitute \(y = ux\), \(y' = u + xu'\) ⇒ \(xu' = g(u) - u\) (separable).
  • Integrate, write the constant as \(\ln|C|\), drop the logs, rename \(K = \pm C\).
  • Roots of \(g(u) = u\) give lines \(y = u_0x\): include them (maybe as \(K = 0\)).
  • Differential form: check \(x = 0\) too.
  • \(y' = \frac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\) (midterm Q4): \(y = \frac{x}{1+Cx^{1/3}}\) and \(y = 0\); also solvable as Bernoulli \(n=2\).

chapters.title: Shifting and clever substitutions
chapters.lead: Equations with linear expressions like (x − 2y + 1) are almost homogeneous — a shift of the origin (or the substitution z = ax + by) fixes them. After this chapter you can do that, and you can use a hint like u = sin y to reduce an equation to a linear one.
chapters.html:
Equations of the form \((a_1x + b_1y + c_1)dx + (a_2x+b_2y+c_2)dy = 0\)

Without the constants \(c_1, c_2\) this would be homogeneous (every term has degree 1). The constants spoil it. Two cases, depending on whether the two lines \(a_1x+b_1y+c_1 = 0\) and \(a_2x+b_2y+c_2=0\) intersect.

\[ \Delta := a_1b_2 - a_2b_1 \]
Theorem 8 (Week+3.pdf p.29) — compute the determinant first
CaseWhat to doYou get
1. \(\Delta\neq0\) (lines intersect)Solve \(a_1h + b_1k + c_1 = 0,\ a_2h+b_2k+c_2 = 0\). Put \(x = u + h\), \(y = v + k\) (so \(dx = du\), \(dy = dv\)).Homogeneous: \((a_1u+b_1v)du + (a_2u+b_2v)dv = 0\)
2. \(\Delta = 0\) (lines parallel)Put \(z = a_1x + b_1y\) (the second bracket is then a multiple of \(z\) plus a constant).Separable in \(z\) and \(x\)
→
Why the shift works
\((h,k)\) is the point where both lines meet. Moving the origin there (\(u = x-h\), \(v = y-k\)) makes both brackets vanish at the new origin, so the constants disappear: \(a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = a_1u + b_1v\). What remains is homogeneous, and you already know how to solve that (\(v = zu\)).

Example 20.1 — Case 1

Example 20.1 · Week+3.pdf p.30–35Solve \((x - 2y + 1)\,dx + (4x - 3y - 6)\,dy = 0\).
  1. \(a_1 = 1, b_1 = -2, a_2 = 4, b_2 = -3\): \(\Delta = 1(-3) - 4(-2) = 5\neq0\) — Case 1.
  2. Solve \(h - 2k + 1 = 0\), \(4h - 3k - 6 = 0\): multiply the first by 4 and subtract: \(-5k = -10\), \(k = 2\), \(h = 3\).
  3. \(x = u + 3\), \(y = v + 2\), \(dx = du\), \(dy = dv\): \((u - 2v)du + (4u - 3v)dv = 0\).
  4. For \(4u - 3v\neq0\), \(u\neq0\): \(\dfrac{dv}{du} = -\dfrac{u-2v}{4u-3v} = -\dfrac{1 - 2\frac vu}{4 - 3\frac vu} = g\big(\tfrac vu\big)\) — homogeneous. (Note \(4u-3v = 0\) and \(u = 0\) are not solutions.)
  5. \(z = \frac vu\), \(v = zu\), \(\frac{dv}{du} = u\frac{dz}{du} + z\): \(u\dfrac{dz}{du} = \dfrac{2z-1}{4-3z} - z = \dfrac{3z^2 - 2z - 1}{4-3z} = \dfrac{(3z+1)(z-1)}{4-3z}\) (separable).
  6. Notice \(z = 1\) and \(z = -\tfrac13\) are solutions of this \(z\)-equation. For \(z\neq1, -\tfrac13\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{4-3z}{(3z+1)(z-1)}dz = \int\frac{du}{u}\).
  7. Partial fractions: \(A = -\tfrac{15}{4}\), \(B = \tfrac14\). So \(-\tfrac54\ln|3z+1| + \tfrac14\ln|z-1| = \ln|u| + \ln|C|\), \(C\neq0\).
  8. \(\tfrac14\ln\dfrac{|z-1|}{|3z+1|^5} = \ln|Cu|\Rightarrow \Big|\dfrac{z-1}{(3z+1)^5}\Big| = \tilde Cu^4\) (\(\tilde C = C^4 \gt 0\)) \(\Rightarrow z - 1 = Ku^4(3z+1)^5\), \(K = \pm\tilde C\neq0\).
  9. \(z = \frac vu\): \(\dfrac vu - 1 = Ku^4\Big(\dfrac{3v+u}{u}\Big)^5\Rightarrow v - u = K(3v + u)^5\).
  10. Back to \(x, y\) (\(u = x-3\), \(v = y-2\)): \(y - x + 1 = K(3y + x - 9)^5\), \(K\neq0\). Since \(z = 1\) is also a solution (that is \(K=0\)), write \(D\in\mathbb R\).
  11. \(z = -\tfrac13\): \(v = -\tfrac13u\Rightarrow y - 2 = -\tfrac13(x-3)\Rightarrow y = -\tfrac13x + 3\). No value of \(D\) gives this line, so it is a singular solution.
General solution \(y - x + 1 = D(3y + x - 9)^5\), \(D\in\mathbb R\); singular solution \(y = -\tfrac13x + 3\).

Example 20.2 — Case 2

Example 20.2 · Week+3.pdf p.35–36Solve \((x + 2y + 3)\,dx + (2x + 4y - 1)\,dy = 0\).
  1. \(a_1 = 1, b_1 = 2, a_2 = 2, b_2 = 4\): \(\Delta = 1\cdot4 - 2\cdot2 = 0\) — Case 2. Note \(2x + 4y = 2(x+2y)\).
  2. \(z = x + 2y\): \(\dfrac{dz}{dx} = 1 + 2\dfrac{dy}{dx}\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac12\dfrac{dz}{dx} - \dfrac12\).
  3. The equation says \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x+2y+3}{2x+4y-1} = -\dfrac{z+3}{2z-1}\). So \(\dfrac12\dfrac{dz}{dx} - \dfrac12 = -\dfrac{z+3}{2z-1}\).
  4. \(\dfrac12\dfrac{dz}{dx} = \dfrac{-2z - 6 + 2z - 1}{2(2z-1)}\Rightarrow \dfrac{dz}{dx} = -\dfrac{7}{2z-1}\) (separable).
  5. For \(2z - 1\neq0\): \(\displaystyle\int(2z-1)dz = -\int7\,dx\Rightarrow z^2 - z = -7x + C\).
  6. Check \(z = \tfrac12\), i.e. \(x + 2y = \tfrac12\): then \(dx + 2dy = 0\); substituting into the given equation gives \((\tfrac12 + 3)dx + 0\cdot dy = 0\), false. So \(x + 2y = \tfrac12\) is not a solution.
\((x+2y)^2 - x - 2y = -7x + C\), or \(4y^2 + 4xy + x^2 - 2y = -6x + C\), \(C\) arbitrary.
!
Substitute the excluded value back — every time
In Example 20.1 the excluded \(z = 1\) was inside the family, \(z = -\frac13\) was a genuinely new (singular) solution, and in Example 20.2 the excluded \(z = \frac12\) was not a solution at all. You only know which by plugging it into the original equation.

Homework Exercises 6.1 (p.37)

Exercise 6.1.3 · Week+3.pdf p.37–38 (last steps completed in this guide)Solve \(2(y+\alpha)^2\,dx - (y + x + \alpha + \beta)^2\,dy = 0\).
  1. Here \(a_1 = 0, b_1 = 1\) (inside the square), \(a_2 = 1, b_2 = 1\): \(\Delta = 0\cdot1 - 1\cdot1 = -1\neq0\) — Case 1.
  2. \(k + \alpha = 0\Rightarrow k = -\alpha\); \(k + h + \alpha + \beta = 0\Rightarrow h = -\beta\). So \(x = u - \beta\), \(y = v - \alpha\).
  3. \(2v^2\,du - (v + u)^2\,dv = 0\Rightarrow \dfrac{du}{dv} = \dfrac12\Big(1 + 2\dfrac uv + \dfrac{u^2}{v^2}\Big)\).
  4. Let \(z = \frac uv\) (here \(u\) is written as a function of \(v\)): \(u = zv\), \(\dfrac{du}{dv} = z + v\dfrac{dz}{dv}\). Then \(z + v\dfrac{dz}{dv} = \dfrac12(1 + 2z + z^2)\Rightarrow v\dfrac{dz}{dv} = \dfrac12(1+z^2)\). (The slide stops here.)
  5. Separate: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dz}{1+z^2} = \frac12\int\frac{dv}{v}\Rightarrow \arctan z = \tfrac12\ln|v| + C\).
  6. Back: \(z = \dfrac uv = \dfrac{x+\beta}{y+\alpha}\), \(v = y + \alpha\).
\(\arctan\dfrac{x+\beta}{y+\alpha} - \tfrac12\ln|y+\alpha| = C\)
i
Which ratio?
In Example 20 the lecturer uses \(z = v/u\); in Exercise 6.1.3 he uses \(z = u/v\) because the equation is easier to write as \(\frac{du}{dv}\). Both are fine — just stay consistent within one problem.

Answers for the other two homework problems (checked with sympy):

  • 6.1.1 \((x - y + \alpha - \beta)dx + (x + y - \alpha - \beta)dy = 0\): \(\Delta = 2\), \((h,k) = (\beta,\alpha)\), homogeneous \((u-v)du + (u+v)dv = 0\). Answer: \(\arctan\dfrac{y-\alpha}{x-\beta} + \tfrac12\ln\big((x-\beta)^2 + (y-\alpha)^2\big) = C\).
  • 6.1.2 \((2x + 2\alpha y - 1)dx + (2\alpha x + 2\alpha^2y - \beta)dy = 0\): \(\Delta = 4\alpha^2 - 4\alpha^2 = 0\), Case 2 with \(z = x + \alpha y\): \(\dfrac{dz}{dx} = \dfrac{\alpha-\beta}{2\alpha z - \beta}\). Answer: \(\alpha z^2 - \beta z - (\alpha-\beta)x = C\) with \(z = x + \alpha y\).

Substitution: no general rule

The slides (p.39) say it honestly: some equations look different from all the standard types, and a special substitution (usually given as a hint) reduces them to something you know. There is no general rule — look for a piece of the equation whose derivative also appears.

Example 21 · Week+3.pdf p.39–40Solve \(\big(1 + 3x\sin y\big)\,dx - x^2\cos y\,dy = 0\) by letting \(u = \sin y\).
  1. \(u = \sin y\Rightarrow du = \cos y\,dy\) (exactly the \(\cos y\,dy\) in the equation).
  2. Then \((1 + 3xu)\,dx - x^2\,du = 0\Rightarrow \dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac{1 + 3xu}{x^2}\Rightarrow \dfrac{du}{dx} - \dfrac3xu = \dfrac{1}{x^2}\) (linear).
  3. \(\mu(x) = e^{-\int\frac3xdx} = \dfrac1{x^3}\): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\Big(\dfrac{u}{x^3}\Big) = \dfrac{1}{x^5}\).
  4. \(\dfrac{u}{x^3} = -\dfrac{1}{4x^4} + C\Rightarrow u = -\dfrac{1}{4x} + Cx^3\).
\(\sin y = -\dfrac{1}{4x} + Cx^3\), \(C\) arbitrary.

Exercises 6.2 (p.41) — which substitution?

EquationSubstitutionResult
1. \(y' = \tan^2(x+y)\)\(u = x + y\)\(u' = 1 + \tan^2u = \sec^2u\): separable
2. \(y' = (\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma)^2\)\(u = \alpha x + \beta y + \gamma\)\(u' = \alpha + \beta u^2\): separable
3. \(y' = \dfrac{(\alpha x+\beta y)^2 + \gamma}{\alpha x + \beta y} - \dfrac\alpha\beta\)\(u = \alpha x + \beta y\)\(u' = \beta\dfrac{u^2+\gamma}{u}\): separable; \(u^2 + \gamma = Ke^{2\beta x}\)
4. \(y' = \dfrac{(x+y^n)^m - 1}{ny^{n-1}}\)\(u = y^n\), then \(z = x + u\)\(z' = z^m\): separable
5. \(ny^{n-1}y' = y^n + x - 1\)\(u = y^n\)\(u' - u = x - 1\): linear; \(y^n = Ce^x - x\)
Exercise 6.2.1 · Week+3.pdf p.41 (solution written for this guide)Solve \(y' = \tan^2(x+y)\).
  1. \(u = x + y\Rightarrow u' = 1 + y' = 1 + \tan^2u = \sec^2u\).
  2. Separate: \(\cos^2u\,du = dx\). Using \(\int\cos^2u\,du = \frac u2 + \frac{\sin2u}{4}\): \(\dfrac u2 + \dfrac{\sin 2u}{4} = x + C\).
  3. Multiply by 4 and put \(u = x+y\) back: \(2(x+y) + \sin(2x+2y) = 4x + C\).
\(2y - 2x + \sin(2x+2y) = C\)
Exercise 6.2.4 · Week+3.pdf p.41–44Solve \(y' = \dfrac{(x+y^n)^m - 1}{n\,y^{n-1}}\), \(n, m\in\mathbb N\).
  1. \(u = y^n\Rightarrow \dfrac{du}{dx} = ny^{n-1}\dfrac{dy}{dx}\). For \(y\neq0\) (note \(y = 0\) is not a solution): \(ny^{n-1}\dfrac{dy}{dx} = (x + y^n)^m - 1\), i.e. \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = (x+u)^m - 1\).
  2. Let \(z = x + u\): \(\dfrac{dz}{dx} = 1 + \dfrac{du}{dx} = z^m\) (separable).
  3. \(z = 0\) satisfies \(z' = z^m\) (for \(m \ge 1\)), so \(z = 0\) is a solution. For \(z\neq0\) and \(m\neq1\), \(m\neq0\): \(\displaystyle\int z^{-m}dz = \int dx\Rightarrow \frac{z^{1-m}}{1-m} = -\frac{1}{m-1}\,\frac{1}{z^{m-1}} = x + C\).
  4. Solve for \(z^{m-1}\): \((x + y^n)^{m-1} = \dfrac{-1}{(m-1)(x + C)} = \dfrac{1}{(1-m)x + \tilde C}\), with \(\tilde C = (1-m)C\).
  5. \(m = 1\): \(\int\frac{dz}{z} = \int dx\Rightarrow \ln|z| = x + C\Rightarrow z = Ke^x\), \(K = \pm e^C\neq0\); with \(z = 0\): \(x + y^n = De^x\), \(D\) arbitrary.
  6. \(m = 0\): \(z' = 1\Rightarrow z = x + L\Rightarrow y^n = L\).
\(m\ge2\): \((x+y^n)^{m-1} = \dfrac{1}{(1-m)x + \tilde C}\) (and \(x + y^n = 0\)); \(m = 1\): \(x + y^n = De^x\); \(m = 0\): \(y^n = L\).
i
A sign slip on the slide
Integrating \(z^{-m}\) gives \(\frac{z^{1-m}}{1-m} = -\frac{1}{(m-1)z^{m-1}}\). The handwritten line on p.42 drops this minus sign and ends (p.43) with \((x+y^n)^{m-1} = \frac{1}{(m-1)x + \tilde C}\). That changes the sign of the \(x\)-term, which a renamed constant cannot fix. The correct family is \((x + y^n)^{m-1} = \dfrac{1}{(1-m)x + \tilde C}\); sympy confirms it (e.g. \(m = 3, n = 2\)) and rejects the slide's version. Quick sanity check with \(m = 2\): \(z' = z^2\) gives \(z = \frac{1}{-x + \tilde C}\).
★
Recognising the hint
\(\cos y\,dy\) next to \(\sin y\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(u = \sin y\). \(ny^{n-1}y'\) next to \(y^n\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(u = y^n\). A single combination like \(x + y\) or \(\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma\) inside a function \(\Rightarrow\) \(u\) = that combination. \(e^{y}y'\) with powers of \(e^{y}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(z = e^y\) (midterm Q3, see the Bernoulli chapter).

In one minute

  • \((a_1x+b_1y+c_1)dx + (a_2x+b_2y+c_2)dy = 0\): compute \(\Delta = a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\).
  • \(\Delta\neq0\): solve for the intersection \((h,k)\); \(x = u+h\), \(y = v+k\) ⇒ homogeneous; then \(v = zu\).
  • \(\Delta = 0\): \(z = a_1x + b_1y\) ⇒ separable in \(z, x\).
  • Excluded values (\(z = z_0\)): substitute back — included, singular, or not a solution.
  • Special substitutions (\(u = \sin y\), \(u = y^n\), \(u = x+y\)) have no general rule; look for "a function and its derivative".
  • Usually the result is linear (use \(\mu\)) or separable.

chapters.title: Riccati and Clairaut equations
chapters.lead: Two named equations with their own tricks. Riccati: if someone hands you one particular solution, a single substitution gives all the others. Clairaut: y = xp + f(p) is solved by straight lines y = cx + f(c), plus one special curve, the singular solution.
chapters.html:
Riccati equations

\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = p(x)\,y^2 + q(x)\,y + r(x) \]
Definition 18 (Week+4.pdf p.1) — Riccati equation

It is "quadratic in \(y\)". Two quick observations from the lecturer:

  • If \(r(x) = 0\), it is \(\frac{dy}{dx} - q(x)y = p(x)y^2\): a Bernoulli equation with \(n = 2\) (p.1).
  • In general (p.2) its solutions cannot be expressed in terms of elementary functions. We need help: one known solution.

Theorem 9: one solution gives all the others

\[ y = y_1 + \frac1u\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{du}{dx} + \big(2p(x)\,y_1 + q(x)\big)\,u = -p(x) \]
Theorem 9 (p.2–4): a particular solution turns Riccati into a linear equation
i
Letters, exactly as on the slides
Theorem 9 writes the substitution as \(y := y_1 + \frac1u\) (new unknown \(u\)); Exercise 7.1 uses \(y := u + y_1\) without the fraction. Some books call the new unknown \(v\) — the same thing. This guide follows the slides.

Where it comes from (p.3–4):

  1. \(y_1\) is a solution: \(y_1' = p\,y_1^2 + q\,y_1 + r\).
  2. \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\Rightarrow y' = y_1' - \frac{1}{u^2}u'\).
  3. Substitute: \(y_1' - \frac{1}{u^2}u' = p\big(y_1 + \frac1u\big)^2 + q\big(y_1 + \frac1u\big) + r = \underbrace{p y_1^2 + q y_1 + r}_{=\,y_1'} + 2py_1\frac1u + p\frac1{u^2} + q\frac1u\).
  4. Cancel \(y_1'\) on both sides: \(-\frac1{u^2}u' = (2py_1 + q)\frac1u + p\frac1{u^2}\).
  5. Multiply by \(-u^2\): \(u' + (2py_1 + q)u = -p\). Linear!
✓
What to write in the exam
"Since \(y_1\) is a particular solution, let \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\)." Then either substitute directly (1st way) or use the ready formula \(u' + (2py_1+q)u = -p\) (2nd way). The lecturer shows both and both get full credit.
!
No particular solution, no method
Theorem 9 needs a particular solution \(y_1\). If none is given, look for an easy one (a constant, \(y = ax+b\), \(y = x^\beta\)) by plugging in — or the problem tells you its form (Exercises 7.3, 7.4). Without \(y_1\) you cannot start.
Example 22 · Week+4.pdf p.4–6Solve \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = y^2 - 2xy + 2\), which has the particular solution \(y_1(x) = 2x\).
  1. \(p = 1\), \(q = -2x\), \(r = 2\), \(y_1 = 2x\). (Check: \(y_1' = 2\) and \(4x^2 - 4x^2 + 2 = 2\).)
  2. \(y = 2x + \frac1u\), \(y' = 2 - \frac1{u^2}u'\).
  3. 1st way — substitute: \(2 - \frac{1}{u^2}u' = \big(2x + \frac1u\big)^2 - 2x\big(2x + \frac1u\big) + 2\). Expand and multiply by \(-u^2\): \(u' = -1 - 4xu + 2xu\), i.e. \(u' = -1 - 2xu\).
  4. 2nd way — formula: \(2py_1 + q = 2\cdot1\cdot2x - 2x = 2x\), so \(u' + 2xu = -1\). Same equation.
  5. Linear: \(\mu = e^{\int2x\,dx} = e^{x^2}\); \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(e^{x^2}u\big) = -e^{x^2}\).
  6. \(e^{x^2}u = -\int e^{x^2}dx + C\), so \(u = e^{-x^2}\Big(-\int e^{x^2}dx + C\Big)\).
\(y(x) = 2x + \dfrac{e^{x^2}}{-\int e^{x^2}dx + C}\), \(C\in\mathbb R\) (the integral \(\int e^{x^2}dx\) has no elementary form — leave it like this).
i
The particular solution itself
The particular solution \(y_1\) itself corresponds to "\(u = \infty\)" and is not produced by any \(C\). If a question says "find all solutions", mention \(y = y_1\) separately.

Homework Exercises 7 (p.7–8)

Exercise 7.3 · Week+4.pdf p.7 (solution written for this guide)Find \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) such that \(y' = y^2 - \dfrac yx + \dfrac{\alpha}{x^2}\) has a particular solution \(y_1 = x^\beta\). Then find the general solution.
  1. Plug in \(y_1 = x^\beta\): \(\beta x^{\beta-1} = x^{2\beta} - x^{\beta-1} + \alpha x^{-2}\).
  2. The \(x^{2\beta}\) term must cancel against the \(x^{\beta-1}\) terms, so \(2\beta = \beta - 1\): \(\beta = -1\) (and then \(\beta - 1 = -2\) also matches the \(\frac{\alpha}{x^2}\) term). Then \(-x^{-2} = x^{-2} - x^{-2} + \alpha x^{-2}\Rightarrow \alpha = -1\).
  3. So \(y_1 = \frac1x\), \(p = 1\), \(q = -\frac1x\): \(2py_1 + q = \frac2x - \frac1x = \frac1x\). Linear: \(u' + \frac1xu = -1\).
  4. \(\mu = x\): \((xu)' = -x\Rightarrow xu = -\frac{x^2}{2} + C\Rightarrow u = \dfrac{2C - x^2}{2x}\).
\(\alpha = -1\), \(\beta = -1\); \(y = \dfrac1x + \dfrac{2x}{K - x^2}\) (with \(K = 2C\)), and \(y = \frac1x\).
Exercise 7.4 · Week+4.pdf p.7 (solution written for this guide)Find the general solution of \(y' = (y - \alpha x + \beta)^2 + \alpha\) if it has a particular solution which is a straight line.
  1. Try \(y_1 = ax + b\): \(a = (ax + b - \alpha x + \beta)^2 + \alpha\) for all \(x\) forces \(a = \alpha\) and \(b = -\beta\). So \(y_1 = \alpha x - \beta\).
  2. Expand: \(y' = y^2 - 2(\alpha x - \beta)y + (\alpha x-\beta)^2 + \alpha\), so \(p = 1\), \(q = -2(\alpha x - \beta)\).
  3. \(2py_1 + q = 2(\alpha x - \beta) - 2(\alpha x - \beta) = 0\): the linear equation is just \(u' = -1\), \(u = C - x\).
\(y = \alpha x - \beta + \dfrac{1}{C - x}\), and \(y = \alpha x - \beta\).
  • Exercise 7.1 (p.7): with \(y = y_1 + u\) (no fraction) the same computation gives \(u' - (2py_1 + q)u = p\,u^2\) — a Bernoulli equation with \(n = 2\). (Then \(\frac1u\) makes it linear — which is exactly why Theorem 9 uses \(y_1 + \frac1u\) directly.)
  • Exercise 7.2 (p.7–8): \(y = -\dfrac{u'}{p\,u}\) turns Riccati into a second-order linear equation. If \(p\) is a constant the result is \(u'' - q\,u' + p\,r\,u = 0\); in general \(u'' - \big(q + \frac{p'}{p}\big)u' + p\,r\,u = 0\). (The handwritten solution writes \(u'' + q u' + rpu = 0\): it loses the sign of the \(q\)-term, because \(q\,y = -q\frac{u'}{pu}\), and it ignores \(p'\).)

Clairaut equations

\[ y = x\,p + f(p),\qquad p := \frac{dy}{dx} \]
Definition 19 (p.9) — Clairaut equation

The unknown slope \(p\) appears inside a function \(f\), so we cannot solve for \(y'\) directly. The trick is to differentiate the whole equation.

Solution technique (p.9–11)

  1. Differentiate with respect to \(x\) (product rule on \(xp\), chain rule on \(f(p)\)): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = p + x\dfrac{dp}{dx} + f'(p)\dfrac{dp}{dx}\).
  2. The left side is \(p\), so \(p\) cancels: \(0 = \dfrac{dp}{dx}\big(x + f'(p)\big)\).
  3. Either \(\dfrac{dp}{dx} = 0\Rightarrow p = c\). Substitute \(c\) for \(p\) in the equation: the general solution is the family of lines
\[ y = cx + f(c),\qquad c \text{ an arbitrary constant} \]
General solution: replace p by a constant c
  1. Or \(x + f'(p) = 0\), i.e. \(f'(p) = -x\). Solve it to find the singular solution: an extra solution which is not a member of the one-parameter family.
\[ x = -f'(p),\qquad y = x\,p + f(p) \;\;\Rightarrow\;\; \text{eliminate } p \]
Singular solution — parametric form, then eliminate the parameter
Example 23 · Week+4.pdf p.12–13Solve \(y = xp + p^2\).
  1. Differentiate: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = p + x\dfrac{dp}{dx} + 2p\dfrac{dp}{dx}\Rightarrow 0 = \dfrac{dp}{dx}(x + 2p)\).
  2. \(\dfrac{dp}{dx} = 0\Rightarrow p = c\): general solution \(y = cx + c^2\).
  3. \(x + 2p = 0\Rightarrow p = -\dfrac x2\), i.e. \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac x2\Rightarrow y = -\dfrac{x^2}{4} + k\) (lecturer's way: integrate the slope).
  4. Which \(k\)? Plug into the original equation with \(p = y' = -\frac x2\): \(-\frac{x^2}{4} + k = x\big(-\frac x2\big) + \frac{x^2}{4} = -\frac{x^2}{4}\Rightarrow k = 0\).
  5. Shortcut (same result): put \(p = -\frac x2\) straight into \(y = xp + p^2\): \(y = -\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^2}{4} = -\frac{x^2}{4}\).
General solution \(y = cx + c^2\); singular solution \(y = -\dfrac{x^2}{4}\).
★
Check the singular solution in 10 seconds
For \(y = -\frac{x^2}{4}\): \(p = -\frac x2\), and \(xp + p^2 = -\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^2}{4} = -\frac{x^2}{4} = y\). It works, and it is a parabola, not a line — so it cannot be one of the \(y = cx + c^2\).

Homework Exercises 8 (p.14)

Exercise 8.1 · Week+4.pdf p.14 (solution written for this guide)Solve the Clairaut equation \(y = xp + p^2 + 1\).
  1. \(f(p) = p^2 + 1\), \(f'(p) = 2p\). Differentiating: \(0 = \frac{dp}{dx}(x + 2p)\).
  2. \(p = c\): \(y = cx + c^2 + 1\).
  3. \(x + 2p = 0\Rightarrow p = -\frac x2\Rightarrow y = -\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^2}{4} + 1 = 1 - \frac{x^2}{4}\).
General: \(y = cx + c^2 + 1\); singular: \(y = 1 - \dfrac{x^2}{4}\).
Exercise 8.2 · Week+4.pdf p.14 (solution written for this guide)Solve the Clairaut equation \(y = xp + e^{-p} + 1\).
  1. \(f(p) = e^{-p} + 1\), \(f'(p) = -e^{-p}\). Differentiating: \(0 = \frac{dp}{dx}\big(x - e^{-p}\big)\).
  2. \(p = c\): \(y = cx + e^{-c} + 1\).
  3. \(x = e^{-p}\Rightarrow p = -\ln x\) (\(x \gt 0\)). Then \(y = x(-\ln x) + x + 1\).
General: \(y = cx + e^{-c} + 1\); singular: \(y = x - x\ln x + 1\), \(x \gt 0\).
i
Lagrange equations (Exercises 8.3–8.4)
The slide also names equations of the form \(y = x\,f(p) + g(p)\) "Lagrange differential equations" and says they are solved "by using the same steps" (differentiate with respect to \(x\)). Clairaut is the special case \(f(p) = p\). No worked solution is given in the slides.

Traps

!
Forgetting the singular solution
"Solve the Clairaut equation" means both the family \(y = cx + f(c)\) and the singular solution from \(x + f'(p) = 0\). The singular one is where most points are lost.
!
Riccati sign
The linear equation is \(u' + (2py_1 + q)u = -p\) — note the minus on the right. Check it by quickly redoing the substitution if unsure.
!
Clairaut vs. Riccati
Clairaut has \(y\) alone on the left and \(p = y'\) inside a function: \(y = xp + f(p)\). Riccati has \(y'\) alone on the left and is quadratic in \(y\): \(y' = py^2 + qy + r\).

In one minute

  • Riccati: \(y' = p y^2 + q y + r\); if \(r = 0\) it is Bernoulli (\(n = 2\)).
  • Needs a particular solution \(y_1\); then \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\).
  • Linear equation: \(u' + (2py_1 + q)u = -p\); solve with \(\mu\); and \(y = y_1\) is also a solution.
  • Find \(y_1\) by trying a guessed form (constant, line, \(x^\beta\)).
  • Clairaut: \(y = xp + f(p)\); differentiate ⇒ \(\frac{dp}{dx}(x + f'(p)) = 0\).
  • General solution: \(y = cx + f(c)\) (replace \(p\) by \(c\)).
  • Singular solution: \(x = -f'(p)\), \(y = xp + f(p)\), eliminate \(p\) (e.g. \(y = xp + p^2\Rightarrow y = -\frac{x^2}{4}\)).

chapters.title: Orthogonal trajectories
chapters.lead: Given a family of curves, find the curves that cross every one of them at a right angle. It is a three-step recipe: get the family's slope, flip it to −1/slope, solve the new (usually separable) equation.
chapters.html:
What we are looking for

This is the first application of first-order equations in the course (p.20: applied problems formulated in terms of first-order differential equations).

✓
Definition 20 (p.21)
Let \(\Phi(x,y,c) = 0\) be a given one-parameter family of curves in the \(xy\)-plane. A curve which intersects the curves of the given family at right angles is called an orthogonal trajectory of the given family.

Example 24 (p.22): every straight line \(y = kx\) through the origin is an orthogonal trajectory of the circles \(x^2 + y^2 = c^2\), and conversely each circle is an orthogonal trajectory of the lines. "Actually, they are orthogonal trajectories of each other."

→
Right angle = slopes multiply to −1
Two lines with slopes \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are perpendicular exactly when \(m_1m_2 = -1\), i.e. \(m_2 = -\dfrac{1}{m_1}\). Two curves cross at right angles when their tangent lines at the crossing point do. The lecturer checks this on Example 24: circles have slope \(m_1 = -\frac xy\), lines have \(m_2 = \frac yx\), and \(m_1m_2 = -\frac xy\cdot\frac yx = -1\).

The recipe (Solution technique, p.23–24)

  1. Slope of the given family. Differentiate \(\Phi(x,y,c) = 0\) implicitly with respect to \(x\).
  2. Eliminate \(c\) using the original equation and the derived one. Result: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = f(x,y)\) — this is \(m_1\), the slope of the family member through \((x,y)\). (In general \(f = -\Phi_x/\Phi_y\).)
  3. Flip: the trajectories have slope \(m_2 = -\dfrac{1}{f(x,y)}\). Their differential equation is
\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{1}{f(x,y)} = \frac{\partial\Phi/\partial y}{\partial\Phi/\partial x} \]
Differential equation of the orthogonal trajectories (p.24)
  1. Solve it. A one-parameter family of solutions \(\Psi(x,y,d) = 0\) is the family of orthogonal trajectories.
!
Eliminate c BEFORE flipping
The slope \(f(x,y)\) must not contain \(c\). For \(y = ce^{x}\): \(y' = ce^{x}\) still has \(c\); replace \(ce^x\) by \(y\) to get \(y' = y\). Only then flip to \(y' = -\frac1y\). If you flip \(ce^x\) you get a "family" that depends on \(c\) — wrong.

Example 25 — circles

Examples 24–25 · Week+4.pdf p.22, 25Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of circles \(x^2 + y^2 = c^2\).
  1. Differentiate: \(2x + 2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac xy\). (\(c\) disappeared by itself.) So \(m_1 = -\frac xy\).
  2. Trajectories: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{1}{m_1} = \dfrac yx\) (separable).
  3. \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dy}{y} = \int\frac{dx}{x}\Rightarrow \ln|y| = \ln|x| + \ln|k|\Rightarrow y = kx\).
The orthogonal trajectories are the lines through the origin, \(y = kx\).

Example 26 — parabolas

Example 26 · Week+4.pdf p.25–26Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of parabolas \(y = kx^2\).
  1. 1st family. \(y = kx^2\Rightarrow k = \dfrac{y}{x^2}\).
  2. \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2kx = 2\dfrac{y}{x^2}x = \dfrac{2y}{x}\) (\(k\) eliminated). So \(m_1 = \dfrac{2y}{x}\).
  3. 2nd family. \(m_2 = -\dfrac{1}{m_1} = -\dfrac{x}{2y}\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{x}{2y}\) (separable).
  4. \(\displaystyle\int2y\,dy = -\int x\,dx\Rightarrow y^2 = -\frac{x^2}{2} + C\).
\(y^2 + \dfrac{x^2}{2} = C\), \(C\) arbitrary — a family of ellipses.

Homework Exercises 9.1 (p.27)

Exercise 9.1.5 · Week+4.pdf p.27–28Obtain the orthogonal trajectories of the family of curves \(y = \dfrac{e^x}{e^x + c}\).
  1. \(e^xy + yc = e^x\Rightarrow c = \dfrac{e^x(1-y)}{y}\).
  2. Quotient rule: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{e^x(e^x + c) - e^x\cdot e^x}{(e^x+c)^2} = \dfrac{ce^x}{(e^x+c)^2}\).
  3. Eliminate \(c\): from the family, \(e^x + c = \dfrac{e^x}{y}\), so \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{c\,y^2}{e^x} = \dfrac{e^x(1-y)}{y}\cdot\dfrac{y^2}{e^x} = (1-y)y\). So \(m_1 = (1-y)y\).
  4. \(m_2 = \dfrac{1}{(y-1)y}\): \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{(y-1)y}\) (separable).
  5. \(\displaystyle\int y(y-1)\,dy = \int dx\Rightarrow \frac{y^3}{3} - \frac{y^2}{2} = x + C\).
\(\dfrac{y^3}{3} - \dfrac{y^2}{2} = x + C\), \(C\) arbitrary.
Exercise 9.1.6 · Week+4.pdf p.29 (last step completed in this guide)Show that the orthogonal trajectories of the family \(y^2 = 2cx + c^2\) is the family itself.
  1. Differentiate: \(2y\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2c\Rightarrow \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac cy\).
  2. Eliminate \(c\): \(y^2 + x^2 = x^2 + 2cx + c^2 = (x+c)^2\Rightarrow x + c = \pm\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Taking \(c = -x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\): \(m_1 = \dfrac{-x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{y}\).
  3. \(m_2 = -\dfrac{1}{m_1} = \dfrac{-y}{-x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}}\) — a homogeneous equation (the lecturer stops here: "Solve it!").
  4. Instead of solving, rationalise: multiply top and bottom by \(x + \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). Since \((-x+\sqrt{x^2+y^2})(x+\sqrt{x^2+y^2}) = y^2\), we get \(m_2 = \dfrac{-x - \sqrt{x^2+y^2}}{y}\).
  5. That is exactly \(\dfrac cy\) for the other root \(c = -x - \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). So the trajectory through \((x,y)\) satisfies the same equation \(y' = \frac cy\), \(y^2 = 2cx + c^2\), with the other value of \(c\).
Through every point pass two curves of the family (one for each root \(c\)), and they meet at a right angle: the family \(y^2 = 2cx + c^2\) is its own family of orthogonal trajectories.

Answers for the other homework problems (all separable after flipping, checked with sympy):

Family\(m_1\) (\(c\) eliminated)Trajectory equationOrthogonal trajectories
9.1.1 \(3x^2 - y^2 = c\)\(\dfrac{3x}{y}\)\(y' = -\dfrac{y}{3x}\)\(xy^3 = K\)
9.1.2 \(y = ce^{x}\)\(y\)\(y' = -\dfrac1y\)\(y^2 = -2x + C\)
9.1.3 \(y = cx^2\)\(\dfrac{2y}{x}\)\(y' = -\dfrac{x}{2y}\)\(x^2 + 2y^2 = C\) (as Example 26)
9.1.4 \(y^3 = cx^2\)\(\dfrac{2y}{3x}\)\(y' = -\dfrac{3x}{2y}\)\(3x^2 + 2y^2 = C\)
★
Shortcut for the slope
From \(\Phi(x,y,c) = 0\) you can also solve for \(c\) first (\(c = G(x,y)\)), then differentiate \(G(x,y) = c\): \(G_x + G_y\,y' = 0\Rightarrow y' = -\frac{G_x}{G_y}\). The constant is gone automatically. E.g. \(c = \frac{y}{x^2}\): \(-\frac{2y}{x^3} + \frac{1}{x^2}y' = 0\Rightarrow y' = \frac{2y}{x}\).

In one minute

  • Orthogonal trajectory: crosses every curve of the family at a right angle.
  • Step 1: differentiate the family implicitly.
  • Step 2: eliminate \(c\) ⇒ \(y' = f(x,y)\) (no \(c\) left!).
  • Step 3: replace \(y'\) by \(-\frac{1}{y'}\): solve \(y' = -\frac{1}{f(x,y)}\).
  • The new equation is usually separable (sometimes homogeneous).
  • Circles \(x^2+y^2 = c^2\) are orthogonal to lines \(y = kx\); parabolas \(y = kx^2\) are orthogonal to ellipses \(y^2 + \frac{x^2}{2} = C\).
  • \(y^2 = 2cx + c^2\) is self-orthogonal.

chapters.title: Applications: cooling, falling bodies, decay and mixtures
chapters.lead: Turn a word problem into a first-order differential equation, solve it with methods you already know, and use the numbers in the story to pin down the constants. Question 1 of the midterm is always one of these.
chapters.html:
The big picture

Every problem in this chapter is the same story told in four costumes: cooling, falling, growth/decay and mixing. In each one, a sentence tells you how fast something changes. You write that sentence as an equation, solve it (it is always separable or linear — methods you already know), and then use the given measurements to find the unknown constants.

→
The 5-step recipe for every word problem
  1. Name the unknown and its units: "Let \(A(t)\) be the grams of A present at time \(t\) hours."
  2. Translate the rate sentence into a differential equation (table below).
  3. Write every number in the story as a condition: "initially 50 g" means \(A(0)=50\); "after 2 hours 10 g" means \(A(2)=10\).
  4. Solve the equation (separable or linear), then use the condition at \(t=0\) to find \(C\), and the second condition to find \(k\).
  5. Answer the actual question (plug in a time, or solve for a time) and write the units.

Translating words into an equation

"The rate of change of A" always means the derivative \(\frac{dA}{dt}\). "Proportional to" always means "equals a constant \(k\) times". The rest is just reading carefully what it is proportional to.

The sentence says…You write…
A changes at a rate proportional to the amount present\(\frac{dA}{dt}=kA\)
A decays / is converted / decreases at a rate proportional to the amount\(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA\), \(k\gt 0\)
… proportional to the square of the amount\(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\)
… proportional to the square root of the amount\(\frac{dA}{dt}=-k\sqrt{A}\)
bacteria grow at a rate proportional to the number present\(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN\), \(k\gt 0\)
temperature changes at a rate proportional to the difference between the body and the surroundings\(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_m)\)
force = gravity minus air resistance proportional to speed\(m\frac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv\)
salt enters at one rate and leaves at another\(\frac{dx}{dt}=r_{\text{in}}-r_{\text{out}}\)
Data sentenceCondition
"Initially 50 g is present"\(A(0)=50\)
"After 2 hours only 10 g remain"\(A(2)=10\)
"Half … disintegrates in 138 years" (half-life)\(N(138)=\tfrac12 N_0\)
"The number doubles every 10 hours"\(N(10)=2N_0\)
"It is cooling at 5° per minute (at the initial time)"\(T'(0)=-5\)
"Dropped without any velocity"\(v(0)=0\)
!
Where does the minus sign go?

If the quantity decreases, its derivative is negative. The slides use two conventions, and both are fine as long as you stay consistent:

  • Write \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA\) with \(k\gt 0\) (printed slides, Week+5.pdf p.20).
  • Write \(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN\) and let the data tell you that \(k\) is negative (handwritten solution of Example 29: \(k=-\frac{\ln 2}{138}\)).

What you must not do is write \(-k\) and then also get a negative \(k\): that would make the amount grow.

★
Two conditions, two unknowns

The general solution always contains two unknowns: the integration constant \(C\) and the proportionality constant \(k\). That is why every problem gives you two measurements (plus maybe a third time where you have to predict). Use the \(t=0\) data first — it usually gives \(C\) immediately.

1. Newton's law of cooling

Intuition. A hot cup of tea in a cold room cools fast at first and then more and more slowly, because the cooling speed depends on how much hotter it is than the room. When the tea reaches room temperature, it stops changing.

\[ \frac{dT}{dt}=-k\,(T-T_m) \]
Newton's law of cooling (Week+5.pdf p.2)
\(T(t)\)
temperature of the body at time \(t\) (the unknown)
\(T_m\)
temperature of the surrounding medium (room, outside air) — a constant
\(k\)
a positive constant of proportionality
\(\frac{dT}{dt}\)
rate of change of the temperature of the body

Why the minus sign? If the body is hotter than the room (\(T-T_m\gt 0\)), it must cool, so \(\frac{dT}{dt}\lt 0\). With \(k\gt 0\), only \(-k(T-T_m)\) has the right sign. The same formula also works for a cold body warming up: then \(T-T_m\lt 0\) and \(\frac{dT}{dt}\gt 0\).

Solving it once and for all. The equation is separable. For \(T\ne T_m\):

\[ \int\frac{dT}{T-T_m}=-\int k\,dt\ \Rightarrow\ \ln|T-T_m|=-kt+\ln C\ \Rightarrow\ T(t)=T_m+\tilde C e^{-kt}. \]

(\(T\equiv T_m\) is also a solution; it is the case \(\tilde C=0\).) Putting \(t=0\) gives \(\tilde C=T_0-T_m\), so

\[ T(t)=T_m+(T_0-T_m)\,e^{-kt} \]
Solution of the cooling law (T0 = starting temperature)
Example 28 · Week+5.pdf p.3–6A thermometer, which has been showing 26 °C inside a house, is placed outside where the temperature is 10 °C. Three minutes later the thermometer reads 12 °C. Predict the thermometer reading at any time.
  1. Unknown: \(T(t)\) = reading after \(t\) minutes. Data: \(T(0)=26\), \(T(3)=12\), \(T_m=10\).
  2. Model: \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-10)\) (temperature is decreasing, so we use \(-k\) with \(k\gt 0\))
  3. Separable. For \(T\ne 10\): \(\frac{dT}{T-10}=-k\,dt\Rightarrow \ln|T-10|=-kt+\ln C\Rightarrow T(t)=\tilde C e^{-kt}+10\). (\(T=10\) is also a solution, covered by \(\tilde C=0\))
  4. \(T(0)=26\): \(\tilde C e^{0}+10=26\Rightarrow \tilde C=16\).
  5. \(T(3)=12\): \(16e^{-3k}+10=12\Rightarrow e^{-3k}=\frac{2}{16}=2^{-3}\Rightarrow -3k=-3\ln 2\Rightarrow k=\ln 2\).
  6. So \(T(t)=16e^{-(\ln 2)t}+10=16\cdot 2^{-t}+10\). (because \(e^{-(\ln 2)t}=(e^{\ln 2})^{-t}=2^{-t}\))
\(T(t)=16\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t}+10=2^{4-t}+10\) °C
★
Shortcut for k: take a ratio

From \(T-T_m=(T_0-T_m)e^{-kt}\): \(\;e^{-kt}=\dfrac{T(t)-T_m}{T_0-T_m}\). So at the measured time \(t_1\), \(e^{-kt_1}\) is just a ratio of differences. In Example 28: \(e^{-3k}=\frac{12-10}{26-10}=\frac18\). You often don't even need \(k\) itself — keep \(e^{-k}\) as a number.

Exercises 10.1 (homework on Week+5.pdf p.7), solved

Exercises 10.1 #1 · Week+5.pdf p.7An object initially at 20 °C is placed in a room kept at 80 °C. One hour later it is 35 °C. What will its temperature be after three hours?
  1. \(T(0)=20\), \(T_m=80\), \(T(1)=35\). Model \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-80)\), solution \(T=80+(20-80)e^{-kt}=80-60e^{-kt}\). (here the body warms up; the same law works)
  2. \(T(1)=35\): \(80-60e^{-k}=35\Rightarrow e^{-k}=\frac{45}{60}=\frac34\).
  3. \(T(3)=80-60\,(e^{-k})^3=80-60\cdot\frac{27}{64}=\frac{875}{16}\).
\(T(3)=\frac{875}{16}\approx 54.69\) °C
Exercises 10.1 #2 · Week+5.pdf p.7A 200 °F cup of tea is left in a 65 °F room. At the initial time the tea is cooling at 5 °F per minute. Write an initial-value problem for the temperature and find the temperature after 5 minutes.
  1. IVP: \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-65)\), \(T(0)=200\). The extra information is about the rate: \(T'(0)=-5\).
  2. Put \(t=0\) into the equation: \(-5=-k(200-65)=-135k\Rightarrow k=\frac{5}{135}=\frac1{27}\).
  3. \(T(t)=65+135e^{-t/27}\), so \(T(5)=65+135e^{-5/27}\approx 177.18\).
\(T(5)\approx 177.2\) °F
i
The slide's handwritten note says T(1)=195
The handwriting on the slide reads the data as \(T(1)=195\). That is an approximation of "cooling at 5° per minute". With \(T(1)=195\) you get \(e^{-k}=\frac{130}{135}\) and \(T(5)\approx 176.8\) °F — almost the same. The exact reading of the sentence is \(T'(0)=-5\).
Exercises 10.1 #3 · Week+5.pdf p.7A room is kept at 68 °F. A pie taken out of a 350 °F oven has cooled to 150 °F after 45 minutes. When will it reach 80 °F?
  1. \(T(t)=68+282e^{-kt}\) (\(T_0-T_m=350-68=282\))
  2. \(T(45)=150\): \(e^{-45k}=\frac{82}{282}\).
  3. Want \(T(\bar t)=80\): \(e^{-k\bar t}=\frac{12}{282}\). Take logs and divide: \(\dfrac{\bar t}{45}=\dfrac{\ln(12/282)}{\ln(82/282)}\).
\(\bar t=45\,\dfrac{\ln(12/282)}{\ln(82/282)}\approx 115\) minutes

2. Problems in mechanics: falling objects

Newton's second law: the rate of change of momentum equals the force. For constant mass:

\[ \frac{d}{dt}(mv)=F \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F=ma=m\frac{dv}{dt} \]
Newton's second law (Week+5.pdf p.8)

\(m\) = mass, \(v\) = velocity, \(a=\frac{dv}{dt}\) = acceleration, \(F\) = total force. Below, \(k\) is the drag coefficient and \(g\) the gravitational constant.

Falling through air. Two forces act: gravity \(mg\) (down, the positive direction) and air resistance \(-kv\) (opposite to the motion, proportional to speed). So

\[ m\frac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{k}{m}v=g \]
Falling body with air resistance (Week+5.pdf p.9)

It is both separable and linear. Solving with \(v(0)=v_0\) (Week+5.pdf p.10):

\[ v(t)=\left(v_0-\frac{mg}{k}\right)e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}+\frac{mg}{k} \]
Velocity of a falling object
→
Terminal (limiting) velocity
As \(t\to\infty\), \(e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}\to 0\), so \(v(t)\to \frac{mg}{k}\). This is the speed at which air resistance exactly cancels gravity: \(mg-kv=0\). You can read it straight from the equation without solving it.

Distance. Velocity is the derivative of position, so the distance fallen is \(x(t)=\int v(t)\,dt\) with \(x(0)=0\).

Exercises 10.2 #1 · Week+5.pdf p.11–16 (handwritten solution)A parachutist bails out at 10 000 ft, falls freely for 20 seconds, then opens her parachute. Air resistance is proportional to speed with \(k_1=0.15\) without the parachute and \(k_2=1.5\) with it. (a) IVP for the free fall; (b) IVP after the parachute opens; (c) total time to land. The lecturer takes \(m=60\), \(g=10\).
  1. (a) \(\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{mg-k_1v}{m}\Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{0.15}{60}v=10\), \(v(0)=0\), for \(0\le t\le 20\).
  2. Linear, \(\mu=e^{\int\frac{k}{m}dt}=e^{\frac{k}{m}t}\): \(\frac{d}{dt}\left(ve^{\frac{k}{m}t}\right)=ge^{\frac{k}{m}t}\Rightarrow v=\frac{mg}{k}+Ce^{-\frac{k}{m}t}\). With \(v(0)=0\): \(C=-\frac{mg}{k}\).
  3. \(\frac{mg}{k_1}=\frac{600}{0.15}=4000\), \(\frac{k_1}{m}=\frac{1}{400}\): \(\;v_1(t)=4000\left(1-e^{-t/400}\right)\).
  4. Distance: \(x_1(t)=\int v_1\,dt=4000t+1\,600\,000\,e^{-t/400}+C\); \(x_1(0)=0\Rightarrow C=-1\,600\,000\), so \(x_1(t)=4000t+1\,600\,000\left(e^{-t/400}-1\right)\).
  5. \(x_1(20)\approx 1967\approx 2000\) and \(v_1(20)=4000(1-e^{-0.05})\approx 195\). (the lecturer rounds to 2000)
  6. (b) Restart the clock when the chute opens: \(\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{600-1.5v}{60}\), \(v_2(0)=v_1(20)\approx 195\). Now \(\frac{mg}{k_2}=400\), \(\frac{k_2}{m}=\frac1{40}\): \(v_2=400+Ce^{-t/40}\), and \(400+C=195\Rightarrow C=-205\).
  7. \(v_2(t)=400-205e^{-t/40}\); \(x_2(t)=400t+8200\left(e^{-t/40}-1\right)\) (\(\int -205e^{-t/40}dt=8200e^{-t/40}\), then \(x_2(0)=0\))
  8. (c) Remaining height \(\approx 10\,000-2000=8000\): solve \(400\bar t+8200\left(e^{-\bar t/40}-1\right)=8000\). This cannot be solved by algebra; trying values gives \(\bar t\approx 31\).
\(v_1=4000(1-e^{-t/400})\), \(v_2=400-205e^{-t/40}\); total time \(\approx 20+31=51\) seconds
i
Units in this exercise
The exercise does not give the mass; the handwritten solution assumes \(m=60\) and \(g=10\) and then treats the 10 000 ft as if it were in the same unit as these numbers. On the exam, use exactly the data you are given; the method (two IVPs, the second starting with the final velocity of the first) is the point.
Exercises 10.2 #2 · Week+5.pdf p.11A 1 kg steel ball is dropped from 793 m with no initial velocity. Air resistance is \(\frac18 v\). (a) Find the limiting velocity. (b) Find approximately how long it takes to hit the ground (\(g=9.8\)).
  1. \(1\cdot\frac{dv}{dt}=9.8-\frac18 v\), \(v(0)=0\). So \(v(t)=78.4\left(1-e^{-t/8}\right)\). (\(\frac{mg}{k}=\frac{9.8}{1/8}=78.4\), \(\frac{k}{m}=\frac18\))
  2. (a) \(\lim_{t\to\infty}v(t)=78.4\) m/s.
  3. (b) \(x(t)=\int_0^t v=78.4t-627.2\left(1-e^{-t/8}\right)\). Set \(x(t)=793\) and solve numerically.
limiting velocity 78.4 m/s; hits the ground after about 17.2 s

3. Rate problems: growth and decay

Intuition. The more nuclei (or bacteria) there are, the more decay (or divide) per second. So the rate is proportional to the amount itself.

\[ \frac{dN}{dt}=kN \;\Rightarrow\; N(t)=N_0e^{kt} \]
Growth (k positive) or decay (k negative) — Week+5.pdf p.17–19

It is separable (the lecturer also solved it as a linear equation with \(\mu=e^{-kt}\)). With the printed convention \(\frac{dx}{dt}=-kx\), \(k\gt 0\), the answer is \(x(t)=x_0e^{-kt}\) — the same thing.

Example 29 · Week+5.pdf p.17–21Half of the original number of Polonium-210 nuclei disintegrate in 138 years. (1) What percentage remains after 414 years? (2) When will only one-tenth remain?
  1. \(N(t)\) = nuclei at time \(t\) years; \(N(0)=N_0\), \(N(138)=\frac{N_0}{2}\).
  2. \(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN\Rightarrow N(t)=Ce^{kt}\); \(N(0)=N_0\Rightarrow C=N_0\).
  3. \(\frac{N_0}{2}=N_0e^{138k}\Rightarrow -\ln 2=138k\Rightarrow k=-\frac{\ln 2}{138}\).
  4. So \(N(t)=N_0e^{-\frac{\ln 2}{138}t}=N_0\,2^{-t/138}=N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/138}\).
  5. (1) \(N(414)=N_0\,2^{-414/138}=N_0\,2^{-3}=\frac{N_0}{8}\), i.e. 12.5%. (414 = 3 half-lives)
  6. (2) \(N_0\,2^{-T/138}=\frac{N_0}{10}\Rightarrow -\frac{T}{138}\ln 2=-\ln 10\Rightarrow T=\frac{138\ln 10}{\ln 2}\).
(1) 12.5% remains; (2) \(T=\frac{138\ln 10}{\ln 2}\approx 458.4\) years (about 458 years and 5 months)
★
Half-life form
If the half-life is \(h\), then directly \(N(t)=N_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/h}\). After 1, 2, 3 half-lives: 50%, 25%, 12.5%. Similarly, "doubles every \(d\) hours" gives \(N(t)=N_0\,2^{t/d}\).

Exercises 10.3 (homework on Week+5.pdf p.22–23), solved

Exercises 10.3 #1 · Week+5.pdf p.22 — this exact problem was Question 1 of the 2023 midtermDuring a chemical reaction, substance A is converted into substance B at a rate proportional to the square of the amount of A. Initially 50 g of A is present, and after 2 hours only 10 g remain. How much A is present after 4 hours?
  1. \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\), \(A(0)=50\), \(A(2)=10\). ("converted" = decreasing, so minus; "square" gives \(A^2\))
  2. Separable. For \(A\ne 0\): \(\int\frac{dA}{A^2}=-\int k\,dt\Rightarrow -\frac1A=-kt-C\Rightarrow A=\frac{1}{kt+C}\).
  3. \(A(0)=50\Rightarrow C=\frac1{50}\Rightarrow A(t)=\frac{50}{50kt+1}\).
  4. \(A(2)=10\Rightarrow \frac{50}{100k+1}=10\Rightarrow 100k=4\Rightarrow k=\frac1{25}\). So \(A(t)=\frac{50}{2t+1}\).
\(A(4)=\frac{50}{9}\approx 5.56\) g
!
Not exponential!
With \(A^2\) the answer is not \(Ce^{kt}\). Students who memorise "rate problems give exponentials" write \(A=50e^{-kt}\) and get 2 g — wrong. Always solve the equation you actually wrote.
Exercises 10.3 #2 · Week+5.pdf p.22A substance A transforms into another substance. After 1 hour 50 g of A remain, after 3 hours 25 g remain. (a) How much was present at the beginning? (b) How much after 5 hours? (c) When will there be 2 g?
  1. No "square" is mentioned, so use the basic rate law \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA\Rightarrow A=A_0e^{-kt}\).
  2. Divide the two data: \(\frac{A(3)}{A(1)}=e^{-2k}=\frac{25}{50}=\frac12\). So the half-life is 2 hours and \(A(t)=A_0\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/2}\).
  3. (a) \(A(1)=A_0\cdot 2^{-1/2}=50\Rightarrow A_0=50\sqrt2\approx 70.7\) g.
  4. (b) \(A(5)\) is one half-life after \(A(3)\): \(12.5\) g.
  5. (c) \(50\left(\tfrac12\right)^{(t-1)/2}=2\Rightarrow \frac{t-1}{2}=\log_2 25\Rightarrow t=1+\frac{2\ln 25}{\ln 2}\).
(a) \(50\sqrt2\approx 70.7\) g; (b) 12.5 g; (c) \(t\approx 10.3\) hours
Exercises 10.3 #3 · Week+5.pdf p.23Bacteria grow at a rate proportional to the number present. (a) If the number doubles every 10 hours, how long until it triples? (b) If there are 5 million after 6 hours and 8 million after 9 hours, how many were there initially?
  1. \(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN\Rightarrow N=N_0e^{kt}\).
  2. (a) \(e^{10k}=2\Rightarrow k=\frac{\ln 2}{10}\). Triple: \(e^{kt}=3\Rightarrow t=\frac{10\ln 3}{\ln 2}\approx 15.85\) h.
  3. (b) \(\frac{N(9)}{N(6)}=e^{3k}=\frac85\). Then \(N_0=N(6)e^{-6k}=5\left(\tfrac58\right)^2=\frac{125}{64}\).
(a) about 15.85 hours; (b) \(\frac{125}{64}\approx 1.95\) million

4. Mixture problems

Intuition. Think of the salt in the tank as money in a bank account: the change per minute is what comes in minus what goes out.

\[ \frac{dx}{dt}=r_{\text{in}}-r_{\text{out}} \]
Mixture law: x = amount in the tank (Week+5.pdf p.25)
  • \(r_{\text{in}}=(\text{inflow rate})\times(\text{concentration coming in})\) — usually a number.
  • \(r_{\text{out}}=(\text{outflow rate})\times\dfrac{x(t)}{V(t)}\) — the concentration in the tank is "salt ÷ volume".
  • Volume: \(V(t)=V_0+(\text{inflow}-\text{outflow})\,t\). If the two flows are equal, the volume is constant.

Check the units: (lt/min)·(kg/lt) = kg/min. Both rates must be in "amount per time".

Example 30 · Week+5.pdf p.25–29A large tank holds 1000 lt of water. Brine with 1 kg/lt of salt flows in at 6 lt/min; the well-stirred solution flows out at 6 lt/min. When will the concentration of salt in the tank reach \(\frac12\) kg/lt?
  1. \(x(t)\) = kg of salt at time \(t\) min; pure water at first, so \(x(0)=0\).
  2. \(r_{\text{in}}=(6\ \text{lt/min})(1\ \text{kg/lt})=6\) kg/min; volume stays 1000 lt, so \(r_{\text{out}}=6\cdot\frac{x}{1000}=\frac{3}{500}x\) kg/min.
  3. IVP: \(\frac{dx}{dt}=6-\frac{3}{500}x\), \(x(0)=0\). Linear: \(\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{3}{500}x=6\), \(\mu=e^{\frac{3}{500}t}\).
  4. \(x(t)=e^{-\frac{3}{500}t}\left(\int 6e^{\frac{3}{500}t}dt+C\right)=1000+Ce^{-\frac{3}{500}t}\); \(x(0)=0\Rightarrow C=-1000\).
  5. \(x(t)=1000\left(1-e^{-\frac{3t}{500}}\right)\), concentration \(\frac{x}{1000}=1-e^{-\frac{3t}{500}}\).
  6. Set concentration \(=\frac12\) (i.e. \(x(T)=500\)): \(e^{-\frac{3T}{500}}=\frac12\Rightarrow T=\frac{500}{3}\ln 2\).
\(T=\frac{500}{3}\ln 2\approx 116\) min; in the long run \(x(t)\to 1000\) kg
Exercises 10.4 #2 · Week+5.pdf p.29 (volume changes!)A tank holds 200 lt of salt water containing 30 g of salt. Brine of 1 g/lt pours in at 4 lt/min; the well-mixed solution pours out at 5 lt/min. Find the amount of salt at time \(t\).
  1. Volume: \(V(t)=200+(4-5)t=200-t\) (it loses 1 lt per minute)
  2. \(r_{\text{in}}=4\cdot 1=4\) g/min; \(r_{\text{out}}=5\cdot\frac{x}{200-t}\).
  3. \(\frac{dx}{dt}+\frac{5}{200-t}x=4\), \(x(0)=30\). Linear with \(\mu=e^{\int\frac{5}{200-t}dt}=e^{-5\ln(200-t)}=(200-t)^{-5}\).
  4. \(\frac{d}{dt}\left[(200-t)^{-5}x\right]=4(200-t)^{-5}\Rightarrow (200-t)^{-5}x=(200-t)^{-4}+C\).
  5. \(x=(200-t)+C(200-t)^5\); \(x(0)=30\Rightarrow C=-\frac{170}{200^5}\).
\(x(t)=(200-t)-170\left(\frac{200-t}{200}\right)^5\) grams, \(0\le t\lt 200\)
Exercises 10.4 #3 · Week+5.pdf p.29A room of 1000 m³ has air with 0.15% CO₂. From \(t=0\), outside air with 0.05% CO₂ is let in at 500 m³/min (and the mixed air leaves at the same rate). (a) Percentage of CO₂ after 3 min? (b) When is it 0.1%?
  1. \(x(t)\) = m³ of CO₂ in the room; \(x(0)=0.0015\cdot 1000=1.5\).
  2. \(r_{\text{in}}=500\cdot 0.0005=0.25\), \(r_{\text{out}}=500\cdot\frac{x}{1000}=\frac{x}{2}\): \(\;\frac{dx}{dt}=0.25-\frac{x}{2}\).
  3. Solution: \(x(t)=0.5+e^{-t/2}\) (steady value \(0.5\); \(x(0)=1.5\) gives the coefficient 1). Percentage \(=\frac{x}{1000}\cdot 100=0.05+0.1e^{-t/2}\)%.
  4. (a) \(t=3\): \(0.05+0.1e^{-1.5}\approx 0.0723\)%. (b) \(0.1e^{-t/2}=0.05\Rightarrow t=2\ln 2\).
(a) about 0.072%; (b) \(t=2\ln 2\approx 1.39\) min
i
Exercises 10.4 #1
On the slide, the concentration of the incoming water is missing ("a salt concentration of lbs/gal"). With an unknown concentration \(c\) lb/gal the set-up would be \(V(t)=600+3t\), \(\frac{dx}{dt}=9c-\frac{6x}{600+3t}\), \(x(0)=5\) — practise the set-up; the number cannot be computed without \(c\).
!
Where students lose points in word problems
  • Forgetting the minus sign for decrease, or putting it twice.
  • Writing \(r_{\text{out}}=(\text{rate})\cdot x\) instead of \((\text{rate})\cdot\frac{x}{V}\).
  • Forgetting that the volume changes when inflow ≠ outflow.
  • Answering with \(k\) or \(C\) instead of the number the question asks for (and without units).
  • Using the exponential formula when the rate is proportional to \(A^2\) or \(\sqrt A\).

In one minute

  • "Rate of change" = derivative; "proportional to" = \(k\times\). Decrease ⇒ minus sign with \(k\gt 0\).
  • Cooling: \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_m)\Rightarrow T=T_m+(T_0-T_m)e^{-kt}\).
  • Falling: \(m\frac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv\Rightarrow v=\left(v_0-\frac{mg}{k}\right)e^{-\frac{k}{m}t}+\frac{mg}{k}\); limiting velocity \(\frac{mg}{k}\); distance = \(\int v\,dt\).
  • Decay/growth: \(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN\Rightarrow N=N_0e^{kt}\); half-life \(h\): \(N=N_0(\frac12)^{t/h}\).
  • Rate ∝ \(A^2\): \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\Rightarrow A=\frac{1}{kt+C}\) (midterm 2023 Q1).
  • Mixture: \(\frac{dx}{dt}=r_{\text{in}}-r_{\text{out}}\), \(r_{\text{out}}=\text{flow}\cdot\frac{x}{V(t)}\), \(V(t)=V_0+(\text{in}-\text{out})t\).
  • Two data points ⇒ find \(C\) (from \(t=0\)) and \(k\); then answer the question with units.

chapters.title: Higher-order linear equations and reduction of order
chapters.lead: Learn the language of n-th order linear equations (operator, IVP, linear independence, Wronskian, fundamental set, general solution) and the reduction-of-order trick that turns one known solution into a second one — that trick is midterm Question 5.
chapters.html:
The big picture

Until now every equation had only \(y'\). Now we allow \(y''\), \(y'''\), …, \(y^{(n)}\). We will not yet learn how to solve these in general. This week is about the rules of the game: when does a solution exist, how many solutions do we need, how do we check they are "really different", and how do we build all solutions from a few. At the end comes one real solving technique: reduction of order.

1. Linear equations of order n

\[ a_0(x)\frac{d^ny}{dx^n}+a_1(x)\frac{d^{n-1}y}{dx^{n-1}}+\cdots+a_{n-1}(x)\frac{dy}{dx}+a_n(x)\,y=f(x) \]
Linear ODE of order n (Week+6.pdf p.1)

"Linear" means: \(y\) and its derivatives appear only to the first power, are not multiplied together, and the coefficients \(a_0,\dots,a_n\) depend only on \(x\). We assume the \(a_i\) and \(f\) are continuous on an interval and \(a_0(x)\ne 0\) there.

For \(n=2\) this is the case you will see most: \(a_0(x)y''+a_1(x)y'+a_2(x)y=f(x)\).

The operator notation

Write \(D\) for "take the derivative": \(D^0y=y\), \(Dy=y'\), \(D^2y=y''\), …, \(D^ny=y^{(n)}\). Then the left side is one machine \(L\) that eats a function and returns a function:

\[ L[y](x):=a_0(x)y^{(n)}(x)+a_1(x)y^{(n-1)}(x)+\cdots+a_n(x)y(x). \]

\(L=L(D)\) is called the n-th order linear differential operator (Definition 22). The equation is simply \(L(D)y=f\).

non-homogeneous term
the right-hand side \(f\)
homogeneous equation
\(f\equiv 0\): \(L(D)y=0\)
linear mapping
\(L(c_1y_1+c_2y_2)=c_1L(y_1)+c_2L(y_2)\) — this one property gives almost every theorem of this chapter

2. The IVP and existence–uniqueness

An n-th order IVP needs the equation plus n conditions, all at the same point \(x_0\):

\[ L(D)y=f(x),\quad y(x_0)=y_0,\ y'(x_0)=y_1,\ \dots,\ y^{(n-1)}(x_0)=y_{n-1}. \]
★
Tip
Second order ⇒ two conditions: a value \(y(x_0)\) and a slope \(y'(x_0)\). Think of a ball: you need where it starts and how fast it starts.
✓
Theorem 10 (Existence and Uniqueness) — Week+6.pdf p.5
Let \(a_0,a_1,\dots,a_n\) and \(f\) be continuous on an interval \(I\) with \(a_0(x)\ne 0\) for all \(x\in I\). Then for any \(x_0\in I\) the IVP above has a unique solution, which exists on the entire interval \(I\).
Example 31 · Week+6.pdf p.6–7Show that \(y''+3xy'+x^3y=e^x\), \(y(1)=2\), \(y'(1)=5\) has a unique solution on \((-\infty,\infty)\).
  1. Read off: \(a_0(x)=1\), \(a_1(x)=3x\), \(a_2(x)=x^3\), \(f(x)=e^x\).
  2. All are continuous for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), and \(a_0=1\ne 0\) everywhere.
  3. By the existence–uniqueness theorem the IVP has a unique solution on \(\mathbb R\).
Unique solution on the whole real line.
→
Corollary 1 (the trivial solution)
If \(\varphi\) solves the homogeneous equation \(L(D)y=0\) and \(\varphi(x_0)=\varphi'(x_0)=\cdots=\varphi^{(n-1)}(x_0)=0\), then \(\varphi\equiv 0\). Reason: \(y\equiv 0\) already solves that IVP, and the solution is unique.

3. Superposition

A linear combination of \(f_1,\dots,f_n\) is \(c_1f_1+c_2f_2+\cdots+c_nf_n\) with constants \(c_i\) (Definition 23).

✓
Theorem 11 (Superposition principle) — Week+6.pdf p.7
If \(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n\) are solutions of the homogeneous linear equation \(L(D)y=0\), then every linear combination \(c_1\varphi_1+\cdots+c_n\varphi_n\) is also a solution.

Why (the lecturer's proof): \(L(D)(c_1\varphi_1+\cdots+c_n\varphi_n)=c_1\underbrace{L(D)\varphi_1}_{0}+\cdots+c_n\underbrace{L(D)\varphi_n}_{0}=0\).

!
Two conditions for superposition
It needs (1) linear and (2) homogeneous. If either fails, a combination of solutions is usually not a solution (see Example 36 below).

4. Linear dependence and independence

Intuition. Functions are dependent if one of them is "made of" the others (like \(3\sin x\) is made of \(\sin x\)). Then it brings nothing new. They are independent if none of them can be built from the others.

✓
Definition 24 — Week+6.pdf p.9
\(f_1,\dots,f_n\) are linearly dependent on \(I\) if there are constants \(c_1,\dots,c_n\), not all zero, with \(c_1f_1(x)+\cdots+c_nf_n(x)=0\) for all \(x\in I\).
They are linearly independent on \(I\) if \(c_1f_1(x)+\cdots+c_nf_n(x)=0\) for all \(x\in I\) implies \(c_1=c_2=\cdots=c_n=0\).
Example 32 · Week+6.pdf p.10–11(1) Show \(f_1=x\), \(f_2=x^2\) are linearly independent on \([0,1]\). (2) Show \(f_1=\sin x\), \(f_2=3\sin x\) are linearly dependent on \([0,\pi]\).
  1. (1) Suppose \(c_1x+c_2x^2=0\) for all \(x\in[0,1]\). A polynomial that is zero at infinitely many points is the zero polynomial: \(c_1x+c_2x^2=0x+0x^2\), so \(c_1=c_2=0\). (compare coefficients)
  2. (2) \(c_1\sin x+3c_2\sin x=(c_1+3c_2)\sin x=0\). Choose \(c_1=-3\), \(c_2=1\): \((-3+3)\sin x=0\) ✓, and the constants are not both zero.
\(x, x^2\) independent; \(\sin x, 3\sin x\) dependent

5. The Wronskian

\[ W[f_1,\dots,f_n](x)=\begin{vmatrix} f_1 & f_2 & \cdots & f_n\\ f_1' & f_2' & \cdots & f_n'\\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\ f_1^{(n-1)} & f_2^{(n-1)} & \cdots & f_n^{(n-1)}\end{vmatrix} \]
Wronskian, Definition 25 (Week+6.pdf p.12)

Row 1: the functions. Row 2: their first derivatives. … The last (\(n\)-th) row: the \((n-1)\)-th derivatives. For two functions:

\[ W[f_1,f_2]=\begin{vmatrix} f_1 & f_2\\ f_1' & f_2'\end{vmatrix}=f_1f_2'-f_2f_1'. \]
✓
Theorems 12, 13 and Corollary 2 — Week+6.pdf p.13–14
Let \(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n\) be solutions of the n-th order homogeneous linear equation \(L(D)y=0\) on \(I\).
  • (Th. 12) They are linearly dependent ⇔ \(W(x)\equiv 0\) on \(I\).
  • (Th. 13) Either \(W(x)\equiv 0\) on \(I\), or \(W(x)\ne 0\) for all \(x\in I\) — nothing in between.
  • (Cor. 2) They are linearly independent ⇔ \(W(x)\ne 0\) for all \(x\in I\).
★
Practical use
Because of Theorem 13, for solutions you only need to check \(W\) at one convenient point. If it is not zero there, it is never zero, and the solutions are independent.
Example 33 · Week+6.pdf p.14–15Show that \(\cos x\) and \(\sin x\) are linearly independent on \((-\infty,\infty)\).
  1. First check they solve one equation: \(\varphi_1=\cos x\), \(\varphi_1''=-\cos x\), so \(\varphi_1''+\varphi_1=0\). Likewise \(\sin x\). Both solve \(y''+y=0\).
  2. \(W(\cos x,\sin x)=\begin{vmatrix}\cos x & \sin x\\ -\sin x & \cos x\end{vmatrix}=\cos^2x+\sin^2x=1\ne 0\) for all \(x\).
  3. So they are independent, \(\{\cos x,\sin x\}\) is a fundamental set, and the general solution of \(y''+y=0\) is \(y=c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x\).
\(W=1\ne 0\) ⇒ independent; \(y=c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x\)
Example 34 and Remark 5 · Week+6.pdf p.16–18Let \(f_1(x)=x|x|\), \(f_2(x)=x^2\) on \([-1,1]\). Show \(W\equiv 0\) but the functions are independent. Why is that not a contradiction?
  1. \(x|x|=x^2\) for \(x\ge 0\) and \(-x^2\) for \(x\lt 0\), so \(\frac{d}{dx}(x|x|)=2|x|\).
  2. \(W=\begin{vmatrix}x|x| & x^2\\ 2|x| & 2x\end{vmatrix}=2x^2|x|-2x^2|x|=0\) for every \(x\in[-1,1]\).
  3. Independence: suppose \(c_1x|x|+c_2x^2=0\) for all \(x\). At \(x=1\): \(c_1+c_2=0\). At \(x=-1\): \(-c_1+c_2=0\). So \(c_1=c_2=0\).
  4. No contradiction with Corollary 2: these two functions cannot both be solutions of one second-order homogeneous linear equation on \([-1,1]\). The Wronskian test is only guaranteed for solutions.
\(W\equiv 0\), yet independent — the Wronskian criterion needs solutions of \(L(D)y=0\).
!
Watch out
"\(W=0\) ⇒ dependent" is only true when the functions are solutions of the same homogeneous linear equation. For arbitrary functions, check the definition directly (plug in points, as in Example 34).

6. Fundamental set and general solution

✓
Theorem 14, Definitions 26–27 — Week+6.pdf p.18–19
An n-th order homogeneous linear equation \(L(D)y=0\) has n linearly independent solutions \(\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n\), and every solution can be written as \(c_1\varphi_1+\cdots+c_n\varphi_n\).
Such a set \(\{\varphi_1,\dots,\varphi_n\}\) of n independent solutions is a fundamental set of solutions (F.S.S.), and \(\varphi=c_1\varphi_1+\cdots+c_n\varphi_n\) is the general solution of \(L(D)y=0\).
→
Recipe: proving a general solution
To show \(y=c_1\varphi_1+c_2\varphi_2\) is the general solution of a 2nd order homogeneous equation: (1) check each \(\varphi_i\) solves it; (2) compute \(W[\varphi_1,\varphi_2]\ne 0\); (3) conclude F.S.S. and write the combination. Order \(n\) ⇒ you need exactly \(n\) independent solutions.

Exercises 11 (homework on Week+6.pdf p.20), solved

Exercises 11 #1 · Week+6.pdf p.20Check linear independence: (a) \(1, x, x^2, (x+1)^2\); (b) \(\cos x, \sin x, \sin 2x\); (c) \(\pi, \tan^2x, \sec^2x\).
  1. (a) \((x+1)^2=1\cdot 1+2\cdot x+1\cdot x^2\). So \(1\cdot 1+2x+x^2-(x+1)^2=0\) with constants \((1,2,1,-1)\), not all zero: dependent.
  2. (b) Suppose \(c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x+c_3\sin 2x=0\) for all \(x\). \(x=0\): \(c_1=0\). \(x=\frac{\pi}{2}\): \(c_2=0\). \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\): \(c_3=0\). Independent. (their Wronskian is \(-3\sin 2x\), not identically zero, which agrees)
  3. (c) \(\sec^2x-\tan^2x=1\), so \(1\cdot\pi+\pi\tan^2x-\pi\sec^2x=\pi(1+\tan^2x-\sec^2x)=0\): dependent.
(a) dependent, (b) independent, (c) dependent
Exercises 11 #2 · Week+6.pdf p.20Show that \(e^{\alpha x}\) and \(e^{\beta x}\) solve \(y''-(\alpha+\beta)y'+\alpha\beta y=0\) and are independent exactly when \(\alpha\ne\beta\).
  1. \(y=e^{\alpha x}\): \(\alpha^2e^{\alpha x}-(\alpha+\beta)\alpha e^{\alpha x}+\alpha\beta e^{\alpha x}=e^{\alpha x}(\alpha^2-\alpha^2-\alpha\beta+\alpha\beta)=0\). Same for \(e^{\beta x}\) by symmetry.
  2. \(W=\begin{vmatrix}e^{\alpha x} & e^{\beta x}\\ \alpha e^{\alpha x} & \beta e^{\beta x}\end{vmatrix}=(\beta-\alpha)e^{(\alpha+\beta)x}\).
  3. The exponential is never 0, so \(W\ne 0\) ⇔ \(\alpha\ne\beta\).
\(W=(\beta-\alpha)e^{(\alpha+\beta)x}\): independent ⇔ \(\alpha\ne\beta\)
Exercises 11 #3 · Week+6.pdf p.20For \(x\gt 0\), find \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) so that \(1, \frac1x, x^2\) solve \(x^3y'''+\alpha x^2y''+\beta xy'+\gamma y=0\); show they are independent; write the general solution.
  1. \(y=1\): all derivatives 0, leaving \(\gamma=0\).
  2. \(y=x^2\): \(y'=2x\), \(y''=2\), \(y'''=0\): \(2\alpha x^2+2\beta x^2=0\Rightarrow \alpha=-\beta\).
  3. \(y=\frac1x\): \(y'=-x^{-2}\), \(y''=2x^{-3}\), \(y'''=-6x^{-4}\): \(\frac{-6+2\alpha-\beta}{x}=0\Rightarrow -6+3\alpha=0\Rightarrow\alpha=2,\ \beta=-2\).
  4. \(W=\begin{vmatrix}1 & x^{-1} & x^2\\ 0 & -x^{-2} & 2x\\ 0 & 2x^{-3} & 2\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot\left(-2x^{-2}-4x^{-2}\right)=-\frac{6}{x^2}\ne 0\).
\(\alpha=2,\ \beta=-2,\ \gamma=0\); independent; \(y=c_1+\frac{c_2}{x}+c_3x^2\)

7. Non-homogeneous equations

✓
Theorem 15 — Week+6.pdf p.21
If \(\varphi\) solves \(L(D)y=f\) and \(\psi\) solves \(L(D)y=0\), then \(\varphi+\psi\) solves \(L(D)y=f\). (Proof: \(L(\psi+\varphi)=L\psi+L\varphi=0+f\).)
complementary solution \(\varphi_c\)
the general solution of the homogeneous equation \(L(D)y=0\)
particular solution \(\varphi_p\)
any one solution of \(L(D)y=f\) without arbitrary constants
general solution of \(L(D)y=f\)
\(\varphi_c+\varphi_p\) (Definition 28)
Example 35 · Week+6.pdf p.24–25Find the general solution of \(y''+y=x\).
  1. Homogeneous \(y''+y=0\): \(\varphi_c=c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x\) (Example 33).
  2. Try \(\varphi_p=x\): \(\varphi_p'=1\), \(\varphi_p''=0\), so \(\varphi_p''+\varphi_p=0+x=x\) ✓.
\(y=c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x+x\)
!
Watch out
Don't forget to add \(\varphi_p\) at the end (the lecturer circles "+x" in red). The complementary part alone is not the general solution of the non-homogeneous equation.
Example 36 · Week+6.pdf p.26 (why linearity matters)\(yy''+(y')^2=0\) on \([0,1]\) has the solutions \(\varphi_1\equiv 1\) and \(\varphi_2=\sqrt{x}\). Is \(c_1+c_2\sqrt{x}\) a solution?
  1. The equation is not linear (\(yy''\) and \((y')^2\) are products), so superposition is not promised.
  2. Indeed, substituting gives \(yy''+(y')^2=-\frac{c_1c_2}{4x^{3/2}}\), which is not zero when \(c_1c_2\ne 0\).
No: superposition fails for non-linear equations (like \(Ax=b\) vs \(Ax=0\) in linear algebra).
✓
Theorem 16 (superposition for the right-hand side) — Week+6.pdf p.27
If \(L(D)\varphi_1=f_1,\ \dots,\ L(D)\varphi_m=f_m\) and \(f=c_1f_1+\cdots+c_mf_m\), then \(\varphi=c_1\varphi_1+\cdots+c_m\varphi_m\) solves \(L(D)y=f\).
Example 37 · Week+6.pdf p.28The equations \(y''-5y'+6y=1\), \(=x\), \(=e^x\) have particular solutions \(\varphi_1=\frac16\), \(\varphi_2=\frac{x}{6}+\frac{5}{36}\), \(\varphi_3=\frac12e^x\). Find a solution of \(y''-5y'+6y=2e^x+36(x+1)\).
  1. Write the right side as a combination: \(f=36\cdot 1+36\cdot x+2\cdot e^x\).
  2. Use the same coefficients: \(\varphi=36\cdot\frac16+36\left(\frac{x}{6}+\frac{5}{36}\right)+2\cdot\frac12e^x=6+6x+5+e^x\).
\(\varphi=e^x+6x+11\)

Exercises 11.1 (homework on Week+6.pdf p.29), solved

Exercises 11.1 #1 · Week+6.pdf p.29\((x+1)y''+xy'-y=(x+1)^2\), \(x\gt -1\). Show \(\varphi_1=x\), \(\varphi_2=e^{-x}\) solve the homogeneous equation and \(\varphi_p=x^2-x+1\) solves the full one. Write the general solution.
  1. \(x\): \(0+x\cdot 1-x=0\) ✓. \(e^{-x}\): \((x+1)e^{-x}-xe^{-x}-e^{-x}=0\) ✓.
  2. \(W[x,e^{-x}]=x(-e^{-x})-e^{-x}=-(x+1)e^{-x}\ne 0\) for \(x\gt -1\): independent.
  3. \(\varphi_p\): \(\varphi_p'=2x-1\), \(\varphi_p''=2\): \(2(x+1)+x(2x-1)-(x^2-x+1)=x^2+2x+1=(x+1)^2\) ✓.
\(y=c_1x+c_2e^{-x}+x^2-x+1\)
Exercises 11.1 #2 · Week+6.pdf p.29\(y''-\tan x\,y'-\sec^2x\,y=\sec x\tan x\) on \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). Verify \(\sec x\), \(\tan x\) solve the homogeneous equation and \(x\sec x\) the full one; give the general solution.
  1. Substituting (with \(\frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x\), \(\frac{d}{dx}\tan x=\sec^2x\)) gives 0 for \(\sec x\) and \(\tan x\), and \(\sec x\tan x\) for \(x\sec x\).
  2. \(W[\sec x,\tan x]=\sec x\cdot\sec^2x-\tan x\cdot\sec x\tan x=\sec x(\sec^2x-\tan^2x)=\sec x\ne 0\).
\(y=c_1\sec x+c_2\tan x+x\sec x\)

8. Reduction of order

Intuition. If you already know one solution \(\varphi_p\) of a homogeneous linear equation, you look for the next one in the form "the known one times an unknown function". Plugging that in kills the \(z\)-term (because \(\varphi_p\) is a solution), and what remains is an equation for \(z'\) of one order lower.

✓
Theorem 17 — Week+6.pdf p.31
Let \(\varphi_p\) be a non-trivial solution of the n-th order homogeneous linear equation \(a_0(x)y^{(n)}+\cdots+a_n(x)y=0\). Then the transformation \(\;y=\varphi_p\,z\;\) reduces it to an \((n-1)\)-st order homogeneous linear equation in the dependent variable \(\;w:=\frac{dz}{dx}\).
i
Notation
On these slides \(\varphi_p\) just means "the known solution" of the homogeneous equation — here the "p" is not "particular solution of the non-homogeneous equation". Remark 6: for a second-order equation you must already know one solution.
\[ y=\varphi_p z,\qquad y'=\varphi_p'z+\varphi_p z',\qquad y''=\varphi_p''z+2\varphi_p'z'+\varphi_p z'' \]
The substitution and its derivatives (handwritten on Week+6.pdf p.31)

What always happens for second order. Put these into \(a_0y''+a_1y'+a_2y=0\) and group by \(z''\), \(z'\), \(z\):

\[ a_0\varphi_p\,z''+\left(2a_0\varphi_p'+a_1\varphi_p\right)z'+\underbrace{\left(a_0\varphi_p''+a_1\varphi_p'+a_2\varphi_p\right)}_{=0\ \text{since }\varphi_p\text{ is a solution}}z=0. \]

So with \(w=z'\):

\[ a_0\varphi_p\,w'+\left(2a_0\varphi_p'+a_1\varphi_p\right)w=0 \]
Reduced equation: first order, linear and separable
★
Use it as a check
Always write the substitution steps on the exam (that is what is graded). But you can use the boxed reduced equation to check your \(z'\) coefficient — the place where most mistakes happen (including in the 2023 midterm's handwritten solution, see Chapter 16). If the \(z\)-coefficient does not come out 0, you made an algebra mistake or \(\varphi_p\) is not a solution.
→
The 6 steps of reduction of order (2nd order)
  1. Check that the given \(y_1\) really is a solution (quick).
  2. Put \(y=y_1z\); write \(y'\) and \(y''\).
  3. Substitute and collect: the \(z\)-term must vanish.
  4. Set \(w=z'\): solve the first-order equation for \(w\) (separate, partial fractions); choose the constant \(=1\).
  5. \(z=\int w\,dx\) (choose the constant \(=0\)); \(y_2=y_1z\).
  6. Write the F.S.S. \(\{y_1,y_2\}\) and the general solution \(y=c_1y_1+c_2y_2\).
Example 38 · Week+6.pdf p.32–36Given that \(\varphi_p(x)=x\) is a solution of \((x^2+1)y''-2xy'+2y=0\), find a linearly independent solution by reduction of order.
  1. \(y=xz\Rightarrow y'=z+xz'\), \(y''=z'+z'+xz''=2z'+xz''\).
  2. Substitute: \((x^2+1)(2z'+xz'')-2x(z+xz')+2xz=0\).
  3. Collect: \(x(x^2+1)z''+z'\left(2x^2+2-2x^2\right)+z(-2x+2x)=0\Rightarrow x(x^2+1)z''+2z'=0\). (the \(z\)-term is 0 — good sign)
  4. \(w=z'\): \(\frac{dw}{dx}+\frac{2}{x(x^2+1)}w=0\) (linear, separable).
  5. Partial fractions: \(\frac{2}{x(x^2+1)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+1}\Rightarrow A=2,\ B=-2,\ C=0\).
  6. \(\mu(x)=e^{\int\left(\frac2x-\frac{2x}{x^2+1}\right)dx}=e^{2\ln x-\ln(x^2+1)}=\frac{x^2}{x^2+1}\), so \(w=C\frac{x^2+1}{x^2}=C\left(1+\frac{1}{x^2}\right)\); choose \(C=1\).
  7. \(z=\int\left(1+\frac1{x^2}\right)dx=x-\frac1x+d\); choose \(d=0\).
  8. \(y_2=x\cdot\left(x-\frac1x\right)=x^2-1\). Check: \((x^2+1)\cdot 2-2x\cdot 2x+2(x^2-1)=0\) ✓; \(W[x,x^2-1]=x^2+1\ne 0\) ✓.
F.S.S. \(=\{x,\ x^2-1\}\); general solution \(y=c_1x+c_2(x^2-1)\)
Example 39 · Week+6.pdf p.32 (homework)Given \(\varphi_p(x)=x\) solves \(y''-2xy'+2y=0\), find the second linearly independent solution.
  1. \(y=xz\): \(y'=z+xz'\), \(y''=2z'+xz''\).
  2. \((2z'+xz'')-2x(z+xz')+2xz=xz''+(2-2x^2)z'=0\).
  3. \(w=z'\): \(\frac{w'}{w}=\frac{2x^2-2}{x}=2x-\frac{2}{x}\Rightarrow \ln|w|=x^2-2\ln|x|\Rightarrow w=\frac{e^{x^2}}{x^2}\).
  4. \(z=\int\frac{e^{x^2}}{x^2}\,dx\). This integral has no elementary antiderivative, so we leave it as an integral.
\(y_2=x\displaystyle\int\frac{e^{x^2}}{x^2}\,dx\); general solution \(y=c_1x+c_2\,x\displaystyle\int\frac{e^{x^2}}{x^2}\,dx\)
i
Note
Leaving an integral is acceptable only when it cannot be done with elementary functions (like \(e^{x^2}\)). If it can be done — e.g. \(\int\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}dx\) — do it ("Solve it!" as the lecturer wrote on the midterm).
Exercises 12 #1 · Week+6.pdf p.37Obtain the general solution of \(y''-\frac{4x}{2x-1}y'+\frac{4}{2x-1}y=0\) for \(x\gt 1\), after finding an exponential solution \(\varphi_p=e^{\lambda x}\).
  1. Put \(y=e^{\lambda x}\) and multiply by \((2x-1)e^{-\lambda x}\): \(\lambda^2(2x-1)-4x\lambda+4=0\), i.e. \(x(2\lambda^2-4\lambda)+(4-\lambda^2)=0\) for all \(x\).
  2. Both brackets must vanish: \(2\lambda(\lambda-2)=0\) and \(\lambda^2=4\) ⇒ \(\lambda=2\). So \(y_1=e^{2x}\).
  3. \(y=e^{2x}z\): \(y'=e^{2x}(2z+z')\), \(y''=e^{2x}(4z+4z'+z'')\). Substituting and dividing by \(e^{2x}\): \(z''+\left(4-\frac{4x}{2x-1}\right)z'=0\), i.e. \((2x-1)w'+(4x-4)w=0\).
  4. \(\frac{w'}{w}=-\frac{4x-4}{2x-1}=-2+\frac{2}{2x-1}\Rightarrow w=(2x-1)e^{-2x}\).
  5. \(z=\int(2x-1)e^{-2x}dx=-xe^{-2x}\) (integration by parts; check by differentiating), so \(y_2=e^{2x}\cdot(-xe^{-2x})=-x\); drop the sign.
\(y=c_1e^{2x}+c_2x\)
!
Where students lose points in reduction of order
  • Wrong \(y''\): it is \(\varphi_p''z+2\varphi_p'z'+\varphi_pz''\) — the middle term has a 2.
  • Algebra slip in the \(z'\) coefficient (expand everything, then collect).
  • Forgetting \(y_2=y_1z\) — giving \(z\) or \(w\) as the answer.
  • Stopping at \(y_2\): the question usually also asks for the general solution \(c_1y_1+c_2y_2\).
  • Leaving an integral that can be computed.

In one minute

  • Linear n-th order: \(a_0y^{(n)}+\cdots+a_ny=f\), written \(L(D)y=f\); homogeneous if \(f\equiv 0\).
  • IVP needs n conditions at one point; continuous coefficients and \(a_0\ne 0\) on \(I\) ⇒ unique solution on all of \(I\).
  • Superposition: combinations of solutions of a linear homogeneous equation are solutions.
  • Dependent = some non-trivial combination is identically 0. Wronskian = determinant of functions and derivatives.
  • For solutions: independent ⇔ \(W\ne 0\) (check one point). \(x|x|, x^2\): \(W\equiv 0\) but independent — they are not solutions.
  • General solution = \(c_1\varphi_1+\cdots+c_n\varphi_n\) from a fundamental set; non-homogeneous: \(\varphi_c+\varphi_p\).
  • Reduction of order: \(y=y_1z\), \(w=z'\), reduced equation \(a_0y_1w'+(2a_0y_1'+a_1y_1)w=0\); then \(y_2=y_1\int w\).

chapters.title: Which method? Recognising the equation
chapters.lead: The exam never tells you which method to use. This chapter is a checklist you can run in your head in under a minute for any first-order equation.
chapters.html:
→
The one habit that wins points
Before you integrate anything, write down the type and the reason: “Not exact, because \(M_y\ne N_x\)”, “Bernoulli with \(n=3\)”, “homogeneous: \(f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\)”. Graders give method points even when the algebra slips, and naming the type makes you check it.

Step 0: get the equation into a standard shape
