Write it in both forms, because different tests need different forms:

\[ \frac{dy}{dx}=f(x,y) \qquad\text{and}\qquad M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0 \]
Derivative form and differential form

To switch: \( \dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{M}{N} \). Move everything to one side and simplify first. Many equations become obviously separable or linear after one line of algebra.

The checklist, in order

Ask the questions in this order. Stop at the first yes.

#Ask yourselfIf yesCh.
1Can I write \(y' = g(x)\,h(y)\)?Separable. Divide by \(h(y)\), integrate both sides. Then check \(h(y)=0\).4
2Is \(y\) (and \(y'\)) only to the first power, never multiplied together? \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)\)Linear. \(\mu = e^{\int p\,dx}\), then \((\mu y)' = \mu q\).7
3In \(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\): is \(M_y = N_x\)?Exact. Build \(F\) with \(F_x=M\), \(F_y=N\). Answer \(F=C\).5
4Not exact, but \(\frac{1}{N}(M_y-N_x)\) has only \(x\)? Or \(\frac{1}{M}(M_y-N_x)\) has only \(y\)?Integrating factor \(\mu(x)=e^{\int f}\) or \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int g}\). Then solve as exact.6
5\(y' + p(x)y = q(x)\,y^n\) with \(n\ne 0,1\)?Bernoulli. \(u = y^{1-n}\) gives a linear equation in \(u\).8
6Does \(y'\) depend only on \(\frac{y}{x}\)? Is \(f(tx,ty)=f(x,y)\)? Do all terms of \(M\) and \(N\) have the same total degree?Homogeneous. \(y=ux\), \(y'=u+xu'\) gives a separable equation.9
7\((a_1x+b_1y+c_1)dx+(a_2x+b_2y+c_2)dy=0\)?Compute \(\Delta=a_1b_2-a_2b_1\). \(\Delta\ne0\): shift \(x=X+h\), \(y=Y+k\) to make it homogeneous. \(\Delta=0\): use \(z=a_1x+b_1y\).10
8\(y' = p(x)y^2+q(x)y+r(x)\) and a solution \(y_1\) is given?Riccati. \(y=y_1+\frac1u\) gives a linear equation in \(u\).11
9\(y = xy' + f(y')\)?Clairaut. General \(y=cx+f(c)\). Singular: \(x=-f'(p)\), \(y=xp+f(p)\), then eliminate \(p\).11
10None of these, but a hint or a repeated piece appears (like \(e^y\), \(\sin y\), \(\ln y\))?Substitute that piece as \(u\). Its derivative is usually already in the equation. You often land on Bernoulli or linear.10
★
Two quick tricks before you give up
  • Flip the roles. If the equation is not linear in \(y\) but \(x\) appears only to the first power, look at \(\frac{dx}{dy}\). It may be linear (or Bernoulli) in \(x\).
  • More than one door can be open. A separable equation can also be exact, and a homogeneous one can also be Bernoulli. Any correct method gets full marks, so pick the one with the easiest integrals.

Signatures: what each type looks like

You see…Think…
\(y'=\dfrac{\text{only }x}{\text{only }y}\)Separable
\(y' + (\dots)\,y = (\dots)\), \(y\) to the power 1Linear
\(y' + (\dots)\,y = (\dots)\,y^{n}\)Bernoulli
\(y'\) built from \(\frac yx\), or \(x^2+y^2\), \(xy\), \(y^2\) all degree 2Homogeneous
\(y^2\) on the right and a known solutionRiccati
You see…Think…
\(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\) with matching \(M_y,N_x\)Exact
Same, but \(M_y\ne N_x\)Integrating factor
\(y = xp + f(p)\)Clairaut
Straight-line coefficients \(ax+by+c\)Shift (Ch. 10)
\(y''\) and “one solution is \(y_1\)”Reduction of order

Recognition drill

Cover the right column and name the method. Each one is a real example from the slides or the midterm.

EquationMethod and the reason
\((y^2+1)\,dx + (x^2+1)\,dy = 0\)Separable: \(\frac{dy}{y^2+1} = -\frac{dx}{x^2+1}\).
\((\tan y + 2x)\,dx + (x - x^2\tan y)\,dy = 0\)Integrating factor: \(M_y=\sec^2y\ne N_x=1-2x\tan y\). \(\frac1M(M_y-N_x)=\tan y\) only has \(y\), so \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int\tan y\,dy}=\cos y\). (Midterm Q2.)
\(e^y y' + e^y = e^{3y+2x}\)Substitution, then Bernoulli: put \(u=e^y\), so \(u'=e^yy'\) and \(u'+u=u^3e^{2x}\), Bernoulli with \(n=3\). (Midterm Q3.)
\(y' = \dfrac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\)Homogeneous (or Bernoulli with \(n=2\)): the right side is \(\frac13\big(\frac yx\big)^2+\frac23\frac yx\). Don’t forget \(y=0\). (Midterm Q4.)
\((x^2+x)y''-2xy'+2y=0\), \(y_1=x\)Reduction of order: \(y=xz\), then \(w=z'\) gives a first-order separable equation. (Midterm Q5.)
\(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{y^2}{1-3xy}\)Linear in \(x\): flip to \(\frac{dx}{dy}+\frac3yx=\frac1{y^2}\).
\((1+3x\sin y)\,dx - x^2\cos y\,dy = 0\)Substitution \(u=\sin y\): \(du=\cos y\,dy\) is already there, and it becomes linear in \(u\).
“Rate of conversion is proportional to the square of the amount of A”Model first: \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\), which is separable. Use the data to find \(C\) and then \(k\). (Midterm Q1.)
!
“Find all solutions” means: don’t lose any
Whenever you divide by something containing \(y\) (\(h(y)\) when separating, \(y^n\) in Bernoulli, \(u\) or \(x\) in homogeneous), that value is thrown away. Check each one in the original equation. If it works and isn’t covered by any value of \(C\), write it next to the general solution as a singular solution. Midterm Q4 lost \(y=0\) for many students.

Second order: only one method in this course

If you see \(y''\) and the question gives you one solution \(y_1\) (often “it is known that \(f(x)=x\) is a solution”), it is reduction of order (Chapter 14): put \(y = y_1 z\), and the \(z\) terms cancel. With \(w = z'\) you get a first-order separable equation. Then the general solution is \(y = c_1y_1 + c_2y_2\).

✓
Write this at the top of every answer
  1. The type, and the test that proves it.
  2. The substitution or integrating factor, with its formula.
  3. The new equation (linear / separable / exact) and its solution.
  4. Back-substitute, and write the answer clearly with the arbitrary constant.
  5. Any solutions lost by dividing, if the question says “all solutions”.

In one minute

  • Put the equation in both forms: \(y'=f(x,y)\) and \(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\).
  • Check in order: separable → linear → exact → integrating factor → Bernoulli → homogeneous → shift → Riccati / Clairaut → substitution.
  • Not linear in \(y\)? Try linear in \(x\).
  • A strange repeated piece (\(e^y\), \(\sin y\)) is a hint: substitute it.
  • Second order with one known solution means reduction of order.
  • Always name the type and the test, and look for lost solutions.

chapters.title: The 2023 midterm, fully solved
chapters.lead: The real MAT 2039 midterm of 17.11.2023: five questions, 20 points each. For each one you get how to recognise it, a clean solution that follows the lecturer's handwritten steps (corrected where the handwriting has a mistake), and the traps that cost points.
chapters.html:
The exam at a glance

QPointsTypeMethod
120Word problem: rate ∝ (amount)²Model \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\), separable, two data points
220\(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\), not exactIntegrating factor \(\mu(y)\), then exact
320Equation with \(e^y\)Substitution \(z=e^y\) ⇒ Bernoulli ⇒ linear
420"Find all solutions"Homogeneous \(y=vx\) (or Bernoulli) + singular solution
520One solution givenReduction of order \(y=xz\), then general solution
i
About the source
The PDF contains the printed exam and the lecturer's handwritten solutions to Questions 1, 2, 3 and 5. There is no handwritten solution for Question 4; the solution below is ours (checked with sympy). The handwritten solution of Question 5 contains an algebra error — the correct version is given here and the difference is explained.

Question 1 (20 points) — rate proportional to the square

During a chemical reaction, substance A is converted into substance B at a rate that is proportional to the square of the amount of A. Initially, 50 grams of A is present, and after 2 hours only 10 grams of A remain unconverted. How much of A is present after 4 hours?

★
How to recognise it
A story with "rate … proportional to …" and two measurements = Week 5 rate problem. The key words are "square of the amount" ⇒ \(A^2\), and "converted" ⇒ A decreases ⇒ minus sign. (This is word for word Exercises 10.3 #1 from Week+5.pdf p.22.)
Midterm 2023 Q1 · 2023-2024 midterm.pdf p.1–2Find \(A(4)\).
  1. Model: \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\), \(A(0)=50\), \(A(2)=10\), find \(A(4)\).
  2. Separable; write it in differential form. For \(A\ne 0\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dA}{A^2}=-\int k\,dt\).
  3. \(-\frac1A=-kt-C\Rightarrow A=\dfrac{1}{kt+C}\).
  4. \(A(0)=\frac{1}{k\cdot 0+C}=50\Rightarrow C=\frac1{50}\), so \(A(t)=\dfrac{50}{50kt+1}\).
  5. \(A(2)=10\Rightarrow \dfrac{50}{100k+1}=10\Rightarrow 5=100k+1\Rightarrow 100k=4\Rightarrow k=\frac1{25}\).
  6. \(A(t)=\dfrac{50}{2t+1}\Rightarrow A(4)=\dfrac{50}{9}\).
\(A(4)=\frac{50}{9}\approx 5.56\) grams
!
Where students lose points
  • Writing \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA\) (ignoring "square") and getting an exponential: \(A(4)=50\left(\frac15\right)^2=2\) g — wrong.
  • Making the integration constant inconsistent: from \(-\frac1A=-kt-C\) you must get \(\frac1A=kt+C\), not \(kt-C\) (or keep the sign and let the data fix it).
  • Answering with \(A(t)\) or \(k\) only; the question asks for a number (with units).

Question 2 (20 points) — integrating factor

Find the general solution of \((\tan y+2x)\,dx+(x-x^2\tan y)\,dy=0\).

★
How to recognise it
Form \(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\) ⇒ test exactness first. If \(M_y\ne N_x\), check whether \(\frac{M_y-N_x}{N}\) depends only on \(x\) or \(\frac{M_y-N_x}{M}\) only on \(y\). The trig identity \(\sec^2y=\tan^2y+1\) (printed as a hint on the exam sheet) is exactly what makes the quotient simplify.
Midterm 2023 Q2 · 2023-2024 midterm.pdf p.2–3Solve \((\tan y+2x)\,dx+(x-x^2\tan y)\,dy=0\).
  1. \(M=\tan y+2x\), \(N=x-x^2\tan y\). \(M_y=\sec^2y\), \(N_x=1-2x\tan y\). Since \(M_y\ne N_x\), it is not exact.
  2. \(\dfrac{M_y-N_x}{M}=\dfrac{\sec^2y-1+2x\tan y}{\tan y+2x}=\dfrac{\tan^2y+2x\tan y}{\tan y+2x}=\dfrac{\tan y(\tan y+2x)}{\tan y+2x}=\tan y\). (depends only on \(y\); uses \(\sec^2y-1=\tan^2y\))
  3. Integrating factor: \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int\tan y\,dy}=e^{-\int\frac{\sin y}{\cos y}dy}=e^{\ln|\cos y|}=|\cos y|\). (On an interval where \(\cos y\ne0\), any constant multiple of an integrating factor also works, so take \(\mu(y)=\cos y\).)
  4. Multiply both sides by \(\cos y\): \((\sin y+2x\cos y)\,dx+(x\cos y-x^2\sin y)\,dy=0\). Call these \(\tilde M,\tilde N\).
  5. Check: \(\tilde M_y=\cos y-2x\sin y=\tilde N_x\) ⇒ the new equation is exact.
  6. \(F_x=\tilde M\Rightarrow F(x,y)=\int(\sin y+2x\cos y)\,dx+g(y)=x\sin y+x^2\cos y+g(y)\).
  7. \(F_y=\tilde N\Rightarrow x\cos y-x^2\sin y+g'(y)=x\cos y-x^2\sin y\Rightarrow g'(y)=0\Rightarrow g(y)=0\).
  8. General solution: \(F(x,y)=C\).
\(x\sin y+x^2\cos y=C\), \(C\) arbitrary constant
!
Where students lose points
  • Sign of the integrating factor exponent: with \(\frac{M_y-N_x}{M}=g(y)\) the factor is \(e^{-\int g\,dy}\). Using \(e^{+\int\tan y\,dy}=\sec y\) does not make the equation exact — always re-check \(\tilde M_y=\tilde N_x\).
  • Dividing by \(N\) instead of \(M\): \(\frac{M_y-N_x}{N}\) is not a function of \(x\) alone here, so that route is a dead end.
  • Forgetting "\(=C\)": \(F(x,y)\) alone is not a solution.

Question 3 (20 points) — substitution, then Bernoulli

Find the general solution of \(e^y\,y'+e^y=e^{3y+2x}\).

★
How to recognise it
You see \(e^y\,y'\), which is exactly \(\frac{d}{dx}(e^y)\). That shouts "put \(z=e^y\)". The right side \(e^{3y}e^{2x}=z^3e^{2x}\) then gives a Bernoulli equation with \(n=3\). (The hint printed under this question, \(\sec^2y=\tan^2y+1\), is not used here — it belongs to Question 2.)
Midterm 2023 Q3 · 2023-2024 midterm.pdf p.3–4Solve \(e^y\,y'+e^y=e^{3y+2x}\).
  1. Rewrite: \(e^yy'+e^y=e^{3y}e^{2x}=(e^y)^3e^{2x}\).
  2. Let \(z=e^y\), so \(z'=e^yy'\). Then \(z'+z=z^3e^{2x}\): Bernoulli with \(n=3\).
  3. \(u=z^{1-n}=z^{-2}\), \(\frac{du}{dx}=-2z^{-3}\frac{dz}{dx}\). Multiply both sides by \(\frac{-2}{z^3}\): \(-\frac{2}{z^3}\frac{dz}{dx}-\frac{2}{z^2}=-2e^{2x}\).
  4. That is \(\frac{du}{dx}-2u=-2e^{2x}\): linear.
  5. \(\mu(x)=e^{-\int 2\,dx}=e^{-2x}\): \(e^{-2x}\frac{du}{dx}-2ue^{-2x}=-2\Rightarrow\frac{d}{dx}\left(e^{-2x}u\right)=-2\).
  6. Integrate: \(e^{-2x}u=-2x+C\Rightarrow u=-2xe^{2x}+Ce^{2x}\).
  7. Back: \(u=\frac1{z^2}=e^{-2y}\).
\(e^{-2y}=-2xe^{2x}+Ce^{2x}\) (equivalently \(y=-x-\frac12\ln(C-2x)\)), \(C\) arbitrary
i
Note
Since \(z=e^y\gt 0\), the Bernoulli "extra" solution \(z=0\) is impossible, so nothing is lost by dividing by \(z^3\).
!
Where students lose points
  • Choosing \(u=z^{-3}\) or \(u=z^{2}\): for Bernoulli the new variable is \(u=z^{1-n}=z^{-2}\).
  • Forgetting to multiply the right side by \(-2/z^3\) too (it becomes \(-2e^{2x}\)).
  • Stopping at \(u\) or \(z\): go back to \(y\).

Question 4 (20 points) — find all solutions

Find all solutions of \(y'=\dfrac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\).

★
How to recognise it
The right side is \(\frac{y^2+2xy}{3x^2}\): every term has total degree 2 on top and bottom ⇒ a function of \(\frac{y}{x}\) only ⇒ homogeneous, use \(y=vx\). "Find all solutions" is the signal that some solution gets lost when you divide — you must find it and list it.
Midterm 2023 Q4 · 2023-2024 midterm.pdf p.1 (no handwritten solution in the PDF)Find all solutions of \(y'=\frac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\), \(x\ne 0\).
  1. \(y'=\frac13\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^2+\frac23\cdot\frac{y}{x}\) depends only on \(\frac yx\): homogeneous. Put \(y=vx\), \(y'=v+xv'\).
  2. \(v+xv'=\frac{v^2+2v}{3}\Rightarrow xv'=\frac{v^2-v}{3}=\frac{v(v-1)}{3}\). (separable)
  3. Before dividing, note the constant solutions: \(v(v-1)=0\Rightarrow v=0\) (i.e. \(y=0\)) and \(v=1\) (i.e. \(y=x\)).
  4. For \(v\ne 0,1\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dv}{v(v-1)}=\int\frac{dx}{3x}\). Partial fractions: \(\frac{1}{v(v-1)}=\frac{1}{v-1}-\frac1v\).
  5. \(\ln\left|\frac{v-1}{v}\right|=\frac13\ln|x|+\ln C\Rightarrow \frac{v-1}{v}=Kx^{1/3}\), \(K\ne 0\).
  6. \(1-\frac1v=Kx^{1/3}\Rightarrow v=\dfrac{1}{1-Kx^{1/3}}\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{x}{1-Kx^{1/3}}\).
  7. Lost solutions: \(K=0\) gives \(y=x\), so \(y=x\) is already in the family (allow \(K=0\)). But \(y=0\) is not obtained for any \(K\) ⇒ it is a singular solution and must be listed separately.
\(y=\dfrac{x}{1-Cx^{1/3}}\) (\(C\) arbitrary) and the singular solution \(y\equiv 0\)
→
Alternative: Bernoulli
The same equation is Bernoulli: \(y'-\frac{2}{3x}y=\frac{1}{3x^2}y^2\) (\(n=2\)). With \(u=y^{-1}\): \(u'+\frac{2}{3x}u=-\frac{1}{3x^2}\), \(\mu=x^{2/3}\), \(\left(x^{2/3}u\right)'=-\frac13x^{-4/3}\Rightarrow x^{2/3}u=x^{-1/3}+C\Rightarrow y=\frac{x}{1+Cx^{1/3}}\) — the same family (rename \(C\to -C\)). Dividing by \(y^2\) loses \(y=0\), which again must be added.
!
Where students lose points
  • Not mentioning \(y=0\) — in a "find all solutions" question this is exactly where points are lost.
  • Listing \(y=x\) as "singular": it is in the family (\(C=0\)), so it is not singular. Say so.
  • Algebra in \(v+xv'=\dots\): subtract \(v\) correctly: \(\frac{v^2+2v}{3}-v=\frac{v^2-v}{3}\).

Question 5 (20 points) — reduction of order

Find a second solution of \((x^2+x)y''-2xy'+2y=0\) if it is known that \(f(x)=x\) is a solution. Write the general solution.

★
How to recognise it
Second-order linear homogeneous, one solution given ⇒ reduction of order (Theorem 17, Week+6.pdf p.31). Put \(y=xz\). It is the same pattern as Example 38, \((x^2+1)y''-2xy'+2y=0\).
Midterm 2023 Q5 · 2023-2024 midterm.pdf p.4–5 (corrected)Find \(y_2\) and the general solution of \((x^2+x)y''-2xy'+2y=0\), given \(y_1=x\).
  1. \(y_2(x)=f(x)z(x)=xz\). Then \(y_2'=z+xz'\), \(y_2''=z'+z'+xz''=2z'+xz''\).
  2. Substitute: \((x^2+x)(2z'+xz'')-2x(z+xz')+2xz=0\).
  3. Collect: \((x^3+x^2)z''+\left(2x^2+2x-2x^2\right)z'+(-2x+2x)z=0\Rightarrow (x^3+x^2)z''+2x\,z'=0\). (\((x^2+x)\cdot 2z'=(2x^2+2x)z'\); the \(2x^2\) cancels with \(-2x\cdot xz'\))
  4. \(w=z'\): \(x^2(x+1)w'+2xw=0\), i.e. \(w'+\frac{2}{x(x+1)}w=0\) (linear and separable).
  5. For \(w\ne 0\): \(\displaystyle\int\frac{dw}{w}=-\int\frac{2}{x(x+1)}dx\). Partial fractions: \(\frac{2}{x(x+1)}=\frac2x-\frac{2}{x+1}\).
  6. \(\ln|w|=-2\ln|x|+2\ln|x+1|+\ln C\Rightarrow w=K\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}\); \(w=0\) is also a solution, so \(w=\alpha\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}\). Choose \(\alpha=1\).
  7. \(z=\displaystyle\int\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}dx=\int\left(1+\frac2x+\frac1{x^2}\right)dx=x+2\ln|x|-\frac1x\) (constant chosen 0).
  8. \(y_2=xz=x^2+2x\ln|x|-1\). Check: \(W[x,y_2]=x\,y_2'-y_2=(x+1)^2\ne 0\) on any interval where \(x^2+x\ne 0\).
\(y_2=x^2+2x\ln|x|-1\); general solution \(y=c_1x+c_2\left(x^2+2x\ln|x|-1\right)\)
i
The handwritten solution has an error
In the handwritten solution (p.4) the \(z'\) coefficient is written as \((2x-2x^2)\) instead of \(2x\): the \(2x^2\) from \((x^2+x)\cdot 2z'\) was dropped. This leads to \(x^2(x+1)w'-2x(x-1)w=0\), \(w=\frac{(x+1)^4}{x^2}\) and \(y_2=x\int\frac{(x+1)^4}{x^2}dx\), which is not a solution of the equation (substituting it leaves \(2(x+1)^4\ne 0\)). The method and all later steps are fine; only that coefficient is wrong. The correct \(w\) is \(\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}\). Also note the lecturer's "Solve it!": the integral must be evaluated.
!
Where students lose points
  • The \(z'\) coefficient (see the note above!). Quick check: it must equal \(2a_0y_1'+a_1y_1=2(x^2+x)-2x\cdot x=2x\).
  • Answering only \(y_2\) and forgetting "Write the general solution": \(y=c_1x+c_2y_2\).
  • Leaving \(\int\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}dx\) unevaluated — it is elementary, so compute it.
  • Forgetting \(y_2=xz\) (giving \(z\) as the second solution).

In one minute

  • Q1: "∝ square" ⇒ \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\Rightarrow A=\frac{50}{2t+1}\), \(A(4)=\frac{50}{9}\) g.
  • Q2: \(\frac{M_y-N_x}{M}=\tan y\) ⇒ \(\mu=\cos y\) ⇒ \(x\sin y+x^2\cos y=C\).
  • Q3: \(z=e^y\) ⇒ Bernoulli \(n=3\) ⇒ \(u=z^{-2}\) ⇒ \(e^{-2y}=(C-2x)e^{2x}\).
  • Q4: homogeneous ⇒ \(y=\frac{x}{1-Cx^{1/3}}\) plus singular \(y=0\).
  • Q5: \(y=xz\) ⇒ \((x^3+x^2)z''+2xz'=0\) ⇒ \(y_2=x^2+2x\ln|x|-1\), \(y=c_1x+c_2y_2\).
  • Always verify: the \(z\)-term must vanish in reduction of order; the new equation must be exact after \(\mu\).

chapters.title: Cheat sheet
chapters.lead: Two dense pages to print and review before the exam
chapters.html:
Basics & IVPs

  • ODE: one independent variable; PDE: partial derivatives. Order = highest derivative (not power).
  • Linear: \(a_0(x)y^{(n)}+\dots+a_n(x)y=f(x)\), \(a_0\neq0\). No \(yy'\), \((y')^2\), \(\sin y\), \(\sqrt y\).
  • Solution on \(I\): \(n\)-times differentiable, satisfies the DE for all \(x\in I\). Explicit \(y=\varphi(x)\) / implicit \(\Phi(x,y)=0\).
  • General: \(n\) arbitrary constants. Particular: none. Singular: not obtainable from the general solution for any constants (e.g. \(y\equiv0\) for \((y')^2=4y\), general \((x+c)^2\)).
  • Thm 1: \(f\) and \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) continuous on \(R:|x-x_0|\le a,|y-y_0|\le b\) \(\Rightarrow\) unique solution of \(y'=f,\ y(x_0)=y_0\) on some \(|x-x_0|\lt h\).
  • Fails? Theorem is silent: \(y'=x\sqrt y,\ y(0)=0\) has \(y\equiv0\) and \(y=\frac{x^4}{16}\).
  • Local only: \(y'=1+y^2,\ y(0)=0\Rightarrow y=\tan x\) on \(\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)\).

Separable

  • \(f(y)y'=g(x)\) or \(y'=g(x)h(y)\). For \(h(y)\neq0\): \(\int\frac{dy}{h(y)}=\int g(x)dx+C\).
  • Then check \(h(y)=0\): each root \(y_1\) gives \(y\equiv y_1\) (lost solution). Singular if no \(C\) gives it.
  • \(y'=-2xy^2\): \(y=\frac1{x^2+C}\), \(y=0\) singular. \(\ y'=2xy\): \(y=Ke^{x^2}\), \(y=0\) is \(K=0\) (not singular).
  • Differential form: dividing by \(x+1\) can lose the line \(x=-1\).
  • \(\int\frac{dy}{y^2-1}=\frac12\ln\left|\frac{y-1}{y+1}\right|\); \(\int\sec y\,dy=\ln|\sec y+\tan y|\); \(\int\ln x=x\ln x-x\).

Exact

  • \(M\,dx+N\,dy=0\) exact \(\iff\) \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\) (Thm 2). Then \(F_x=M,\ F_y=N\), answer \(F(x,y)=C\).
  • 1st way: \(F=\int M\,dx+g(y)\), \(F_y=N\Rightarrow g'(y)\) (only \(y\)!).
  • 2nd way: \(F=\int N\,dy+h(x)\), \(F_x=M\Rightarrow h'(x)\).
  • Ex. 12: \(2xe^ydx+(x^2e^y+\cos y)dy=0\Rightarrow x^2e^y+\sin y=C\).

Integrating factors

  • \(\mu\neq0\) with \(\mu M\,dx+\mu N\,dy=0\) exact. PDE: \(N\mu_x-M\mu_y=\mu(M_y-N_x)\).
  • Case 1: \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)=f(x)\Rightarrow\mu(x)=e^{\int f(x)dx}\).
  • Case 2: \(\frac1M(M_y-N_x)=g(y)\Rightarrow\mu(y)=e^{\boldsymbol{-}\int g(y)dy}\).
  • Steps: not exact \(\to\) factor \(M_y-N_x\) \(\to\) divide by \(N\), then \(M\) \(\to\) \(\mu\) \(\to\) re-check \(\tilde M_y=\tilde N_x\) \(\to\) build \(F\).
  • \(x^my^n\) / \((xy)^n\) given: multiply, match coefficients (Ex. 14: \(\mu=xy^2\)).
  • \(e^{-2\ln|x|}=x^{-2}\), \(e^{5\ln|y|}=y^5\), \(e^{\ln|\sin y|}=\sin y\).

Linear (1st order)

  • Standard form \(y'+p(x)y=q(x)\) (divide by the coefficient of \(y'\) first!).
  • \(\mu=e^{\int p(x)dx}\), \(\ (\mu y)'=\mu q\), \(\ y=\frac1\mu\left(\int\mu q\,dx+C\right)\). Contains all solutions.
  • Domain: \(p,q\) continuous on \(I\ni x_0\); avoid zeros of the leading coefficient, \(\tan\) at \(\frac\pi2+k\pi\), \(\cot\) at \(k\pi\).
  • Ex. 15: \(y'+xy=xe^{x^2/2},\ y(0)=1\Rightarrow y=\frac12e^{x^2/2}+\frac12e^{-x^2/2}\).
  • Not linear in \(y\)? Try \(\frac{dx}{dy}+p(y)x=q(y)\): \(y^2dx+(3xy-1)dy=0\Rightarrow xy^3=\frac{y^2}2+C\).

Bernoulli

  • Form: \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)y^n\) (\(n = 0, 1\): already linear).
  • \(u = y^{1-n}\), \(u' = (1-n)y^{-n}y'\). Multiply the equation by \((1-n)y^{-n}\):
  • \(\boxed{u' + (1-n)p\,u = (1-n)q}\) — linear, \(\mu = e^{\int(1-n)p\,dx}\), \((\mu u)' = \mu(1-n)q\).
  • \(y = 0\) is a solution when \(n \gt 0\) — list it.
  • Hidden Bernoulli: \(z = e^{y}\) (\(e^yy'\) present), \(z = \sin y\) (\(\cos y\,y'\)), \(u = y^n\) (\(ny^{n-1}y'\)). Midterm Q3: \(e^yy' + e^y = e^{3y+2x}\) \(\to\) \(z' + z = e^{2x}z^3\).
  • Power of \(x\) instead of \(y\)? Flip to \(\frac{dx}{dy}\), unknown \(x(y)\).

Homogeneous & shifts

  • Homogeneous: \(y' = g(y/x)\) \(\iff\) \(f(\lambda x,\lambda y) = f(x,y)\) \(\iff\) \(M, N\) homogeneous of the same degree (\(F(\lambda x,\lambda y) = \lambda^nF\)).
  • \(y = ux\), \(\boxed{y' = u + xu'}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(xu' = g(u) - u\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\int\frac{du}{g(u)-u} = \ln|x| + C\).
  • Roots \(u_0\) of \(g(u) = u\) \(\Rightarrow\) lines \(y = u_0x\): in the family (some constant) or extra? In \(M\,dx + N\,dy = 0\) form also test \(x = 0\).
  • Midterm Q4: \(y' = \frac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(y = \frac{x}{1 + Cx^{1/3}}\) and \(y = 0\).
  • \((a_1x+b_1y+c_1)dx + (a_2x+b_2y+c_2)dy = 0\): \(\Delta = a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\). \(\Delta\neq0\): \(x = u+h\), \(y = v+k\) (\((h,k)\) = intersection) \(\Rightarrow\) homogeneous. \(\Delta = 0\): \(z = a_1x + b_1y\) \(\Rightarrow\) separable.

Riccati & Clairaut

  • Riccati: \(y' = py^2 + qy + r\). Needs a particular solution \(y_1\) (try const, \(ax+b\), \(a/x\), \(x^\beta\)).
  • \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(\boxed{u' + (2py_1 + q)u = -p}\) (linear). \(y = y_1\) is also a solution.
  • \(r = 0\): Bernoulli \(n = 2\). (\(y = y_1 + w\): Bernoulli in \(w\).)
  • Clairaut: \(y = xp + f(p)\), \(p = y'\). Differentiate: \(\frac{dp}{dx}\big(x + f'(p)\big) = 0\).
  • General: \(\boxed{y = cx + f(c)}\). Singular: \(x = -f'(p)\), \(y = xp + f(p)\), eliminate \(p\).
  • \(y = xp + p^2\): \(y = cx + c^2\); singular \(y = -\frac{x^2}{4}\).

Orthogonal trajectories & toolkit

  • 1) Differentiate \(\Phi(x,y,c) = 0\); 2) eliminate \(c\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(y' = f(x,y)\); 3) solve \(y' = -\frac{1}{f(x,y)}\).
  • \(x^2+y^2 = c^2\) \(\to\) \(y = kx\); \(y = kx^2\) \(\to\) \(y^2 + \frac{x^2}{2} = C\); \(y = ce^x\) \(\to\) \(y^2 = -2x + C\); \(y^2 = 2cx + c^2\) self-orthogonal.
  • \(\int\tan = -\ln|\cos|\), \(\int\cot = \ln|\sin|\), \(\int\frac{f'}{f} = \ln|f|\), \(\int xe^{-x} = -(x+1)e^{-x}\), \(\int\frac{\ln x}{x^2} = -\frac{\ln x + 1}{x}\).
  • \(e^{-\ln f} = \frac1f\), \(e^{a\ln x} = x^a\). \(\ln|z| = \ln|x| + \ln|C|\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(z = Kx\) \(\Rightarrow\) add lost \(z = 0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(D\in\mathbb R\).

Word problems → DE

  • "rate of change of A" = \(\frac{dA}{dt}\); "∝" = \(k\cdot\); decreasing ⇒ \(-k\), \(k\gt 0\)
  • ∝ amount: \(A'=-kA\Rightarrow A=A_0e^{-kt}\); ∝ square: \(A'=-kA^2\Rightarrow A=\frac1{kt+C}\); ∝ \(\sqrt A\): \(2\sqrt A=-kt+C\)
  • Half-life \(h\): \(N=N_0(\frac12)^{t/h}\); doubles every \(d\): \(N=N_0 2^{t/d}\)
  • Data: "initially" ⇒ \(t=0\) gives \(C\); 2nd reading gives \(k\); "cooling at 5°/min" ⇒ \(T'(0)=-5\)
  • Midterm '23: \(A(0)=50,A(2)=10\Rightarrow A=\frac{50}{2t+1}\), \(A(4)=\frac{50}9\)

Cooling · falling · mixing

  • Cooling: \(T'=-k(T-T_m)\Rightarrow T=T_m+(T_0-T_m)e^{-kt}\); \(e^{-kt_1}=\frac{T(t_1)-T_m}{T_0-T_m}\)
  • Falling: \(mv'=mg-kv\Rightarrow v=(v_0-\frac{mg}k)e^{-kt/m}+\frac{mg}k\); terminal \(\frac{mg}k\); \(x=\int v\,dt\)
  • Mixture: \(x'=r_{\text{in}}-r_{\text{out}}\), \(r_{\text{in}}=\text{flow}\cdot c_{\text{in}}\), \(r_{\text{out}}=\text{flow}\cdot\frac{x}{V(t)}\), \(V=V_0+(\text{in}-\text{out})t\)
  • Ex. 30: \(x'=6-\frac{3}{500}x\), \(x=1000(1-e^{-3t/500})\)

Linear n-th order theory

  • \(a_0y^{(n)}+\cdots+a_ny=f\); IVP: \(y,y',\dots,y^{(n-1)}\) at one \(x_0\)
  • \(a_i,f\) continuous, \(a_0\ne0\) on \(I\) ⇒ unique solution on all of \(I\)
  • Superposition: needs linear + homogeneous
  • \(W=\begin{vmatrix}f_1&f_2\\f_1'&f_2'\end{vmatrix}\). For solutions: indep ⇔ \(W\ne0\); \(W\equiv0\) or never 0
  • \(x|x|,x^2\): \(W\equiv0\) but independent (not solutions)
  • General: \(c_1\varphi_1+\dots+c_n\varphi_n\) (F.S.S.); non-hom.: \(\varphi_c+\varphi_p\)

Reduction of order

  • Know \(y_1\): \(y=y_1z\), \(y''=y_1''z+2y_1'z'+y_1z''\); \(z\)-term must cancel
  • \(w=z'\): \(a_0y_1w'+(2a_0y_1'+a_1y_1)w=0\) (separable) → \(w\), \(C=1\)
  • \(y_2=y_1\int w\,dx\); answer \(y=c_1y_1+c_2y_2\)
  • Ex. 38: \((x^2+1)y''-2xy'+2y=0\), \(y_1=x\Rightarrow y_2=x^2-1\)
  • Mid '23: \((x^2+x)y''-2xy'+2y=0\), \(y_1=x\Rightarrow w=\frac{(x+1)^2}{x^2}\), \(y_2=x^2+2x\ln|x|-1\)

quiz.q: What is the order of \(\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^3=y^2\)?
quiz.why: Order = highest derivative that occurs. Only \(y'\) appears; the cube is a power, not a third derivative.

quiz.q: Which of these equations is linear?
quiz.why: In \(xy''+\frac{1}{1+x^2}y'=\sin x\) the unknown and its derivatives appear to the first power with coefficients depending only on \(x\). The others put \(y'\) or \(y\) inside \(\sin\), \(\sqrt{\ }\) or a square.

quiz.q: \(\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}+\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial y^2}=0\) is …
quiz.why: \(u\) depends on two variables \(x,y\) (partial derivatives), so it is a PDE; the highest derivative is second order.

quiz.q: Order and linearity of \(\frac{d^4y}{dx^4}+\left(\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}\right)^2+\cos x=0\)?
quiz.why: Highest derivative \(y^{(4)}\): order 4. The square of \(y''\) makes it non-linear (\(\cos x\) alone is harmless).

quiz.q: \(y=(x+c)^2\) is the general solution of \(\left(y'\right)^2-4y=0\). The solution \(y\equiv0\) is …
quiz.why: \(y\equiv0\) satisfies the equation, but \((x+c)^2\) equals 0 for all \(x\) for no \(c\) (\(c=0\) gives \(x^2\), not 0). So it is singular.

quiz.q: \(x^2+y^2=4\) is an implicit solution of \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac xy\). On which interval are its explicit solutions valid?
quiz.why: At \(x=\pm2\), \(y=0\) and the equation (division by \(y\)) is undefined, so the endpoints are excluded.

quiz.q: Theorem 1 (existence and uniqueness) for \(y'=f(x,y),\ y(x_0)=y_0\) requires …
o: \(f\) and \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) continuous on a rectangle around \((x_0,y_0)\)
quiz.why: The slide's hypothesis: \(f\) and \(\partial f/\partial y\) continuous on \(R=\{|x-x_0|\le a,|y-y_0|\le b\}\). The derivative is with respect to \(y\), not \(x\).

quiz.q: For \(y'=x\sqrt y,\ y(0)=0\), which statement is true?
o: Theorem 1 does not apply, and \(y\equiv0\) and \(y=\frac{x^4}{16}\) are both solutions
quiz.why: \(\partial f/\partial y=\frac{x}{2\sqrt y}\) is not continuous at \(y=0\), so the theorem is silent; indeed two solutions pass through \((0,0)\).

quiz.q: Theorem 1 guarantees the solution of the IVP exists …
o: on the whole interval \(|x-x_0|\le a\) of the rectangle
quiz.why: The conclusion is local: a unique solution in some interval \(|x-x_0|\lt h\). Its size is not given by the theorem.

quiz.q: For \(y'=y^{2/3}\), Theorem 1 guarantees a unique solution through \((x_0,y_0)\) exactly when …
quiz.why: \(f=y^{2/3}\) is continuous everywhere, but \(f_y=\frac23y^{-1/3}\) fails only at \(y=0\); negative \(y_0\) is fine (cube roots). Through \((0,0)\) both \(0\) and \(x^3/27\) are solutions.

quiz.q: Why does \(y'+p(x)y=q(x),\ y(x_0)=y_0\) (with \(p,q\) continuous) have a unique solution near \(x_0\)?
o: Because \(f=q(x)-p(x)y\) and \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=-p(x)\) are continuous
quiz.why: Exactly the hypotheses of Theorem 1: \(f\) and \(f_y=-p(x)\) are continuous on any rectangle around \((x_0,y_0)\).

quiz.q: The IVP \(y'=y^2,\ y(0)=1\) has the solution \(y=\frac{1}{1-x}\). On which interval does it exist?
quiz.why: The solution must be on an interval containing \(x_0=0\); it blows up at \(x=1\), so it lives on \((-\infty,1)\), even though \(f=y^2\) is continuous everywhere.

quiz.q: Which equation is separable?
quiz.why: \(\frac{dy}{dx}=x^2+x^2y^2=x^2(1+y^2)\) factors as \(g(x)h(y)\). The other right-hand sides do not factor.

quiz.q: Solving \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-2y^2x\) gives \(y=\frac{1}{x^2+C}\). What about \(y\equiv0\)?
o: It is a solution not obtainable from \(\frac{1}{x^2+C}\): a singular solution
It is a particular solution obtained as \(C\to0\)
quiz.why: \(y=0\) gives \(0=0\), so it solves the equation, but \(\frac{1}{x^2+C}\) is never 0. It was lost when dividing by \(y^2\).

quiz.q: For \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2xy\) the general solution is \(y=Ke^{x^2}\). Is \(y\equiv0\) singular?
quiz.why: A lost solution is singular only if no constant gives it. Here \(K=0\) does, so it is contained in the general solution.

quiz.q: Which constant functions solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=(y^2-1)\ln x\)?
quiz.why: \(h(y)=y^2-1=0\) at \(y=\pm1\); then \(y'=0=0\cdot\ln x\). The slide warns: be careful for \(y=\mp1\).

quiz.q: General solution of \((y^2+1)\,dx+(x+1)\,dy=0\)?
quiz.why: \(\frac{dy}{1+y^2}=-\frac{dx}{x+1}\Rightarrow\arctan y=-\ln|x+1|+C\). The vertical line \(x=-1\) is an extra (singular) solution.

quiz.q: For \(\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos y\sin x\), which are the singular solutions?
quiz.why: Dividing by \(\cos y\) loses its zeros \(y=\frac\pi2+k\pi\). They satisfy the equation and are not in \(\ln|\sec y+\tan y|=-\cos x+C\).

quiz.q: \(M(x,y)\,dx+N(x,y)\,dy=0\) is exact (Theorem 2) if and only if …
quiz.why: \(M=F_x\), \(N=F_y\), so \(M_y=F_{xy}=F_{yx}=N_x\). Cross the letters: \(M\) by \(y\), \(N\) by \(x\).

quiz.q: General solution of \(2xy\,dx+(x^2+3y^2)\,dy=0\)?
quiz.why: \(M_y=2x=N_x\). \(F=\int2xy\,dx+g=x^2y+g(y)\); \(F_y=x^2+g'=x^2+3y^2\Rightarrow g=y^3\).

quiz.q: Which equation is exact?
For which \(k\) is \((x^2+kxy)\,dx+(2x^2+y)\,dy=0\) exact?
quiz.why: \(M_y=kx\) must equal \(N_x=4x\), so \(k=4\).

quiz.q: Building \(F\) the 1st way: after \(F=\int M\,dx+g(y)\), what is the next step?
o: Differentiate \(F\) with respect to \(y\) and set it equal to \(N\)
Differentiate \(F\) with respect to \(x\) and set it equal to \(N\)
quiz.why: \(F_y=N\) determines \(g'(y)\). (\(F_x=M\) is already true by construction.)

quiz.q: General solution of \(2xe^y\,dx+(x^2e^y+\cos y)\,dy=0\) (Example 12)?
quiz.why: \(F=x^2e^y+g(y)\); \(F_y=x^2e^y+g'=x^2e^y+\cos y\Rightarrow g=\sin y\).

quiz.q: If \(\frac1N\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right)=f(x)\), an integrating factor is …
quiz.why: Theorem 4, Case 1: \(\mu(x)=\exp\{\int^xf(\eta)d\eta\}\), from the separable equation \(\frac{d\mu}{dx}=\mu f(x)\).

quiz.q: With \(g(y)=\frac1M\left(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}-\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\right)\), the slide's integrating factor depending only on \(y\) is …
quiz.why: Theorem 4, Case 2: \(\mu(y)=\exp\{-\int^yg(\zeta)d\zeta\}\). The minus comes from \(-M\mu_y\) in the PDE \((\ast)\); the lecturer marked it with a red “!”.

quiz.q: An integrating factor for \(3xy\,dx+(9x^2+4y)\,dy=0\) is …
quiz.why: \(\frac1M(M_y-N_x)=\frac{3x-18x}{3xy}=-\frac5y=g(y)\), so \(\mu=e^{-\int g}=e^{5\ln y}=y^5\). Forgetting the minus gives \(y^{-5}\), which does not work.

quiz.q: For \((2x^2+y)\,dx+x(xy-1)\,dy=0\) (Example 13), the integrating factor is …
quiz.why: \(M_y-N_x=-2(xy-1)\); dividing by \(N=x(xy-1)\) gives \(-\frac2x\), so \(\mu=e^{-2\ln|x|}=\frac{1}{x^2}\).

quiz.q: An integrating factor for \((x^2+y^2+x)\,dx+xy\,dy=0\) is …
quiz.why: \(M_y-N_x=2y-y=y\); \(\frac{y}{N}=\frac{y}{xy}=\frac1x=f(x)\). So \(\mu=e^{\ln x}=x\).

quiz.q: Example 14: \(\mu=x^my^n\) is an integrating factor for \(y(3x-2y^2)\,dx+x(3x-5y^2)\,dy=0\) when …
The integrating factor of \(y'+\frac2xy=x^2\) (\(x\gt0\)) is …
quiz.why: \(\mu=e^{\int p}=e^{\int\frac2xdx}=e^{2\ln x}=x^2\). Then \(y=\frac{x^3}5+\frac{C}{x^2}\).

quiz.q: For \(xy'-3y=x^2\), what is \(p(x)\) in the standard form \(y'+p(x)y=q(x)\)?
quiz.why: Divide by \(x\) first: \(y'-\frac3xy=x\). Reading \(p=-3\) without dividing is the classic mistake. (Solution: \(y=-x^2+Cx^3\).)

quiz.q: The integrating factor of \(y'-\tan(x)\,y=\sec x\) on \(\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)\) is …
quiz.why: \(p=-\tan x\), \(\mu=e^{-\int\tan x\,dx}=e^{\ln|\cos x|}=\cos x\). Then \((y\cos x)'=1\), \(y=(x+C)\sec x\).

quiz.q: General solution of \(y'+2y=1\)?
quiz.why: \(\mu=e^{2x}\): \((e^{2x}y)'=e^{2x}\Rightarrow e^{2x}y=\frac12e^{2x}+C\Rightarrow y=\frac12+Ce^{-2x}\).

quiz.q: General solution of \(y'+\frac1xy=3x\) (\(x\gt0\))?
quiz.why: \(\mu=x\): \((xy)'=3x^2\Rightarrow xy=x^3+C\Rightarrow y=x^2+\frac Cx\). The constant is divided by \(\mu\) too.

quiz.q: Theorem 5 says that for \(y'+p(x)y=q(x)\) the family \(y=\frac{1}{\mu}\left[\int\mu q+c\right]\) …
quiz.why: “Furthermore, this one-parameter family of solutions includes all solutions”, so a linear equation has no singular solutions.

quiz.q: \(\displaystyle\int\tan x\,dx = \;?\)
quiz.why: With \(z = \cos x\), \(dz = -\sin x\,dx\): \(\int\frac{\sin x}{\cos x}dx = -\int\frac{dz}{z} = -\ln|\cos x|\). \(\sec^2 x\) is the derivative of \(\tan x\), not its integral.

quiz.q: The integrating factor \(\mu = e^{-\int\frac{3}{x}dx}\) simplifies to
quiz.why: \(e^{-3\ln x} = e^{\ln x^{-3}} = x^{-3}\). Forgetting the minus sign gives \(x^3\).

quiz.q: \(\displaystyle\int x\,e^{-x}\,dx = \;?\)
quiz.why: By parts with \(f = x\), \(g' = e^{-x}\): \(-xe^{-x} + \int e^{-x}dx = -xe^{-x} - e^{-x}\). Differentiate to check.
quiz.src: Integration toolkit (by parts; needed in problem m-p-b-01)

quiz.q: You reach \(\ln|z| = \ln|x| + \ln|C|\) (\(C\neq0\)) after dividing by \(z\), and \(z = 0\) also solves the equation. How does the lecturer write the final answer?
quiz.why: \(|z| = |Cx|\Rightarrow z = \pm Cx = Kx\) (\(K\neq0\)); adding the lost solution \(z = 0\) allows \(K = 0\), so any real \(D\).

quiz.q: Partial fractions: \(\dfrac{1}{u(u-1)} = \;?\)
quiz.why: Cover-up: at \(u = 0\) the coefficient is \(\frac{1}{0-1} = -1\), at \(u = 1\) it is \(\frac11 = 1\).

quiz.q: Which equation is a Bernoulli equation?
quiz.why: Bernoulli means \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)y^n\). The others are Riccati (needs a constant term \(r\)), Clairaut and homogeneous.

quiz.q: For \(y' + \dfrac2x y = x^2y^4\), which substitution makes the equation linear?
quiz.why: \(n = 4\), so \(u = y^{1-n} = y^{-3}\). Using \(y^{-n}\) instead of \(y^{1-n}\) is the classic slip.

quiz.q: Substituting \(u = y^{-2}\) into \(y' + \dfrac{y}{x} = x\,y^3\) gives
quiz.why: \(u' + (1-n)p\,u = (1-n)q\) with \(n = 3\): both \(p = \frac1x\) and \(q = x\) are multiplied by \(1 - n = -2\).

quiz.q: The general solution of \(y' - y = e^{x}y^2\) is
A student solves \(y' + p(x)y = q(x)y^2\) with \(u = 1/y\) and gets a one-parameter family. In a find all solutions question, what must still be added?
quiz.why: Dividing by \(y^2\) needs \(y\neq0\). Since \(n = 2 \gt 0\), \(y \equiv 0\) satisfies \(0 + p\cdot0 = q\cdot0\) but no constant in \(1/y = \ldots\) produces it.

quiz.q: In Example 21, \((1 + 3x\sin y)dx - x^2\cos y\,dy = 0\) with \(u = \sin y\) becomes
quiz.why: \(du = \cos y\,dy\), so \((1 + 3xu)dx - x^2du = 0\), i.e. \(u' = \frac{1 + 3xu}{x^2}\): linear, solved with \(\mu = x^{-3}\).

quiz.q: Which equation is homogeneous (i.e. \(f(\lambda x,\lambda y) = f(x,y)\) for \(y' = f(x,y)\))?
quiz.why: In \(\frac{x^2+y^2}{xy}\) every term has degree 2, so all \(\lambda\)'s cancel. In the others a term of a different degree (the 1, the \(x\)) survives.

quiz.q: With \(y = ux\), \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \;?\)
quiz.why: Product rule: \(\frac{d}{dx}(ux) = u'x + u\cdot1\). Dropping the \(+u\) is the most common error.

quiz.q: For \((x^2 - 3y^2)dx + 2xy\,dy = 0\), which statement is correct?
o: \(M\) has degree 2 and \(N\) degree 1, so it is not homogeneous
\(M\) and \(N\) are both homogeneous of degree 2, so the equation is homogeneous
It is homogeneous because \(N\) has degree 0
It is not homogeneous because \(M\) contains a minus sign
quiz.why: \(M(\lambda x,\lambda y) = \lambda^2M\) and \(N(\lambda x,\lambda y) = \lambda^2(2xy) = \lambda^2N\): same degree 2 (Conclusion 1).

quiz.q: The general solution of \(y' = \dfrac{x+y}{x}\) is
quiz.why: \(y = ux\): \(u + xu' = 1 + u\Rightarrow xu' = 1\Rightarrow u = \ln|x| + C\), so \(y = x\ln|x| + Cx\).

quiz.q: Solving \(y' = \dfrac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\) with \(y = ux\) gives the family \(y = \dfrac{x}{1 + Cx^{1/3}}\). Which solution must be listed separately?
quiz.why: The \(u\)-equation \(xu' = \frac13u(u-1)\) has constant solutions \(u = 0\) and \(u = 1\). \(u = 1\) (\(y = x\)) is \(C = 0\); \(u = 0\) (\(y = 0\)) is not in the family. \(x = 0\) is outside the domain of this derivative form.

quiz.q: In Example 19, \((x^2 - 3y^2)dx + 2xy\,dy = 0\), why is \(x = 0\) also a solution?
o: In differential form, \(dx = 0\) and \(2xy\,dy = 0\) on the line \(x = 0\)
Every homogeneous equation has \(x = 0\) as a solution
Because it is the case \(D = 0\) of the family
quiz.why: On \(x = 0\): \(dx = 0\) and \(N = 2xy = 0\), so both terms vanish. This only works because the equation is written as \(M\,dx + N\,dy = 0\).

quiz.q: For the Riccati equation \(y' = p y^2 + q y + r\) with known solution \(y_1\), the substitution \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\) gives
quiz.why: After cancelling \(y_1' = py_1^2 + qy_1 + r\): \(-\frac{u'}{u^2} = (2py_1 + q)\frac1u + \frac{p}{u^2}\); multiply by \(-u^2\).

quiz.q: What do you need before you can use \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\) on a Riccati equation?
quiz.why: Theorem 9 starts from a known solution \(y_1\); in general Riccati solutions cannot be found with elementary functions without it.

quiz.q: \(y' = y^2 - \dfrac yx + \dfrac{\alpha}{x^2}\) has a particular solution \(y_1 = x^{\beta}\). Then \(\beta = \;?\)
quiz.why: Plugging in: \(\beta x^{\beta-1} = x^{2\beta} - x^{\beta-1} + \alpha x^{-2}\). The \(x^{2\beta}\) term must match \(x^{\beta-1}\): \(2\beta = \beta-1\), \(\beta = -1\) (and then \(\alpha = -1\)).

quiz.q: Example 22: \(y' = y^2 - 2xy + 2\), \(y_1 = 2x\). The linear equation for \(u\) (\(y = 2x + \frac1u\)) is
The general solution of the Clairaut equation \(y = xp + f(p)\), \(p = y'\), is
quiz.why: Differentiating gives \(\frac{dp}{dx}(x + f'(p)) = 0\); \(\frac{dp}{dx} = 0\) means \(p = c\), and you just replace \(p\) by \(c\).

quiz.q: The singular solution of \(y = xp + p^2\) is
quiz.why: \(x + 2p = 0\Rightarrow p = -\frac x2\), then \(y = -\frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^2}{4} = -\frac{x^2}{4}\). \(y = cx + c^2\) is the general solution, not the singular one.

quiz.q: Differentiating \(y = xp + f(p)\) with respect to \(x\) leads to
quiz.why: \(y' = p + x\frac{dp}{dx} + f'(p)\frac{dp}{dx}\) and \(y' = p\), so \(p\) cancels.

quiz.q: The singular solution of \(y = xp - p^2\) is
After differentiating the family \(\Phi(x,y,c) = 0\), what is the next step to get the orthogonal trajectories?
quiz.why: The slope \(f(x,y)\) of the family must be free of \(c\); the trajectories satisfy \(y' = -1/f(x,y)\) because perpendicular slopes multiply to \(-1\).

quiz.q: The orthogonal trajectories of the hyperbolas \(xy = c\) are
quiz.why: \(y + xy' = 0\Rightarrow y' = -\frac yx\); trajectories \(y' = \frac xy\Rightarrow y\,dy = x\,dx\Rightarrow y^2 - x^2 = C'\).

quiz.q: The orthogonal trajectories of the circles \(x^2 + y^2 = c^2\) are
quiz.why: \(y' = -\frac xy\), so the trajectories solve \(y' = \frac yx\): \(y = kx\), the lines through the origin (Example 24).

quiz.q: For the family \(y = ce^{x}\), the slope with \(c\) eliminated is
quiz.why: \(y' = ce^x\) and \(ce^x = y\). \(y' = -\frac1y\) is the trajectories' equation, the next step.

quiz.q: Example 26: the orthogonal trajectories of the parabolas \(y = kx^2\) are
quiz.why: \(m_1 = \frac{2y}{x}\), so \(y' = -\frac{x}{2y}\Rightarrow 2y\,dy = -x\,dx\Rightarrow y^2 = -\frac{x^2}{2} + C\): ellipses.

quiz.q: "A substance decomposes at a rate proportional to the cube of the amount present." Which equation models this?
quiz.why: "Rate" = \(\frac{dA}{dt}\), "proportional to the cube" = \(k\cdot A^3\), "decomposes" = decreasing, so a minus sign with \(k\gt 0\).

quiz.q: A pie is cooling in a room kept at 25 °C. With \(T(t)\) the pie's temperature, Newton's law of cooling reads:
quiz.why: The rate is proportional to the difference body − surroundings, \(T-T_m\), with \(-k\), \(k\gt 0\). Using \(25-T\) would make a hot pie heat up.

quiz.q: "A population grows at a rate proportional to the square root of the population." Which is correct?
quiz.why: Grows ⇒ positive rate; proportional to \(\sqrt P\) ⇒ \(k\sqrt P\) with \(k\gt 0\).

quiz.q: In Example 28 the thermometer reading is \(T(t)=16\cdot 2^{-t}+10\) (°C, \(t\) in minutes). What does it read after 6 minutes?
quiz.why: \(16\cdot 2^{-6}=\frac{16}{64}=0.25\), so \(T(6)=10.25\) °C — getting close to the outside temperature 10 °C.

quiz.q: Half of a Polonium-210 sample disintegrates in 138 years. What percentage remains after 414 years?
quiz.why: 414 = 3 × 138, i.e. three half-lives: \(\left(\frac12\right)^3=\frac18=12.5\%\).

quiz.q: After 20 days only \(\frac1{16}\) of a radioactive sample is left. What is its half-life?
quiz.why: \(\frac1{16}=\left(\frac12\right)^4\): 20 days = 4 half-lives, so \(h=5\) days.

quiz.q: A tank holds 500 lt of brine with \(x(t)\) kg of salt; the well-stirred mixture flows out at 4 lt/min (and enters at 4 lt/min). What is \(r_{\text{out}}\)?
quiz.why: \(r_{\text{out}}=(\text{outflow})\times(\text{concentration})=4\cdot\frac{x}{500}\). Forgetting to divide by the volume is a classic mistake.

quiz.q: A tank initially contains 100 lt. Liquid enters at 3 lt/min and leaves at 5 lt/min. The volume at time \(t\) is
An object of mass \(m=2\) kg falls with air resistance \(-kv\), \(k=0.5\), \(g=9.8\). Its limiting (terminal) velocity is
quiz.why: Limit of \(v(t)\) is \(\frac{mg}{k}=\frac{2\cdot 9.8}{0.5}=39.2\) m/s (where \(mg-kv=0\)).

quiz.q: Using \(\frac{dN}{dt}=kN\) (no minus sign) for a decay with half-life 138 years, the constant is
quiz.why: \(N_0e^{138k}=\frac{N_0}{2}\Rightarrow 138k=-\ln 2\). Without a minus in the model, the data make \(k\) negative.

quiz.q: Substance A is converted at a rate proportional to the square of its amount; \(A(0)=20\) g and \(A(1)=10\) g. How much is left at \(t=3\)?
quiz.why: \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\Rightarrow\frac1A=kt+\frac1{20}\); \(A(1)=10\Rightarrow k=\frac1{20}\). Then \(\frac1{A(3)}=\frac{4}{20}\), \(A(3)=5\) g. (2.5 g is the exponential answer.)

quiz.q: A body at 100 °C is placed in a 20 °C room and is at 60 °C after 1 minute. Its temperature after 2 minutes is
quiz.why: \(T=20+80e^{-kt}\), \(e^{-k}=\frac{40}{80}=\frac12\). So \(T(2)=20+80\cdot\frac14=40\) °C (the difference halves every minute, not the temperature).

quiz.q: How many initial conditions does an IVP for a third-order linear equation need?
quiz.why: An n-th order IVP needs \(y,y',\dots,y^{(n-1)}\) at the same point \(x_0\).

quiz.q: For \((x-2)y''+3y=x\), \(y(0)=1\), \(y'(0)=0\), the existence–uniqueness theorem guarantees a unique solution on
quiz.why: \(a_0(x)=x-2\) must be non-zero on the interval, which must contain \(x_0=0\): the largest such interval is \((-\infty,2)\).

quiz.q: \(W[e^x,e^{2x}]\) equals
quiz.why: \(\begin{vmatrix}e^x&e^{2x}\\e^x&2e^{2x}\end{vmatrix}=2e^{3x}-e^{3x}=e^{3x}\).

quiz.q: \(W[x,x^2]\) equals
quiz.why: \(x\cdot 2x-x^2\cdot 1=x^2\).

quiz.q: Which pair of functions is linearly dependent?
quiz.why: \(-3\cdot\sin x+1\cdot 3\sin x=0\) with constants not all zero (Example 32).

quiz.q: For \(f_1=x|x|\) and \(f_2=x^2\) on \([-1,1]\), which statement is correct?
o: They are both solutions of one 2nd order homogeneous linear equation
quiz.why: Example 34: \(W=2x^2|x|-2x^2|x|=0\), yet \(c_1=c_2=0\) is forced. No contradiction: they cannot both solve one such equation (Remark 5).

quiz.q: For which equation does superposition fail (i.e. \(c_1\varphi_1+c_2\varphi_2\) need not be a solution)?
quiz.why: Superposition needs a linear homogeneous equation. \(yy''+(y')^2=0\) is not linear (Example 36).

quiz.q: The general solution of \(y''+y=x\) is
quiz.why: \(\varphi_c=c_1\cos x+c_2\sin x\) and \(\varphi_p=x\) (\(0+x=x\)); general solution \(=\varphi_c+\varphi_p\).

quiz.q: In reduction of order with \(y=xz\), the second derivative is
Substituting \(y=xz\) into \((x^2+1)y''-2xy'+2y=0\) gives
quiz.why: \((x^2+1)(2z'+xz'')-2x(z+xz')+2xz\): the \(z\)-terms cancel and \(z'(2x^2+2-2x^2)=2z'\) (Example 38).

quiz.q: \(\varphi_1,\varphi_2\) solve \(y''+p(x)y'+q(x)y=0\) on \(I\) and \(W[\varphi_1,\varphi_2](1)=5\) (with \(1\in I\)). Then
o: \(W(x)\ne 0\) for all \(x\in I\), so they are independent
quiz.why: Theorem 13: for solutions, either \(W\equiv 0\) or \(W\) is never zero. Since \(W(1)\ne 0\), it is never zero ⇒ independent (Corollary 2).

quiz.q: \(y''-5y'+6y=1,\ =x,\ =e^x\) have particular solutions \(\frac16\), \(\frac x6+\frac5{36}\), \(\frac12e^x\). A solution of \(y''-5y'+6y=2e^x+36(x+1)\) is
quiz.why: \(f=36\cdot 1+36\cdot x+2\cdot e^x\) ⇒ \(\varphi=36\cdot\frac16+36\left(\frac x6+\frac5{36}\right)+2\cdot\frac12e^x=e^x+6x+11\) (Theorem 16).

cards.back: An equation involving one or more derivatives of an unknown function.
ODE: unknown depends on one variable (ordinary derivatives). PDE: unknown depends on several variables (partial derivatives).
The order of the highest derivative occurring. \(\left(y'\right)^3=y^2\) has order 1.
An \(n\)-times differentiable \(y(x)\) on \(I\) that satisfies the equation identically for all \(x\in I\).
Explicit: \(y=\varphi(x)\). Implicit: a relation \(\Phi(x,y)=0\) that defines one or more explicit solutions on \(I\).
General: \(n\) arbitrary constants. Particular: no constants. Singular: cannot be obtained from the general solution by any choice of constants.
If \(f\) and \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) are continuous on \(R=\{|x-x_0|\le a,\ |y-y_0|\le b\}\), the IVP has a unique solution on some \(|x-x_0|\lt h\).
\(f_y=\frac{x}{2\sqrt y}\) fails at \(y=0\); two solutions: \(y\equiv0\) and \(y=\frac{x^4}{16}\).
Find the general solution, substitute \(x_0,y_0\), solve for \(C\), state the interval containing \(x_0\).
Unique (\(f,f_y\) continuous). Solution \(y=\tan x\), only on \(\left(-\frac\pi2,\frac\pi2\right)\).
Dividing by \(h(y)\) assumes \(h(y)\neq0\). Roots \(h(y_1)=0\) give constant solutions \(y\equiv y_1\); singular if not in the general solution.
\(y=Ke^{x^2}\); \(y=0\) comes back with \(K=0\), so it is not singular.
\(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}\) (on a rectangle where they are continuous).
A non-zero \(\mu(x,y)\) such that \(\mu M\,dx+\mu N\,dy=0\) is exact.
Multiply, compute \(\tilde M_y,\tilde N_x\), match coefficients of equal powers, solve for \(m,n\).
\(y=e^{-\int p}\left(\int e^{\int p}q\,dx+C\right)\); contains all solutions.

cards.front: Linear equation \(u' + P(x)u = Q(x)\): the routine
cards.back: \(\mu = e^{\int P\,dx}\); \((\mu u)' = \mu Q\); \(u = \frac1\mu\big(\int\mu Q\,dx + C\big)\)
\(y = Kx\), \(K = \pm C\neq0\); if \(y = 0\) also solves it: \(y = Dx\), \(D\in\mathbb R\)

cards.front: Bernoulli: which solution does the substitution lose?
Equation with \(x^3\) on the right after flipping to \(dx/dy\)?
\(q(x)\) with a jump (Example 17): how to get a continuous solution?
cards.back: Solve on each side with its own constant, then match the one-sided limits at the jump
\(y' = g(y/x)\); test: \(f(\lambda x,\lambda y) = f(x,y)\), or \(M, N\) homogeneous of the same degree
Roots \(u_0\) of \(g(u) = u\) give lines \(y = u_0x\): check if a constant value reproduces them, else list them
Solve for the intersection \((h,k)\); \(x = u+h\), \(y = v+k\) gives a homogeneous equation
\(z = a_1x + b_1y\) gives a separable equation in \(z\) and \(x\)

cards.front: Riccati with particular solution \(y_1\): substitution and result
Riccati: how to find \(y_1\) when only its form is given
cards.back: Plug the form (\(a/x\), \(x^\beta\), \(ax+b\), constant) into the equation and match powers/coefficients

cards.front: Clairaut equation and its general solution
cards.back: \(y = xp + f(p)\), \(p = y'\); general solution \(y = cx + f(c)\)
From \(x + f'(p) = 0\): \(x = -f'(p)\), \(y = xp + f(p)\), eliminate \(p\). E.g. \(y = xp + p^2\Rightarrow y = -\frac{x^2}{4}\)
Differentiate the family, eliminate \(c\) to get \(y' = f(x,y)\), solve \(y' = -1/f(x,y)\)

cards.front: Trajectories of \(x^2 + y^2 = c^2\) and of \(y = kx^2\)

cards.back: The family itself (self-orthogonal): the two roots \(c = -x\pm\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) give perpendicular slopes

cards.front: "Rate proportional to the square of the amount" (decreasing) — equation and solution?
In the cooling law, what are \(T\), \(T_m\), \(k\)?
cards.back: \(T\): body temperature; \(T_m\): temperature of the surrounding medium; \(k\): positive constant of proportionality

cards.front: Falling object with air resistance \(-kv\): equation and solution
Limiting (terminal) velocity of a falling body

cards.back: \(a_i, f\) continuous on \(I\), \(a_0\ne 0\) on \(I\) ⇒ unique solution on the entire \(I\)
Linear combinations of solutions of a linear homogeneous equation are again solutions
\(W(x)\ne 0\) for all \(x\in I\) (and \(W\) is either \(\equiv 0\) or never 0)
\(W\equiv 0\) but linearly independent — no conflict, they cannot both solve one 2nd-order homogeneous linear equation
n independent solutions of \(L(D)y=0\); general solution \(c_1\varphi_1+\cdots+c_n\varphi_n\)

exams.title: Real midterm 2023–2024
exams.blurb: The actual 17.11.2023 midterm. 5 questions × 20 points, with the lecturer-style solutions.

items.q: During a chemical reaction, substance A is converted into substance B at a rate that is proportional to the square of the amount of A. Initially, 50 grams of A is present, and after 2 hours only 10 grams of A remain unconverted. How much of A is present after 4 hours?
items.hint: "Proportional to the square" and "converted" (decreasing): \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA^2\). Separable; use \(A(0)\) for \(C\), \(A(2)\) for \(k\).

items.q: Find the general solution of \((\tan y+2x)\,dx+(x-x^2\tan y)\,dy=0\).
items.hint: Not exact; \(\frac{M_y-N_x}{M}=\tan y\) depends only on \(y\), so \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int\tan y\,dy}=\cos y\). Use \(\sec^2y-1=\tan^2y\).
steps: \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int\tan y\,dy}=e^{\ln|\cos y|}=|\cos y|\). On any interval where \(\cos y\ne0\), a constant multiple of an integrating factor still works, so we can take \(\mu(y)=\cos y\).
New equation: \((\sin y+2x\cos y)dx+(x\cos y-x^2\sin y)dy=0\); \(\tilde M_y=\cos y-2x\sin y=\tilde N_x\): exact.
\(F=\int(\sin y+2x\cos y)dx+g(y)=x\sin y+x^2\cos y+g(y)\); \(F_y=\tilde N\Rightarrow g'(y)=0\Rightarrow g=0\).

items.q: Find the general solution of \(e^y\,y'+e^y=e^{3y+2x}\).
items.hint: \(e^yy'\) is the derivative of \(e^y\): put \(z=e^y\) to get the Bernoulli equation \(z'+z=z^3e^{2x}\) (\(n=3\)), then \(u=z^{-2}\).

items.q: Find all solutions of \(y'=\dfrac{y(y+2x)}{3x^2}\).
items.hint: Right side is a function of \(y/x\): homogeneous, put \(y=vx\). "All solutions": check the constant solutions \(v=0\), \(v=1\) lost when dividing.
steps: \(K=0\) gives \(y=x\) (in the family). \(y=0\) is not in the family: singular solution.

items.q: Find a second solution of \((x^2+x)y''-2xy'+2y=0\) if it is known that \(f(x)=x\) is a solution of the given differential equation. Write the general solution.
items.hint: Reduction of order: \(y=xz\), then \(w=z'\). The \(z'\) coefficient must come out \(2x\).

exams.title: Mock midterm 1
exams.blurb: Same blueprint as the real midterm: word problem, integrating factor, substitution, “find all solutions”, reduction of order.

items.q: A cup of coffee at 90 °C is placed in a room whose temperature is kept at 20 °C. After 10 minutes the coffee is at 60 °C. Assuming Newton's law of cooling, when will the coffee reach 30 °C?
items.hint: Newton's law: \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-20)\), solution \(T=20+70e^{-kt}\); the 10-minute reading gives \(e^{-10k}\).

items.q: Find the general solution of \((x^2+y^2+x)\,dx+xy\,dy=0\).
items.hint: Not exact. Compute \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)\): it depends on \(x\) only, so use Case 1 of Theorem 4.
steps: \(M=x^2+y^2+x\), \(N=xy\). \(\frac{\partial M}{\partial y}=2y\neq\frac{\partial N}{\partial x}=y\). Not exact.
\(M_y-N_x=y\). \(\frac1M(M_y-N_x)=\frac{y}{x^2+y^2+x}\) is not a function of \(y\) only; \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)=\frac{y}{xy}=\frac1x=f(x)\).
items.src: modeled on Week 2-2.pdf p.13, 16–18 (Theorem 4 Case 1, Example 13)

items.q: Find the general solution of \( \cos(y)\,y' + \sin(y) = x\sin^2(y) \). (Hint: let \(z = \sin y\).)
items.hint: \(z = \sin y\) gives \(z' = \cos y\,y'\), and the equation becomes Bernoulli in \(z\) with \(n = 2\).
steps: Let \(z = \sin y\). Then \(\dfrac{dz}{dx} = \cos y\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}\), so the equation is \(z' + z = x\,z^2\): a Bernoulli equation with \(p = 1\), \(q = x\), \(n = 2\).
Integrating factor \(\mu = e^{-\int dx} = e^{-x}\): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}\big(e^{-x}u\big) = -x e^{-x}\).
items.answer: \(\sin y = \dfrac{1}{x + 1 + Ce^{x}}\), \(C\) arbitrary; and the constant solutions \(y = k\pi\) (\(\sin y = 0\)).
items.src: modeled on Week+3.pdf p.3–4 (Theorem 6) and midterm 2023 Q3

items.q: Find all solutions of \(\frac{dy}{dx}=2x\left(y^2-1\right)\).
items.hint: Separable with \(h(y)=y^2-1\). Solve for \(y\neq\mp1\), then check \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) separately.
steps: If \(y^2-1=0\): \(y=1\) and \(y=-1\) give \(y'=0=2x\cdot0\). Both are solutions (lost solutions).
\(K=0\) gives \(y=1\), so \(y=1\) is contained in the family. \(\frac{1+A}{1-A}=-1\) would need \(1=-1\): no \(K\) gives \(y=-1\).
items.answer: \(y=\frac{1+Ke^{2x^2}}{1-Ke^{2x^2}}\), \(K\) arbitrary (contains \(y=1\) for \(K=0\)), and the singular solution \(y=-1\).

items.q: Given that \(y_1=x^2\) is a solution of \(x^2y''-3xy'+4y=0\) for \(x\gt 0\), find a second linearly independent solution and write the general solution.
items.hint: Reduction of order: \(y=x^2z\); the \(z\)-term cancels and you get a first-order equation for \(w=z'\).

exams.title: Mock midterm 2
exams.blurb: Same blueprint as the real midterm: word problem, integrating factor, substitution, “find all solutions”, reduction of order.

items.q: A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the amount present. It is observed that 20% of the original amount has decayed after 5 years. (a) Find the half-life. (b) What percentage of the original amount remains after 20 years?
items.hint: \(\frac{dN}{dt}=-kN\Rightarrow N=N_0e^{-kt}\). "20% decayed" means 80% remains: \(N(5)=0.8N_0\).

items.q: Find the general solution of \((2y^2+2xy+y)\,dx+(x+2y)\,dy=0\).
items.hint: Factor \(M_y-N_x\) and compare it with \(N\).
steps: \(M_y-N_x=2x+4y=2(x+2y)=2N\). So \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)=2=f(x)\) (a constant is a function of \(x\) only).
items.src: modeled on Week 2-2.pdf p.13 and Exercises 3.3 #1 (p.20)

items.q: Find the general solution of \( x^2\,y' + x = e^{y} \).
items.hint: Write it as \(y' + \frac1x = \frac{e^{y}}{x^2}\); with \(z = e^{y}\) it is Bernoulli (\(n=2\)), so \(u = z^{-1} = e^{-y}\) makes it linear.
steps: Let \(z = e^{y}\), \(z' = e^{y}y' = z\Big(\dfrac{z}{x^2} - \dfrac1x\Big)\). So \(z' + \dfrac1x z = \dfrac{1}{x^2}z^2\): Bernoulli with \(n = 2\). (\(z = e^y\) is never 0, so nothing is lost.)
items.src: modeled on midterm 2023 Q3 and Week+3.pdf p.3–4

items.q: Find all solutions of \(\frac{dy}{dx}=e^{x}\cos^2y\).
items.hint: Separable with \(h(y)=\cos^2y\). Divide only where \(\cos y\neq0\); the zeros of \(\cos y\) give constant solutions.
steps: At \(y=\frac\pi2+k\pi\), \(\tan y\) is undefined, so no \(C\) produces them: singular solutions.
items.answer: \(\tan y=e^x+C\) (\(C\) arbitrary), together with the singular solutions \(y=\frac\pi2+k\pi\), \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\).

items.q: Given that \(y_1=e^x\) is a solution of \(xy''-(x+1)y'+y=0\), \(x\gt 0\), find a second linearly independent solution by reduction of order and write the general solution.
items.hint: Put \(y=e^xz\); the reduced equation is \(xw'+(x-1)w=0\) with \(w=z'\).
steps: \(z=\int xe^{-x}dx=-(x+1)e^{-x}\) (by parts) \(\Rightarrow y_2=e^xz=-(x+1)\); drop the constant factor \(-1\).

exams.title: Mock midterm 3
exams.blurb: Same blueprint as the real midterm: word problem, integrating factor, substitution, “find all solutions”, reduction of order.

items.q: A tank initially contains 100 lt of pure water. Brine containing 2 g of salt per litre flows into the tank at 5 lt/min, and the well-stirred mixture flows out at the same rate. (a) Find the amount of salt after 20 minutes. (b) When will the concentration in the tank be 1 g/lt?
items.hint: \(\frac{dx}{dt}=r_{\text{in}}-r_{\text{out}}\) with \(r_{\text{in}}=5\cdot 2\) and \(r_{\text{out}}=5\cdot\frac{x}{100}\); linear.

items.q: Find the general solution of \(y\,dx+\left(2x-ye^{y}\right)dy=0\).
items.hint: \(\frac1N(M_y-N_x)\) still contains \(y\); try \(\frac1M(M_y-N_x)\) and remember the minus sign in \(\mu(y)=e^{-\int g}\).
items.src: modeled on Week 2-2.pdf p.14 (Theorem 4 Case 2) and 2023 midterm Q2

items.q: Show that \(y_1 = e^{x}\) is a particular solution of the Riccati equation \( y' = e^{-x}y^2 + y - e^{x} \) and find its general solution.
items.hint: Use \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\); the linear equation is \(u' + (2py_1 + q)u = -p\) with \(p = e^{-x}\), \(q = 1\).
steps: Check: \(y_1' = e^{x}\) and \(e^{-x}e^{2x} + e^{x} - e^{x} = e^{x}\). So \(y_1 = e^x\) is a particular solution.

items.q: Find all solutions of \( x^2\,y' = y^2 + 2xy \).
items.hint: Homogeneous (\(y' = (y/x)^2 + 2(y/x)\)): put \(y = ux\); watch the roots of \(u^2 + u = 0\). (It is also Bernoulli with \(n = 2\).)
steps: For \(x\neq0\): \(y' = \Big(\dfrac yx\Big)^2 + 2\dfrac yx = g\big(\tfrac yx\big)\) — homogeneous.
\(y = ux\), \(y' = u + xu'\): \(u + xu' = u^2 + 2u\Rightarrow x\dfrac{du}{dx} = u(u+1)\) (separable).
Lost values: \(u = 0\) (\(y = 0\)) solves the equation and is \(K = 0\). \(u = -1\) (\(y = -x\)): \(x^2(-1) = x^2 - 2x^2\) holds, so it is a solution, but no \(K\) gives it.

Check with the Bernoulli way: \(y' - \frac2xy = \frac{1}{x^2}y^2\), \(u = 1/y\): \((x^2u)' = -1\Rightarrow \frac1y = \frac{C - x}{x^2}\), i.e. \(y = \frac{x^2}{C - x}\) — now \(C = 0\) gives \(y = -x\), and \(y = 0\) is the extra one. Same set of solutions.
items.answer: \(y = \dfrac{x^2}{C - x}\), \(C\in\mathbb R\) (contains \(y = -x\) for \(C = 0\)), together with \(y = 0\). Equivalently \(y = \dfrac{Kx^2}{1-Kx}\), \(K\in\mathbb R\), together with \(y = -x\).
items.src: modeled on Week+4.pdf p.18–19 (quiz) and Week+3.pdf p.21–25

items.q: Given that \(y_1=x\) is a solution of \(x^2y''+xy'-y=0\), \(x\gt 0\), find a second linearly independent solution and the general solution.
items.hint: \(y=xz\Rightarrow x^3z''+3x^2z'=0\).

exams.title: Mock midterm 4
exams.blurb: Same blueprint as the real midterm: word problem, integrating factor, substitution, “find all solutions”, reduction of order.

items.q: A substance dissolves in water at a rate proportional to the square root of the amount still undissolved. Initially there are 100 g; after 1 hour 64 g are still undissolved. (a) How much is undissolved after 2 hours? (b) When is it completely dissolved?
items.hint: "Square root of the amount", decreasing: \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-k\sqrt A\). Separable: \(\int A^{-1/2}dA=-\int k\,dt\).

items.q: Find the general solution of \((2x+y)\,dx+\left(x^2+xy+x\right)dy=0\).
items.hint: Compute \(M_y-N_x\) and compare it with \(M\).
items.src: modeled on Week 2-2.pdf p.14 (Theorem 4 Case 2) and 2023 midterm Q2

items.q: The Riccati equation \( y' = y^2 - \dfrac{2}{x^2} \) has a particular solution of the form \(y_1 = \dfrac{a}{x}\). Find a suitable \(a\) and the general solution.
items.hint: Plug \(y_1 = a/x\) in to get an equation for \(a\); then \(y = y_1 + \frac1u\).
steps: \(y_1 = \dfrac ax\Rightarrow y_1' = -\dfrac{a}{x^2}\). Plug in: \(-\dfrac{a}{x^2} = \dfrac{a^2}{x^2} - \dfrac{2}{x^2}\Rightarrow a^2 + a - 2 = 0\Rightarrow a = 1\) or \(a = -2\). Take \(a = 1\): \(y_1 = \dfrac1x\).
\(\mu = e^{\int\frac2xdx} = x^2\): \(\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^2u) = -x^2\Rightarrow x^2u = -\dfrac{x^3}{3} + C\Rightarrow u = \dfrac{3C - x^3}{3x^2}\).
items.answer: \(a = 1\) (or \(a = -2\)); \(y = \dfrac1x + \dfrac{3x^2}{K - x^3}\), \(K\) arbitrary; and \(y = \dfrac1x\). (Note \(y = -\frac2x\) is the case \(K = 0\).)

items.q: Find all solutions of \( x\,y' + y = y^2\ln x \), \(x \gt 0\).
items.hint: Divide by \(x\): Bernoulli with \(n = 2\). Remember \(y = 0\).
steps: \(y = 0\) is a solution (\(0 + 0 = 0\)). For \(y\neq0\): \(u = y^{-1}\), \(u' = -y^{-2}y'\). Multiply by \(-y^{-2}\): \(u' - \dfrac1x u = -\dfrac{\ln x}{x}\) (linear).
By parts, \(\int\frac{\ln x}{x^2}dx = -\frac{\ln x + 1}{x}\). So \(\dfrac ux = \dfrac{\ln x + 1}{x} + C\Rightarrow u = \ln x + 1 + Cx\).

items.q: Given that \(f(x)=x\) is a solution of \((x^2-1)y''-2xy'+2y=0\) on \(x\gt 1\), find a second solution and write the general solution.
items.hint: Same pattern as the 2023 midterm Q5: \(y=xz\); expect \(x(x^2-1)z''-2z'=0\) and partial fractions.
items.src: modeled on 2023-2024 midterm.pdf Q5 and Week+6.pdf p.32

exams.title: Concept check 1
exams.blurb: Quick multiple-choice test of recognising methods and key facts.

items.q: \(\displaystyle\int\frac{\ln x}{x^2}\,dx = \;?\)
items.why: By parts, \(f = \ln x\), \(g' = x^{-2}\): \(-\frac{\ln x}{x} + \int\frac{1}{x^2}dx = -\frac{\ln x}{x} - \frac1x\). \(\frac{(\ln x)^2}{2}\) is \(\int\frac{\ln x}{x}dx\).
items.src: Integration toolkit (by parts; needed in problem m-p-b-06)

items.q: For which \(\alpha\) is \(y=e^{\alpha x}(c_1x+c_2)\) the general solution of \(y''-4y'+4y=0\)?
items.why: Substituting gives \(e^{\alpha x}\left[(\alpha-2)^2(c_1x+c_2)+(2\alpha-4)c_1\right]=0\) for all \(c_1,c_2\), so \(\alpha=2\).
General solution \(y=\frac{1}{x^2+C}\); \(y(0)=\frac1C=-1\) gives \(C=-1\). The formula breaks at \(x=\pm1\), so the solution lives on \((-1,1)\).

items.q: Solve \(e^{y^2}\ln x\,dx-y\,dy=0\).
items.why: \(\int ye^{-y^2}dy=-\frac12e^{-y^2}\) and \(\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x\). Multiply by \(-2\): the \(x\) term becomes \(+2x\) (the handwritten line has \(+x\), a slip).

items.q: Which \(M\) makes \(M(x,y)\,dx+(2x^2y-1)\,dy=0\) exact?
items.why: Need \(M_y=N_x=4xy\); integrating in \(y\) gives \(2xy^2\) plus anything depending only on \(x\). Solution (with \(k=0\)): \(x^2y^2-y=C\).

items.q: An integrating factor for \((x+y-1)y\,dx+(x+2y-2)\,dy=0\) is …
Best way to solve \(y^2\,dx+(3xy-1)\,dy=0\)?
items.why: \(M_y=2y\neq N_x=3y\), and it is not linear in \(y\). Flipping gives a linear equation for \(x(y)\); then \(xy^3=\frac{y^2}{2}+C\).

items.q: Example 17: the continuous solution of \(y' + y = q(x)\), \(y(0) = 0\), with \(q = 1\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(q = -1\) for \(x \lt 0\), is, for \(x \lt 0\):
items.why: For \(x \lt 0\), \(y = -1 + \tilde Ce^{-x}\); continuity at 0 with \(1 - e^{-x}\) (value 0) forces \(\tilde C = 1\).

items.q: In \((x + 2y + 3)dx + (2x + 4y - 1)dy = 0\) the separation step needs \(x + 2y \neq \tfrac12\). What is the line \(x + 2y = \tfrac12\)?
o: The member \(C = 0\) of the general solution
items.why: On \(x + 2y = \frac12\): \(dx + 2dy = 0\) and the second bracket is 0, so the equation gives \((\frac12 + 3)dx = 0\), false. Always substitute excluded values back.

items.q: If \(r(x) = 0\), the Riccati equation \(y' = p(x)y^2 + q(x)y + r(x)\) is
items.why: \(y' - q(x)y = p(x)y^2\) is Bernoulli with \(n = 2\) (handwritten note on the definition slide).

items.q: The orthogonal trajectories of \(y = cx^3\) are
items.why: \(c = \frac{y}{x^3}\), \(y' = 3cx^2 = \frac{3y}{x}\); trajectories \(y' = -\frac{x}{3y}\Rightarrow 3y\,dy = -x\,dx\Rightarrow 3y^2 + x^2 = C\).

items.q: A bacteria colony grows at a rate proportional to its size and doubles every 3 hours. How long does it take to become 8 times as large?
items.why: \(N=N_0\,2^{t/3}\); \(8=2^3\Rightarrow t/3=3\Rightarrow t=9\) h.

items.q: A drug is eliminated from the blood at a rate proportional to the amount present. When 50 mg is present, it is eliminated at 10 mg/h. The model is
items.why: \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA\) and \(-10=-k\cdot 50\Rightarrow k=0.2\). A rate given at a moment fixes \(k\) directly (like the tea exercise).

items.q: \(y_1=x\) solves \(x^2y''+xy'-y=0\) (\(x\gt 0\)). Reduction of order gives the second solution
items.why: \(y=xz\Rightarrow x^3z''+3x^2z'=0\Rightarrow w=x^{-3}\), \(z=-\frac1{2x^2}\), \(y_2=-\frac1{2x}\sim\frac1x\). Check: \(\frac{2}{x}-\frac1x-\frac1x=0\).

items.q: The functions \(\pi,\ \tan^2x,\ \sec^2x\) are
o: linearly independent, because \(\pi\) is a constant
items.why: \(1\cdot\pi+\pi\tan^2x-\pi\sec^2x=\pi(1+\tan^2x-\sec^2x)=0\) for all \(x\), with constants not all zero.

exams.title: Concept check 2
exams.blurb: Quick multiple-choice test of recognising methods and key facts.

items.q: Which equation has no general solution (its only solution is \(y\equiv1\))?
items.why: A sum of squares is 0 only if \(y'=0\) and \(y=1\). No arbitrary constant appears, so there is no general solution (Remark 1).

items.q: \(y'=1+y^2,\ y(0)=0\) has the unique solution \(y=\tan x\). What is the largest interval containing 0 where it exists?
items.why: \(\tan x\) blows up at \(\pm\frac\pi2\). Theorem 1 only promises some interval \(|x|\lt h\), even though \(f=1+y^2\) is continuous everywhere.

items.q: All solutions of \(\frac{dy}{dx}=x(y^2-4)\) are \(y=\frac{2(1+Ke^{2x^2})}{1-Ke^{2x^2}}\) (\(K\) arbitrary) plus constant solutions. Which constant solution is singular for this family?
items.why: Both \(y=\pm2\) solve the equation. \(K=0\) gives \(y=2\), but no \(K\) gives \(-2\). So only \(y=-2\) is singular.

items.q: General solution of \(e^y\,dx+(xe^y+2y)\,dy=0\)?
items.why: \(M_y=e^y=N_x\). \(F=xe^y+g(y)\); \(F_y=xe^y+g'(y)=xe^y+2y\Rightarrow g=y^2\).

items.q: An integrating factor for \(y\,dx+(2x-ye^y)\,dy=0\) is …

items.why: \(\mu=e^x\): \((e^xy)'=1\Rightarrow e^xy=x+C\Rightarrow y=(x+C)e^{-x}\); \(y(0)=C=0\).

items.q: Which substitution turns \(e^{y}y' + e^{y} = e^{3y+2x}\) into a Bernoulli equation, and what is \(n\)?
items.why: \(z = e^y\), \(z' = e^yy'\): \(z' + z = e^{2x}z^3\) — Bernoulli with \(n = 3\). Then \(u = z^{-2} = e^{-2y}\) is the linearising substitution (a second step).

items.q: For \((x - 2y + 1)dx + (4x - 3y - 6)dy = 0\), compute \(\Delta = a_1b_2 - a_2b_1\) and choose the next step.
items.why: \(\Delta = 1(-3) - 4(-2) = 5\neq0\), Case 1; the lines meet at \((h,k) = (3,2)\), so shift \(x = u + 3\), \(y = v + 2\) to get a homogeneous equation.

items.q: The general solution of \(y' = y^2 - 2xy + x^2 + 1\), which has the particular solution \(y_1 = x\), is
For \(y = xp + p^3\), eliminating \(p\) from \(x = -3p^2\), \(y = -2p^3\) gives the singular solution
items.why: \(y^2 = 4p^6 = 4\big(-\frac x3\big)^3 = -\frac{4x^3}{27}\) (so \(x \le 0\)). The sign matters: \(p^2 = -\frac x3\).

items.q: The orthogonal trajectories of the circles \(x^2 + y^2 = 2cx\) are
items.why: Eliminating \(c\): \(y' = \frac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy}\). The trajectory equation \(y' = \frac{2xy}{x^2 - y^2}\) is homogeneous; \(y = ux\) gives \(\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2} = K'x\), i.e. \(x^2 + y^2 = Ky\).

items.q: In Example 30, \(x(t)=1000\left(1-e^{-3t/500}\right)\) kg. Which statement is true?
o: The salt reaches 1000 kg after \(\frac{500}{3}\) minutes
items.why: \(e^{-3t/500}\to 0\), so \(x\to 1000\) kg (concentration → 1 kg/lt, the inflow concentration) but never reaches it. At \(T=\frac{500}{3}\ln 2\) the concentration is \(\frac12\).

items.q: A cup at 90 °C is in a 30 °C room; at the initial moment it is cooling at 3 °C per minute. In \(\frac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-30)\), \(k\) equals
items.why: Put \(t=0\) in the equation: \(-3=-k(90-30)\Rightarrow k=\frac{3}{60}=\frac1{20}\).

items.q: \(W[1,x,x^2]\) equals
items.why: \(\begin{vmatrix}1&x&x^2\\0&1&2x\\0&0&2\end{vmatrix}\) is upper triangular: \(1\cdot 1\cdot 2=2\).

items.q: In \((x^2+x)y''-2xy'+2y=0\) put \(y=xz\). The coefficient of \(z'\) after collecting terms is
items.why: \((x^2+x)\cdot 2z'=(2x^2+2x)z'\) and \(-2x\cdot xz'=-2x^2z'\): total \(2xz'\). The handwritten 2023 solution wrote \(2x-2x^2\) — an error.

exams.title: Problem bank
exams.blurb: Extra exam-style problems on every topic. No rush: open the steps whenever you’re stuck.

items.q: Consider \(\frac{dy}{dx}=3y^{2/3}\). (a) Where does Theorem 1 guarantee a unique solution through \((x_0,y_0)\)? (b) Show that the IVP with \(y(0)=0\) has at least two solutions.
items.hint: Check where \(f\) and \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\) are continuous; \(y^{-1/3}\) breaks at \(y=0\).
steps: \(\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}=2y^{-1/3}=\frac{2}{\sqrt[3]{y}}\) is continuous only for \(y\neq0\).
(a) For \(y_0\neq0\) a small rectangle around \((x_0,y_0)\) avoids \(y=0\): unique solution on some \(|x-x_0|\lt h\).
(b) At \((0,0)\) the theorem does not apply. \(y\equiv0\): \(0=3\cdot0\). ✓
items.answer: (a) Every \((x_0,y_0)\) with \(y_0\neq0\). (b) \(y\equiv0\) and \(y=x^3\) both solve the IVP, so uniqueness fails.

items.q: Solve the IVP \(e^{y}\frac{dy}{dx}=x\cos x,\ y(0)=0\).
items.hint: Separable (Example 11 (1)): integrate \(e^y\,dy=x\cos x\,dx\), then use the initial condition.
steps: \(e^y=x\sin x+\cos x+C\) (by parts on the right).
\(y=\ln\left(x\sin x+\cos x\right)\), valid on the interval around \(0\) where \(x\sin x+\cos x\gt0\).
items.answer: \(y=\ln\left(x\sin x+\cos x\right)\) (near \(x=0\), where the argument is positive).
items.src: modeled on Week+1-3.pdf p.31 (Example 11 (1)) and p.22–23 (IVP)

items.q: Solve \(\frac{dy}{dx}=-2xy^2,\ y(0)=-1\). Give the largest interval on which the solution exists.
items.hint: Separate for \(y\neq0\); the solution must live on an interval containing \(x_0=0\).
steps: The formula is undefined at \(x=\pm1\); the interval containing \(0\) is \((-1,1)\).

items.q: Find all solutions of \(\left(y^2+1\right)dx+xy\,dy=0\).
items.hint: Differential form: put \(y\)-terms with \(dy\), \(x\)-terms with \(dx\). Dividing by \(x\) may lose the line \(x=0\); then check whether some value of the constant brings it back.
steps: For \(x=0\): \(dx=0\) and \(xy\,dy=0\). So the line \(x=0\) is a solution (lost when we divided by \(x\)).

Is it in the family? With \(K=0\): \(x^2(y^2+1)=0\iff x=0\) (because \(y^2+1\gt0\)). So \(x=0\) is the member \(K=0\), and it is not singular. Compare Exercise 3.1 #1, where \(x=-1\) is not in \(\arctan y+\ln|x+1|=C\) for any \(C\), so there it is singular.
items.answer: \(x^2\left(y^2+1\right)=K\), \(K\ge0\) arbitrary (\(K=0\) gives the solution \(x=0\)); there is no singular solution.

items.q: Solve \(\left(2xy-\sec^2x\right)dx+\left(x^2+2y\right)dy=0,\ y\!\left(\frac\pi4\right)=1\).
items.hint: Check \(M_y=N_x\), build \(F\), then use the initial point to find \(C\).

items.q: Find the general solution of \(\left(y\cos x+2xe^y\right)dx+\left(\sin x+x^2e^y-1\right)dy=0\).
items.hint: Test exactness, then integrate \(M\) in \(x\) (or \(N\) in \(y\)).

items.q: Solve the initial value problem \(y'+3y=x,\ y(0)=1\).
items.hint: Linear with \(p=3\): \(\mu=e^{3x}\).
steps: By parts: \(\int xe^{3x}dx=\frac x3e^{3x}-\frac19e^{3x}\). So \(e^{3x}y=\frac x3e^{3x}-\frac19e^{3x}+C\).

items.q: Solve \(y'-\tan(x)\,y=\sec x,\ y(0)=2\), and state the interval of validity.
items.hint: \(p(x)=-\tan x\) (watch the sign); \(\mu=e^{-\int\tan x\,dx}\).
steps: \(p=-\tan x\), \(q=\sec x\); both are continuous on \(-\frac\pi2\lt x\lt\frac\pi2\), the interval containing \(x_0=0\).

items.hint: Divide by \(x\) first to get standard form; work on \(x\gt0\).
items.src: modeled on Week 2-2.pdf p.22–25 (standard form, Theorem 5)

items.q: Find the general solution of \(y\,dx+\left(2x-y^2\right)dy=0\).
items.hint: Not linear in \(y\), but linear in \(x\): write \(\frac{dx}{dy}+p(y)x=q(y)\).

items.q: Find all solutions of \( y' + \dfrac{y}{x} = x\,y^3 \), \(x \gt 0\).
items.hint: Bernoulli with \(n = 3\): \(u = y^{-2}\), multiply by \(-2y^{-3}\).

items.q: Find all solutions of \( (x + y + 1)\,dx + (2x + 2y - 1)\,dy = 0 \).
items.hint: \(\Delta = 1\cdot2 - 2\cdot1 = 0\): Case 2 of Theorem 8, put \(z = x + y\).
steps: Back: \(2(x+y) + 3\ln|x+y-2| = x + C\Rightarrow x + 2y + 3\ln|x + y - 2| = C\).
\(z = 2\): \(x + y = 2\), \(dy = -dx\): \((3)dx + (3)(-dx) = 0\) holds. It is a solution and not in the family.
items.answer: \(x + 2y + 3\ln|x + y - 2| = C\), and the line \(x + y = 2\).

items.q: Solve \( y' = (x + y + 1)^2 \) by a suitable substitution.
items.hint: As in Exercises 6.2: \(u = x + y + 1\).
steps: \(u = x + y + 1\Rightarrow u' = 1 + y' = 1 + u^2\) (separable; \(1 + u^2\) is never 0).

items.q: Solve the Clairaut equation \( y = xp + \dfrac1p \), \(p = \dfrac{dy}{dx}\). Find the general and the singular solution.
items.hint: Differentiate: \(\frac{dp}{dx}\big(x - \frac{1}{p^2}\big) = 0\).
steps: Then \(y = xp + \dfrac1p = \pm\big(\sqrt x + \sqrt x\big) = \pm2\sqrt x\), i.e. \(y^2 = 4x\).
items.answer: General solution \(y = cx + \dfrac1c\); singular solution \(y^2 = 4x\) (\(y = \pm2\sqrt x\)).

items.q: Solve \( y = xy' - (y')^3 \).
items.hint: Clairaut with \(f(p) = -p^3\). Singular solution: \(x = 3p^2\), then eliminate \(p\).
items.answer: General solution \(y = cx - c^3\); singular solution \(27y^2 = 4x^3\).

items.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of circles \( x^2 + y^2 = 2cx \).
items.hint: Eliminate \(c\) to get \(y' = \frac{y^2-x^2}{2xy}\); the trajectory equation is homogeneous.
steps: Differentiate: \(2x + 2yy' = 2c\). From the family, \(2c = \dfrac{x^2+y^2}{x}\). So \(2yy' = \dfrac{x^2+y^2}{x} - 2x = \dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{x}\), \(m_1 = \dfrac{y^2 - x^2}{2xy}\).
Back: \(\dfrac{y/x}{1 + y^2/x^2} = \dfrac{xy}{x^2+y^2} = Kx\Rightarrow y = K(x^2+y^2)\). (\(u = 0\), i.e. \(y = 0\), is the case \(K = 0\).)
items.answer: \(x^2 + y^2 = Dy\) (circles tangent to the \(x\)-axis at the origin), together with \(y = 0\).

items.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family \( y = \dfrac{c}{1 + x^2} \).
items.hint: \(c = y(1+x^2)\); eliminate it from \(y'\), then flip.

items.q: A tank holds 200 lt of salt water containing 30 g of salt. Brine with 1 g/lt pours in at 4 lt/min and the well-mixed solution pours out at 5 lt/min. Find the amount of salt at time \(t\).
items.hint: Volume changes: \(V(t)=200-t\). \(\frac{dx}{dt}=4-\frac{5x}{200-t}\) is linear.

items.q: A 1 kg steel ball is dropped from 793 m with no initial velocity. The air resistance is \(\frac18v\). Find (a) the velocity \(v(t)\) and the limiting velocity, (b) the distance fallen \(x(t)\) (\(g=9.8\) m/s²).
items.hint: \(m\frac{dv}{dt}=mg-kv\) with \(m=1\), \(k=\frac18\): linear; limiting velocity \(\frac{mg}{k}\).

items.q: A chemical substance A transforms into another substance. After 1 hour 50 g of A remain, after 3 hours 25 g remain. (a) How much A was present initially? (b) How much remains after 5 hours? (c) When will there be 2 g?
items.hint: Basic rate law \(\frac{dA}{dt}=-kA\); the ratio \(A(3)/A(1)\) gives the half-life directly.

items.q: For \(x\gt 0\), determine \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) so that \(1,\ \frac1x,\ x^2\) are solutions of \(x^3y'''+\alpha x^2y''+\beta xy'+\gamma y=0\). Show they are linearly independent and write the general solution.
items.hint: Substitute each function: \(y=1\) gives \(\gamma\), then \(x^2\) and \(\frac1x\) give two equations for \(\alpha,\beta\). Then compute the \(3\times 3\) Wronskian.

items.q: Obtain the general solution of \(y''-\frac{4x}{2x-1}y'+\frac{4}{2x-1}y=0\) for \(x\gt 1\), after finding an exponential solution \(e^{\lambda x}\).
items.hint: Put \(e^{\lambda x}\) in and make the coefficient of \(x\) and the constant both zero; then reduce the order with \(y=e^{2x}z\).

items.q: Show that \(\varphi_1=x\) and \(\varphi_2=e^{-x}\) are solutions of the homogeneous equation associated with \((x+1)y''+xy'-y=(x+1)^2\), \(x\gt -1\), and that \(\varphi_p=x^2-x+1\) solves the full equation. Write the general solution.
items.hint: Substitute; check independence with the Wronskian; general solution = \(\varphi_c+\varphi_p\).

items.q: Given that \(\varphi_p(x)=x\) is a solution of \(y''-2xy'+2y=0\), find the second linearly independent solution.
items.hint: \(y=xz\Rightarrow xz''+(2-2x^2)z'=0\). The final integral is not elementary — leave it as an integral.
